days.guide: The child writes a safe-ride plan: don't get in, call a parent (no-questions-asked agreement), code word, ride-share with parent's account, stay over.

questions.q: Your ride has been drinking. What do you do?
questions.a: Do not get in; call or text a parent or trusted adult for a ride, use a code word if needed, and stay with sober friends until help arrives.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) depressant 2) only time lowers BAC 3) factors: weight, sex, food, number of drinks, time 4) prefrontal cortex develops into mid-20s 5) CA under-21 limit 0.01%, adults 0.08%. Safe-ride plan (4): refuses ride, names two alternatives, contact numbers, code word/agreement with parent.

weeks.prep: Parental preview: overdose content. Watch a naloxone (Narcan) nasal-spray training video (SAMHSA, CDPH or manufacturer) first. Use a doll or pillow and an empty spray bottle as a model. Learn California's Good Samaritan law (Health & Safety Code 11376.5).
misconceptions: Thinking pills from friends or social media are safe if they look real. Correct: counterfeit pills often contain fentanyl; one pill can kill.
Believing naloxone is dangerous if the person didn't take opioids. Correct: naloxone has no effect on someone without opioids in their system and is safe to give if overdose is suspected.

days.guide: Explain opioids (oxycodone, heroin, fentanyl) bind receptors in the brainstem and slow breathing; fentanyl is 50 times stronger than heroin and 2 mg can be fatal.

questions.q: Why do opioid overdoses kill?
questions.a: Opioids slow or stop breathing, so the brain and body don't get oxygen.

questions.q: Why are counterfeit pills so dangerous?
questions.a: They can contain unknown, lethal amounts of fentanyl and look identical to real prescription pills.

days.guide: List overdose signs together: pinpoint pupils, unresponsive/can't wake, slow or stopped breathing, gurgling/snoring sounds, blue or gray lips/fingertips, limp body.

questions.q: Name three signs of opioid overdose.
questions.a: Pinpoint pupils, unresponsiveness, slow or no breathing, blue/gray lips or nails, choking or gurgling sounds, limp body.

days.guide: Watch the video, then practice: shout and rub sternum, call 911, tilt head back, insert nozzle into a nostril and press plunger, place in recovery position, give second dose in 2–3 minutes if no response, stay until help arrives.

questions.q: After giving naloxone, what next?
questions.a: Stay with the person, give rescue breathing/CPR if trained and needed, put them in the recovery position, and give a second dose after 2–3 minutes if they don't respond; naloxone can wear off, so they still need medical care.

days.guide: Explain the Good Samaritan law: a person who seeks medical help for an overdose is protected from arrest/prosecution for small amounts of drugs for personal use.

questions.q: Why does California have a Good Samaritan overdose law?
questions.a: To encourage people to call 911 without fear of being arrested for minor drug possession, saving lives.

days.guide: The child orders shuffled step cards for responding to an overdose and explains each.

questions.q: What is the first thing to do if someone won't wake up?
questions.a: Try to wake them (shout, rub sternum) and call 911 immediately.

weeks.assessment_key: Correct sequence: 1) Check responsiveness (shout, sternum rub) 2) Call 911 3) Give naloxone into one nostril 4) Support breathing (rescue breaths/CPR if trained) 5) Recovery position on side 6) Second dose after 2–3 minutes if no response 7) Stay until EMS arrives and tell them what happened. Proficient: all steps in order with reasons.

weeks.prep: Print NIDA for Teens pages on prescription stimulants, inhalants, caffeine and marijuana. Make a blank drug-facts chart (drug, effects, risks, CA law). Have energy-drink/soda labels for caffeine counts.
misconceptions: Thinking prescription drugs are safe because a doctor prescribed them. Correct: safe only for the person prescribed at the right dose; misuse can cause heart problems, addiction and overdose.
Believing cannabis today is the same as decades ago. Correct: THC potency has risen from about 4% in the 1990s to often 20%+ in flower and 60–90%+ in concentrates/vapes.

days.guide: Explain ADHD stimulants (Adderall, Ritalin) help people with ADHD but misuse can cause rapid heart rate, anxiety, insomnia and addiction; sharing or selling a prescription is illegal.

questions.q: Do 'study drugs' improve grades for people without ADHD?
questions.a: Research shows no real improvement in grades; they carry risks such as heart problems, anxiety and dependence.

days.guide: Read about inhalants (aerosols, glue, gasoline). Explain 'sudden sniffing death' can happen the first time from heart failure.

questions.q: How can inhalants kill on first use?
questions.a: They can cause the heart to beat irregularly and stop (sudden sniffing death), or cause suffocation.

days.guide: The child lists all caffeine for a typical week (soda ~35–45 mg/12 oz, tea ~30–50 mg/8 oz, coffee ~95 mg/8 oz, energy drinks 80–300 mg) and compares to ≤100 mg/day.

questions.q: A teen drinks two 12-oz colas (35 mg each) and one 8-oz coffee (95 mg) in a day. Is that over 100 mg?
questions.a: Yes: 35 + 35 + 95 = 165 mg, which is 65 mg over 100 mg.

days.guide: Compare THC levels then and now and discuss risks to the teen brain: memory, attention, mood, addiction (cannabis use disorder), psychosis risk with high-potency use; illegal under 21 in CA.

questions.q: Why are high-potency vapes and edibles riskier for teens?
questions.a: Higher THC raises risk of addiction, anxiety, psychosis and impaired memory/learning; edibles take 30 minutes–2 hours to work, leading people to take too much.

days.guide: The child fills the drug-facts chart for stimulants, inhalants, caffeine and cannabis.

questions.q: What is California's legal age for cannabis?
questions.a: 21 (18 with a medical recommendation).

weeks.assessment_key: Drug-facts chart key: Prescription stimulants – increase alertness/heart rate; risks: heart problems, anxiety, insomnia, addiction; sharing/selling is illegal. Inhalants – brief high; risks: brain damage, sudden sniffing death, suffocation; selling certain products to minors is restricted. Caffeine – stimulant; risks: jitters, insomnia, rapid heartbeat; teens ≤100 mg/day, avoid energy drinks. Cannabis – THC alters perception/memory; risks: addiction, impaired learning, psychosis; illegal under 21. Proficient: accurate in all four rows.

weeks.prep: Find 2–3 online examples of vape, alcohol or cannabis ads (or Truth Initiative examples). Print a media-literacy checklist (who made it, target audience, techniques, what's left out). Read about California's flavored tobacco ban (SB 793, upheld by voters with Prop 31 in 2022).
misconceptions: Thinking ads only target adults. Correct: flavors, bright packaging, cartoons and influencers appeal to youth, who are 'replacement customers.'
Believing vapes are just water vapor. Correct: aerosol contains nicotine, heavy metals and ultrafine particles.

days.guide: List tactics: flavors (candy, fruit), influencer posts, sleek packaging, sponsorships of events/music, small discreet devices, 'free' samples.

questions.q: Why do companies use sweet flavors?
questions.a: Flavors hide the harsh taste and appeal especially to young people, making it easier to start.

days.guide: Analyze two ads with the checklist and write findings.

questions.q: What does an alcohol ad usually leave out?
questions.a: Risks: hangovers, impaired driving, addiction, health problems, violence, and the legal age.

days.guide: Explain the flavored tobacco ban: California prohibits retail sale of most flavored tobacco products, including menthol and flavored vapes, approved by voters (Prop 31) in 2022.

questions.q: Why did California ban flavored tobacco sales?
questions.a: Most youth who use tobacco start with flavored products; the ban aims to reduce youth vaping and smoking.

days.guide: The child sketches a counter-ad that exposes one tactic (e.g., 'They flavor it like candy because they want kids hooked').

questions.q: What makes a counter-ad effective?
questions.a: It reveals the hidden tactic or truth, targets the audience clearly and uses a strong image and short message.

days.guide: The child presents the counter-ad and explains the tactic and evidence.

questions.q: Who are 'replacement smokers'?
questions.a: Young people the industry needs to recruit to replace customers who quit or die.

weeks.assessment_key: Counter-ad rubric: 4 = names a specific tactic, accurate fact, clear target audience, strong visual and slogan, explained confidently; 3 = tactic and message clear, weaker design; 2 = general anti-drug message without tactic; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Read NIDA for Teens 'Drugs and the Brain' and a recovery story (NIDA, SAMHSA or a reputable news profile). Health journal ready.
misconceptions: Thinking addiction is a lack of willpower. Correct: it is a chronic, treatable brain disease involving changes in reward, motivation and self-control circuits.
Believing relapse means treatment failed. Correct: relapse rates are similar to other chronic diseases like asthma; it signals a need to adjust treatment.

days.guide: Explain dopamine and the reward system, tolerance (needing more for the same effect) and dependence/withdrawal.

questions.q: What is tolerance?
questions.a: When the body adapts so a person needs more of a drug to get the same effect.

days.guide: Explain why addiction is called a chronic disease: lasting brain changes, compulsive use despite harm, can be managed but relapse is possible.

questions.q: Why is addiction called a disease rather than a choice?
questions.a: Repeated use changes brain circuits for reward, stress and self-control, making it very hard to stop even when the person wants to; the first use is a choice, but addiction is not.

days.guide: The child researches treatments: counseling/behavioral therapy, medications (e.g., buprenorphine, methadone, naltrexone for opioids), support groups, inpatient/outpatient.

questions.q: Name two types of addiction treatment.
questions.a: Behavioral counseling (e.g., CBT), medication for opioid use disorder, support groups (12-step, SMART Recovery), residential or outpatient programs.

days.guide: Read or watch a recovery story and list supports that helped (family, treatment, new friends, purpose).

questions.q: What supports help people stay in recovery?
questions.a: Ongoing treatment, supportive family and friends, sober activities, support groups, coping skills and purpose.

days.guide: The child writes a paragraph explaining addiction to a younger student in simple words.

questions.q: What's a simple way to explain addiction?
questions.a: 'Drugs can change how your brain works so it feels like you need them, even when they hurt you. It's a sickness that doctors can help treat.'

weeks.assessment_key: Explanatory paragraph: 4 = explains dopamine/reward and tolerance in simple terms, calls addiction a treatable disease, mentions treatment and where to get help, age-appropriate; 3 = accurate with one gap; 2 = mostly 'just say no' without explanation; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Prepare scenario cards and a jeopardy grid (categories: Alcohol, Opioids, Other Drugs, Marketing, Addiction). Note SAMHSA National Helpline 1-800-662-4357. Write the unit test.
misconceptions: Thinking telling an adult is 'snitching.' Correct: getting help for a friend's health and safety is caring, not betrayal.
Confronting a friend while they are high. Correct: talk when they are sober, in private, using I-messages.

days.guide: List signs a friend may be using: changes in friends, grades, mood, sleep, secrecy, smell, missing money, paraphernalia.

questions.q: Name three signs.
questions.a: Dropping grades, new friend group, mood swings, secrecy, red eyes or smell of smoke/vape, losing interest in activities, missing money.

days.guide: Teach I-messages ('I feel worried when I see you vaping before school because I care about you'). Role-play; switch roles.

questions.q: Write an I-message for a friend who's drinking at parties.
questions.a: 'I feel worried when you drink at parties because I care about you and don't want you to get hurt. Can we talk?'

days.guide: List adults (parent, counselor, coach, doctor) and hotlines: SAMHSA 1-800-662-4357, 911 in emergencies.

questions.q: What is the SAMHSA National Helpline?
questions.a: 1-800-662-HELP (4357), free, confidential, 24/7 treatment referral and information.

days.guide: Play jeopardy reviewing weeks 19–23.

questions.q: What drug can reverse an opioid overdose?
questions.a: Naloxone (Narcan).

days.guide: Give the unit test; review.

questions.q: What does the Good Samaritan law do?
questions.a: Protects people who call 911 for an overdose from arrest for small-amount drug possession.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit test key: 1) only time lowers BAC 2) under-21 driving limit 0.01% 3) fentanyl in counterfeit pills 4) overdose signs: pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, unresponsive 5) naloxone steps 6) Good Samaritan law 7) inhalants can cause sudden death 8) teen caffeine ≤100 mg 9) higher THC potency risks 10) marketing tactics: flavors, influencers 11) CA flavored tobacco ban 12) addiction = chronic treatable brain disease 13) tolerance definition 14) I-messages and telling an adult. Role-play: proficient = I-message, caring tone, offers help, involves adult.

weeks.prep: Watch the AHA Hands-Only CPR video (cpr.heart.org) together. Use a firm pillow or manikin on the floor. Pick a song at 100–120 bpm ('Stayin' Alive'). Find an AED demonstration video. Print a CPR skills checklist.
misconceptions: Compressing too gently or too slowly. Correct: push hard (at least 2 inches for adults) and fast (100–120/min), letting the chest recoil fully.
Fearing you'll hurt someone or get sued. Correct: without CPR the person will likely die; California's Good Samaritan laws protect people giving emergency care in good faith.

days.guide: Review Check (scene safe, tap and shout), Call (911, get AED), Care. Practice a 911 script: location, what happened, breathing status.

questions.q: What should you tell the 911 dispatcher?
questions.a: Exact location, what happened, number of victims, whether the person is conscious and breathing; stay on the line and follow instructions.

days.guide: Practice hand position (heel of hand on center of chest, other hand on top, arms straight) and compressions to the beat for 2 minutes.

questions.q: What are the two steps of hands-only CPR?
questions.a: Call 911, then push hard and fast in the center of the chest at 100–120 compressions per minute, at least 2 inches deep for adults.

questions.q: When can you stop?
questions.a: When EMS or someone trained takes over, an AED is ready, the person starts breathing, the scene becomes unsafe or you're too exhausted to continue.

days.guide: Watch the AED video. The child sequences: turn on, follow voice prompts, bare chest, attach pads, stand clear for analysis, press shock if advised, resume CPR immediately.

questions.q: What is the first step when an AED arrives?
questions.a: Turn it on and follow the voice prompts.

days.guide: Teach the universal choking sign (hands at throat). Ask 'Are you choking?' Show hand placement for abdominal thrusts (fist above navel, below ribs) without real thrusts.

questions.q: If someone can cough forcefully, what should you do?
questions.a: Encourage them to keep coughing; give abdominal thrusts only if they can't cough, speak or breathe.

days.guide: Run a scenario: someone collapses. The parent checks each step on the checklist.

questions.q: Why start compressions right away?
questions.a: Brain damage begins within minutes without oxygen; compressions circulate oxygenated blood until help arrives.

weeks.assessment_key: CPR skills checklist (1 pt each): checks scene safety; taps and shouts; calls 911 and sends for AED; correct hand position; rate 100–120/min; depth ~2 inches with full recoil; minimal interruptions; uses AED steps correctly; states choking sign and thrust placement. 8–9 = proficient.

weeks.prep: Bookmark AirNow.gov and a first-aid guide (Red Cross app). Learn rip-current escape. Write a scenario quiz (key below).
misconceptions: Thinking heat stroke victims always sweat. Correct: in heat stroke, skin may be hot and dry or still sweaty; confusion and body temperature of 103°F+ are key — call 911.
Swimming straight back to shore against a rip current. Correct: swim parallel to shore until out of the current, or float and signal for help.

days.guide: Compare heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, cool clammy skin, nausea, dizziness) and heat stroke (high body temp, confusion, hot skin, possible fainting). First aid: move to cool place, loosen clothing, cool with water; heat stroke = call 911 and cool rapidly.

questions.q: What's the main difference and what do you do for heat stroke?
questions.a: Heat stroke involves very high body temperature and confusion/altered mental status; it is a medical emergency — call 911 and cool the person rapidly (cold water, ice packs).

days.guide: Teach reach-throw-don't go: reach with a pole or towel, throw a flotation device, don't swim out. Show how a rip current looks and how to escape.

questions.q: How do you escape a rip current?
questions.a: Stay calm, don't fight it; swim parallel to the shore until out of the current, then swim back at an angle, or float/tread water and wave for help.

days.guide: Check today's AQI on AirNow and learn the color scale (0–50 good, 51–100 moderate, 101–150 unhealthy for sensitive groups, 151+ unhealthy).

questions.q: At what AQI should sensitive groups limit outdoor activity?
questions.a: Above 100 (orange, unhealthy for sensitive groups); above 150 everyone should reduce outdoor exertion.

days.guide: The child writes a family plan: cooling spots, water, check on elderly neighbors, close windows, HEPA/air purifier, N95 masks, indoor activities.

questions.q: Name two steps for a wildfire smoke day.
questions.a: Stay indoors with windows closed, run a HEPA air purifier or AC on recirculate, wear a well-fitted N95 outdoors, avoid exercise outside.

days.guide: Give the scenario quiz.

questions.q: A teammate is confused and has hot skin after practice in the heat. What do you do?
questions.a: Suspect heat stroke: call 911, move them to shade, cool them rapidly with water/ice, and stay with them.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario quiz key: 1) heavy sweating, nausea, dizziness = heat exhaustion: move to cool place, fluids, rest 2) confusion and very high temp = heat stroke: 911 + rapid cooling 3) friend struggling in a pool: reach or throw, don't go 4) caught in rip current: swim parallel to shore 5) AQI 160: everyone limit outdoor activity 6) smoke day: stay inside, HEPA, N95 outdoors. 5/6 proficient.

weeks.prep: Find teen pedestrian/cyclist data (NHTSA or CA Office of Traffic Safety). Set up a cone (or shoe) path for the distraction test. Check bike and helmet fit.
misconceptions: Thinking pedestrians and cyclists are always seen by drivers. Correct: drivers have blind spots and may be distracted; make eye contact and wear bright/reflective gear.
Believing you can text and walk safely. Correct: distraction reduces awareness and slows reaction time.

days.guide: Read the data together and identify patterns (time of day, distraction, ages, helmet use).

questions.q: When are pedestrian deaths most common?
questions.a: After dark (most occur at night) and in urban areas away from intersections.

days.guide: The child walks the cone path once normally and once while typing a message; record errors and time.

questions.q: What did the distraction test show?
questions.a: More errors (hitting cones, drifting) and/or slower time while texting — attention can't fully focus on two tasks.

days.guide: Sit in the driver's seat of a parked car with the child walking around it to find blind spots (behind, sides, in front of large vehicles).

questions.q: How can a cyclist be more visible?
questions.a: Wear bright/reflective clothing, use front white light and rear red reflector/light at night, ride predictably with traffic, make eye contact with drivers.

days.guide: Agree on a family code word and no-questions-asked pickup. Practice refusing a ride from a distracted or impaired driver.

questions.q: What might you say to refuse a ride?
questions.a: 'No thanks, my mom is picking me up,' or text the code word to a parent.

days.guide: The child creates a walking/biking safety checklist.

questions.q: Does California require helmets for cyclists under 18?
questions.a: Yes — riders under 18 must wear a helmet on a bicycle, scooter, skateboard or skates.

weeks.assessment_key: Safety checklist: 4 = at least 8 accurate items covering helmet (required under 18 in CA), visibility, phone away, crosswalks and eye contact, riding with traffic, lights at night, safe-ride code word; 3 = 6–7 items; 2 = 4–5; 1 = fewer.

weeks.prep: Prepare scenario cards (in person and online harassment). Read loveisrespect.org and the 5 D's (Right To Be/Hollaback). Know how your school or co-op reports harassment.
misconceptions: Thinking harassment only counts if it's physical. Correct: unwelcome comments, jokes, gestures, images or messages of a sexual nature are harassment.
Believing bystanders can only confront directly. Correct: the 5 D's give safer options.

days.guide: Define sexual harassment and list examples in person and online.

questions.q: Give two examples of online sexual harassment.
questions.a: Sending unwanted sexual messages or images, spreading sexual rumors, sharing someone's photo without consent, sexual comments on posts.

days.guide: Teach the 5 D's: Direct, Distract, Delegate, Delay, Document.

questions.q: Explain 'Delegate' and 'Delay.'
questions.a: Delegate: get help from someone with authority (teacher, coach, adult). Delay: check in with the person afterward to support them.

days.guide: Role-play three scenarios using different D's.

questions.q: Someone is being teased in a group chat. What could you do?
questions.a: Distract by changing the subject, message the target privately (Delay), screenshot (Document), and tell an adult (Delegate).

days.guide: List reporting options: parent, school counselor/Title IX coordinator, platform reports, police for assault, RAINN hotline 1-800-656-4673.

questions.q: Where can someone report sexual assault?
questions.a: Tell a trusted adult, call 911 or police, contact RAINN 1-800-656-HOPE (4673), or a school Title IX coordinator.

days.guide: The child writes how they would support a friend who was harassed.

questions.q: What should you say first to a friend who discloses harassment or assault?
questions.a: 'I believe you. It's not your fault. I'm here for you,' then help them get adult support.

weeks.assessment_key: Bystander role-play rubric: 4 = uses at least two D's appropriately, prioritizes safety, supports the target and involves an adult; 3 = one D used well; 2 = hesitant/unsafe; 1 = no action. Reflection: believes, supports, connects to help.

weeks.prep: Parental preview: weapons and threats. Review Sandy Hook Promise 'Say Something' resources. Know whether firearms are in your home or relatives' homes and how they're stored. Prepare scenario cards.
misconceptions: Thinking a found gun is safe to pick up if it looks like a toy or unloaded. Correct: never touch it — leave the area and tell an adult.
Believing threats online are 'just jokes.' Correct: always report threats; adults will assess them.

days.guide: Teach: Stop, don't touch, leave the area, tell an adult. Explain safe storage (locked, unloaded, ammunition separate).

questions.q: You find a gun at a friend's house. What do you do?
questions.a: Don't touch it, leave the room/area immediately, and tell an adult right away.

days.guide: List warning signs someone may hurt themselves or others: threats, fascination with weapons/violence, withdrawal, posts about violence, severe anger.

questions.q: Name two warning signs of potential violence.
questions.a: Making threats (in person or online), talking about bringing a weapon, obsession with weapons or past attacks, sudden withdrawal and anger, social posts about hurting others.

days.guide: Practice showing a parent a screenshot of a threat and explaining it. Learn anonymous options (Say Something app, school tip line, 911 if imminent).

questions.q: If you see a threat online, what should you do?
questions.a: Don't share it; screenshot it, tell a trusted adult immediately or use an anonymous tip line; call 911 if there's immediate danger.

days.guide: Practice de-escalation: calm low voice, give space, don't block exits, acknowledge feelings, walk away and get help.

questions.q: Name two de-escalation strategies.
questions.a: Speak calmly, keep a safe distance, listen and acknowledge feelings, avoid insults or threats, leave and get an adult.

days.guide: The child completes a scenario worksheet.

questions.q: Why report even if you aren't sure it's serious?
questions.a: Adults trained to assess threats can decide; reporting may prevent harm and get help for the person.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario worksheet key: 1) found gun – don't touch, leave, tell adult 2) classmate posts a threat – screenshot, tell adult/tip line 3) friend talks about hurting themselves – Ask-Listen-Tell, 988 4) heated argument – calm voice, space, leave 5) imminent danger – 911. Proficient: all five correct.

weeks.prep: Gather a first-aid kit and the Red Cross checklist, a CPR pillow, flashcards and the unit test (key below).
misconceptions: Thinking a family plan isn't needed because 911 exists. Correct: phones and roads can fail; you need meeting places and out-of-area contacts.
Forgetting that supplies expire. Correct: check dates and restock regularly.

days.guide: Inventory the kit against a Red Cross list (bandages, gauze, tape, gloves, antiseptic wipes, scissors, tweezers, thermometer, cold pack, emergency blanket) and list items to buy.

questions.q: Why include disposable gloves?
questions.a: To protect against contact with blood and body fluids.

days.guide: Create a plan: emergency contacts, out-of-area contact, meeting place near home and outside neighborhood, evacuation routes, go-bag.

questions.q: Why choose an out-of-area contact?
questions.a: Long-distance calls/texts may get through when local lines are overloaded; everyone can check in with one person.

days.guide: The child demonstrates hands-only CPR and choking response; check with the week 25 checklist.

questions.q: What is the compression rate?
questions.a: 100–120 per minute.

days.guide: Review flashcards for weeks 25–29.

questions.q: Reach, throw, don't ___?
questions.a: Go — don't swim out to rescue someone unless trained.

days.guide: Give the unit test.

questions.q: What do the 5 D's stand for?
questions.a: Direct, Distract, Delegate, Delay, Document.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit test key: 1) Check-Call-Care 2) CPR 100–120/min, ~2 in 3) AED: turn on first 4) choking sign = hands at throat 5) heat stroke = 911 6) rip current: swim parallel 7) AQI >150 unhealthy for all 8) helmet required under 18 9) 5 D's 10) found gun: don't touch, leave, tell 11) threats: report. Skills demo: proficient on week 25 checklist.

weeks.prep: Print a family health history form (CDC 'My Family Health Portrait') and CDC fact sheets on heart disease, type 2 diabetes, cancer and asthma. Be ready to share family history sensitively.
misconceptions: Thinking chronic diseases only affect old people. Correct: habits started in youth (diet, activity, tobacco) shape lifetime risk; type 2 diabetes and asthma occur in teens.
Believing family history means you're destined to get a disease. Correct: it raises risk, but controllable behaviors can lower it.

days.guide: Review communicable vs. noncommunicable diseases and list chronic examples.

questions.q: Name four chronic noncommunicable diseases.
questions.a: Heart disease, type 2 diabetes, cancer, asthma (also stroke, COPD, arthritis).

days.guide: Sort risk factors: controllable (diet, activity, tobacco, sleep, sun exposure) vs. uncontrollable (age, genetics, family history, sex).

questions.q: Is family history controllable?
questions.a: No — but knowing it helps you control other risk factors and get screenings.

days.guide: Fill out the family health history together for parents, grandparents, siblings.

questions.q: Why share family health history with a doctor?
questions.a: It helps the doctor assess risk and recommend earlier screening or prevention.

days.guide: The child researches one disease and writes a prevention plan with 3 behaviors.

questions.q: Name two ways to lower type 2 diabetes risk.
questions.a: Regular physical activity (60 min/day for teens), balanced diet with fewer sugary drinks, healthy weight, enough sleep.

days.guide: The child presents to a family member.

questions.q: What does asthma do and how is it managed?
questions.a: It inflames and narrows airways; managed by avoiding triggers and using controller and quick-relief (rescue) inhalers as prescribed.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric: 4 = defines the disease, explains causes and at least three risk factors (controllable vs. not), gives at least three prevention behaviors and cites 2 valid sources; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = facts without prevention plan; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Find three health product ads (acne cream, weight loss, sleep aid). Print a CRAAP checklist (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose). Have a brand-name and generic label (e.g., ibuprofen).
misconceptions: Thinking testimonials prove a product works. Correct: testimonials are individual stories, often paid; look for scientific evidence.
Believing generic medicine is weaker. Correct: FDA requires generics to have the same active ingredient, strength and effect as the brand.

days.guide: Analyze ads for testimonials, bandwagon, 'clinically proven' without citation, before/after photos.

questions.q: What's wrong with 'Doctors recommend!' with no details?
questions.a: It doesn't say which doctors or what evidence — an unsupported claim.

days.guide: Apply CRAAP to three health websites.

questions.q: What does 'Purpose' ask?
questions.a: Why the information exists — to inform, sell, persuade or entertain; sites selling products may be biased.

days.guide: Explain quackery signs (miracle cure, secret formula, works for many diseases, money-back pressure) and that the FTC fights deceptive advertising (FDA regulates labels/safety).

questions.q: What does the FTC do?
questions.a: The Federal Trade Commission protects consumers from false or deceptive advertising and fraud.

days.guide: Compare labels: same active ingredient (e.g., ibuprofen 200 mg), different price and inactive ingredients.

questions.q: A brand costs $9.99 for 100 tablets and generic $4.99 for 100. Same active ingredient — which is better value?
questions.a: The generic — same medicine at half the price ($0.05 vs. $0.10 per tablet).

days.guide: The child writes a consumer guide for one category (sunscreen, acne, protein bars): what to look for, red flags, trusted sources.

questions.q: What should you look for in sunscreen?
questions.a: Broad spectrum, SPF 30 or higher, water-resistant; reapply every 2 hours.

weeks.assessment_key: Consumer guide: 4 = clear criteria for choosing products, at least three red flags, compares cost/unit price, cites valid sources (FDA, AAD, NIH), practical tips; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = general opinions; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Bookmark CDC, CDPH and your county health department websites. Prepare a simple map and case list for an outbreak activity (e.g., John Snow's 1854 cholera map). Find career profiles (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook).
misconceptions: Thinking public health is only about hospitals. Correct: public health prevents disease in populations (vaccines, clean water, food inspections, tracking outbreaks).
Believing all health careers require medical school. Correct: many need a certificate, associate's or bachelor's degree.

days.guide: Compare roles: CDC (national), CDPH (state), county (local inspections, clinics, vaccines).

questions.q: Which agency inspects local restaurants?
questions.a: The county (or city) environmental health department.

days.guide: Plot cases on the map and find the cluster/source, like John Snow's Broad Street pump.

questions.q: What did John Snow discover in 1854?
questions.a: Mapping cholera deaths in London showed a cluster around the Broad Street water pump, showing cholera spread through contaminated water.

days.guide: Research two careers: duties, education, salary (BLS).

questions.q: What education does a registered nurse need?
questions.a: An associate's degree or bachelor's in nursing (ADN or BSN) and passing the NCLEX-RN licensing exam.

days.guide: Interview someone in a health job or watch a career video and take notes.

questions.q: What is one good interview question?
questions.a: Examples: 'What does a typical day look like?' 'What training did you need?' 'What's the hardest part?'

days.guide: The child makes a career profile card.

questions.q: What is an epidemiologist?
questions.a: A public health scientist who studies patterns and causes of disease in populations.

weeks.assessment_key: Career profile card: 4 = job title, duties, education/training, workplace, salary range (BLS), one interesting fact and personal connection; 3 = one element missing; 2 = vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Prepare a campaign planning template (issue, data, audience, message, call to action, materials, timeline). Help locate valid sources.
misconceptions: Choosing a topic too broad ('health'). Correct: narrow to one behavior and audience ('getting 9 hours of sleep for middle schoolers').
Using opinions as evidence. Correct: cite data from valid sources.

days.guide: The child chooses a topic from the year and explains why it matters.

questions.q: Why is youth vaping a good advocacy topic?
questions.a: Example: many teens use or are exposed; nicotine is addictive and harms the developing brain; teens can influence peers.

days.guide: Gather three valid sources and two statistics.

questions.q: Give one valid source type.
questions.a: Government (.gov: CDC, CDPH), medical organizations (AAP, AHA), or university/hospital sites.

days.guide: Define audience and a specific call to action.

questions.q: Example call to action for a sleep campaign?
questions.a: 'Charge your phone outside your bedroom tonight.'

days.guide: Plan materials and timeline.

questions.q: Why match materials to audience?
questions.a: Different audiences use different media (video for teens, letter for officials).

days.guide: Share plan with a parent and revise.

questions.q: What makes advocacy different from just informing?
questions.a: Advocacy persuades people to take a specific healthy action or supports a change.

weeks.assessment_key: Campaign plan: 4 = focused issue, 3 valid sources with data, defined audience, specific call to action, planned materials and timeline; 3 = one weak element; 2 = vague topic or no sources; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather art supplies or video tools. Prepare a short audience survey (before/after questions).
misconceptions: Thinking sharing once means success. Correct: measure impact with feedback or a survey.
Ignoring feedback. Correct: revise based on audience reactions.

days.guide: The child creates materials using the plan.

questions.q: Does your material include a clear message and call to action?
questions.a: Yes — check that both are visible and accurate.

days.guide: Revise with feedback.

questions.q: What feedback did you get and what did you change?
questions.a: Answers vary; a good answer names specific changes (clearer wording, bigger visual).

days.guide: Share with audience.

questions.q: Who saw your campaign?
questions.a: Answers vary; should match the target audience.

days.guide: Survey the audience on knowledge and intent.

questions.q: How can a survey measure impact?
questions.a: Ask what they learned or whether they plan to change a behavior; compare before and after answers.

days.guide: Write reflection.

questions.q: What would you do differently?
questions.a: Answers vary; a good answer uses survey evidence.

weeks.assessment_key: Campaign and reflection: 4 = polished, accurate materials, shared with target audience, survey data reported, thoughtful reflection on impact and improvements; 3 = shared with some data; 2 = materials only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find the grade 7 wellness wheel (or draw one: physical, mental/emotional, social, safety, environmental, intellectual). Prepare a cumulative final (key below).
misconceptions: Making vague goals. Correct: use SMART goals with tracking.
Forgetting resources. Correct: list specific names and numbers (counselor, doctor, 988).

days.guide: Re-rate each wedge 1–10 and compare with grade 7.

questions.q: Which area improved most?
questions.a: Answers vary; the child should explain why.

days.guide: Write a high school wellness plan with SMART goals for physical, mental, social and safety health.

questions.q: Give one SMART physical goal.
questions.a: Example: 'I will be active 60 minutes a day at least 5 days a week for the fall semester, tracked in a log.'

days.guide: List supports: counselor, doctor, family, coaches, 988.

questions.q: Name two high school resources.
questions.a: School counselor, school nurse, teachers/coaches, clubs, wellness center.

days.guide: Review key concepts from all units.

questions.q: What does Ask-Listen-Tell mean?
questions.a: Ask directly about suicide, listen without judgment, tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: Give the final and share the plan.

questions.q: What reverses an opioid overdose?
questions.a: Naloxone.

weeks.assessment_key: Final key (sample): resilience definition; 988; protective factors; calcium 1,300 mg; supplements not FDA-approved before sale; abstinence 100%; consent clear/ongoing; minors 12+ STI consent; 0.01% under-21 BAC; naloxone; addiction = treatable disease; CPR 100–120/min; reach-throw-don't go; 5 D's; FTC false ads; CDC/CDPH roles. Wellness plan: 4 = SMART goals in four areas, supports, tracking plan.

HSS.overview: U.S. History 8 runs from the ideas behind the Revolution to industrial America, with primary sources every week. Teach each lesson as source work: read the document together (aloud if hard), ask who made it, when, why and how reliable it is, then have your child answer a question using evidence from the text. Keep the 1750–1900 timeline growing, require claim–evidence–explanation in written answers, and preview the weeks on slavery, Indian Removal, Klan violence and Plains wars (15, 16, 30, 31) so you can discuss them with care.

weeks.prep: Set up a notebook and a long paper timeline marked 1750–1900. Print National Archives/Avalon Project excerpts: Magna Carta (clauses 12, 39, 40), English Bill of Rights (1689), Mayflower Compact (1620), Locke's Second Treatise (ch. 2 and 9 excerpts) and Montesquieu's Spirit of the Laws (Book XI, ch. 6).
misconceptions: Thinking Magna Carta created democracy for everyone. In 1215 it protected mainly barons and free men from King John; its lasting importance is the idea that the ruler is under the law.
Believing Americans invented rights ideas from scratch. Colonists drew on English rights traditions and Enlightenment writers like Locke and Montesquieu.

days.guide: Set up the notebook and timeline. Model sourcing on any document: Who wrote it? When? Why? How reliable? Your child sources a short document (e.g., the Mayflower Compact heading).

questions.q: What four questions do historians ask when sourcing a document?
questions.a: Who created it, when, for what purpose/audience, and how reliable is it (was the author in a position to know, any bias)?

days.guide: Read the excerpts; list the limits each placed on the king.

questions.q: Name one limit Magna Carta (1215) placed on King John.
questions.a: No free man could be imprisoned or lose property except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land; certain taxes required the 'common counsel' of the realm.

questions.q: Name two rights in the English Bill of Rights (1689).
questions.a: The monarch cannot levy taxes or keep a peacetime standing army without Parliament's consent; free elections; free speech in Parliament; right to petition; no excessive bail or cruel and unusual punishments.

days.guide: Read the Mayflower Compact and annotate self-government and consent.

questions.q: What did the Pilgrims agree to do in the Mayflower Compact?
questions.a: To 'combine ourselves together into a civil body politic' and make and obey 'just and equal laws' for the general good — self-government by consent.

questions.q: Why was it written before landing?
questions.a: They were outside the Virginia Company's territory and wanted order and agreed rules before going ashore.

days.guide: Read Locke and Montesquieu; chart each idea and its American connection.

questions.q: What were Locke's natural rights, and what could people do if government violated them?
questions.a: Life, liberty and property; people may alter or abolish a government that violates them (government rests on consent).

questions.q: What did Montesquieu argue?
questions.a: Separating government into legislative, executive and judicial powers protects liberty — the basis of the three branches.

days.guide: Your child writes the document-based paragraph; score with the rubric.

questions.q: What is the social contract?
questions.a: The idea that people agree to form a government and give it power in exchange for protection of their rights.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric (1–4): Claim — answers the question (e.g., 'American ideas about rights came from English legal tradition and Enlightenment philosophy'); Evidence — cites two documents accurately (e.g., Magna Carta's guarantee that no free man be imprisoned except by lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land; Locke's natural rights to life, liberty and property and government by consent; the Mayflower Compact's 'civil body politic' making 'just and equal laws'); Explanation — connects each to American ideas (trial by jury, consent of the governed); Conventions. 4 = claim + 2 accurate cited documents + explanation.

weeks.prep: Map of the 13 colonies; a short Whitefield or Edwards sermon excerpt; Paul Revere's engraving 'The Bloody Massacre' (1770); Captain Thomas Preston's account; depositions from Lexington (e.g., from Avalon Project or teachinghistory.org).
misconceptions: Thinking colonists objected to taxes because they were high. Their main complaint was taxation without representation in Parliament.
Accepting Revere's engraving as an accurate photo-like record. It was propaganda: soldiers in a neat line firing on command, an officer ordering fire, and a 'Butcher's Hall' sign.

days.guide: Read a Great Awakening sermon excerpt; discuss how revivals encouraged people to think for themselves.

questions.q: How did the Great Awakening encourage questioning authority?
questions.a: It taught that individuals could have a direct relationship with God without relying on established ministers, created new churches and splits, and encouraged people to challenge traditional leaders.

days.guide: Build a cause-effect chain from French and Indian War debt to taxes and boycotts.

questions.q: Why did Britain tax the colonies after 1763?
questions.a: To pay the huge debt from the French and Indian War and the cost of defending the colonies.

questions.q: How did colonists resist the Stamp Act?
questions.a: Boycotts of British goods (nonimportation), the Stamp Act Congress, protests by the Sons of Liberty; it was repealed in 1766.

days.guide: Compare Revere's engraving with Preston's account.

questions.q: How does Revere's engraving show point of view?
questions.a: It portrays soldiers as cruel attackers firing on calm, defenseless colonists — patriot propaganda.

questions.q: Who defended Preston in court, and what was the result?
questions.a: John Adams; Preston was acquitted (two soldiers were convicted of manslaughter).

days.guide: Read the depositions; decide who fired first using evidence.

questions.q: Can historians prove who fired first at Lexington?
questions.a: No — eyewitness accounts conflict, each side blamed the other; the best answer is 'unknown,' supported by contradictory testimony.

days.guide: Give the timeline quiz and short sourcing response.

questions.q: What were the Intolerable Acts?
questions.a: 1774 laws punishing Massachusetts for the Tea Party — closed Boston Harbor, limited town meetings, allowed quartering of troops.

weeks.assessment_key: Sourcing response rubric (1–4): identifies author, date and purpose of each source (Revere — Boston patriot silversmith, 1770, to rouse anger against Britain; Preston — the British captain, writing to defend himself), notes differences (Revere shows orderly firing on peaceful citizens; Preston describes a threatening mob with clubs, snowballs and a confused order), judges reliability considering bias. Timeline quiz key: French and Indian War 1754–1763; Proclamation of 1763; Stamp Act 1765; Townshend Acts 1767; Boston Massacre March 5, 1770; Boston Tea Party December 16, 1773; Intolerable (Coercive) Acts 1774; First Continental Congress 1774; Lexington and Concord April 19, 1775.

weeks.prep: Declaration of Independence transcript (National Archives); Common Sense excerpts; a map of the Revolution; the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789). Write the unit 1 test.
misconceptions: Thinking independence was declared on July 4. Congress voted for independence on July 2, 1776, and adopted the Declaration's text on July 4.
Assuming all colonists were Patriots. Many were Loyalists or neutral.

days.guide: Read Common Sense excerpts; identify Paine's three strongest arguments.

questions.q: Name two of Paine's arguments for independence.
questions.a: It is absurd for an island to rule a continent; hereditary monarchy is unnatural; independence would free trade and keep America out of Britain's wars; reconciliation was impossible after bloodshed.

questions.q: Why was Common Sense so influential?
questions.a: It was written in plain language, sold widely (well over 100,000 copies in 1776), and was read aloud, persuading ordinary colonists.

days.guide: Close-read the preamble; paraphrase key phrases; list 5 grievances.

questions.q: Paraphrase 'deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed.'
questions.a: Government only has legitimate power when the people agree to it.

questions.q: List three grievances against the king.
questions.a: Imposing taxes without consent; keeping standing armies in peacetime without consent; quartering troops; cutting off trade; depriving colonists of trial by jury; dissolving colonial legislatures.

days.guide: Map Saratoga, Valley Forge, Yorktown; explain the French alliance and contributions of James Armistead and Mercy Otis Warren.

questions.q: Why was Saratoga (1777) a turning point?
questions.a: The American victory convinced France to ally with the United States (1778), bringing troops, money and a navy.

questions.q: Who was James Armistead (Lafayette)?
questions.a: An enslaved man from Virginia who served as a double agent spy for Lafayette, providing intelligence before Yorktown; he later gained his freedom.

questions.q: Who was Mercy Otis Warren?
questions.a: A Massachusetts writer whose plays and later history of the Revolution supported the Patriot cause.

days.guide: Venn diagram: Declaration of Independence vs Rights of Man (1789).

questions.q: Name one similarity between the two documents.
questions.a: Both state that people have natural rights (liberty, property, etc.) and that government's purpose is to protect them; power comes from the people/nation.

days.guide: Give the unit 1 test and constructed response.

questions.q: According to the Declaration, what is the purpose of government?
questions.a: To secure people's unalienable rights, including life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test (suggested): Magna Carta 1215 limited the king; Locke — natural rights/consent; Montesquieu — separation of powers; Stamp Act 1765; Boston Massacre 1770; Lexington and Concord 1775; Common Sense 1776 (Paine); Declaration July 4, 1776 (Jefferson main author); Saratoga 1777 turning point that brought the French alliance (1778); Valley Forge winter 1777–78; Yorktown 1781 (Cornwallis surrendered, with French army and navy help); Treaty of Paris 1783 recognized independence with borders to the Mississippi. Constructed response rubric: explains that government exists to secure unalienable rights (life, liberty, pursuit of happiness), gets its just powers from the consent of the governed, and the people may alter or abolish a government that destroys these ends; cites the text.

weeks.prep: Excerpts of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776) and Massachusetts Constitution (1780); Articles of Confederation; graph paper for a township grid; Northwest Ordinance; Washington's and Jefferson's letters about Shays' Rebellion.
misconceptions: Thinking the Articles accomplished nothing. They won the war, negotiated the Treaty of Paris and created the land ordinances.
Thinking Shays' Rebellion was against Britain. It was Massachusetts farmers (1786–87) protesting debts, taxes and farm foreclosures.

days.guide: Compare the Virginia Declaration of Rights and Massachusetts Constitution; list common principles.

questions.q: Name two principles both documents share.
questions.a: All power comes from the people; natural rights; freedom of the press; trial by jury; limits on government (separation of powers in MA).

days.guide: Read selected articles; sort strengths and weaknesses.

questions.q: Why couldn't the Confederation Congress pay its debts?
questions.a: It had no power to tax; it could only ask the states for money.

questions.q: How many states had to approve an amendment?
questions.a: All 13 (unanimous).

days.guide: Draw a township grid (6 × 6 miles, 36 one-square-mile sections of 640 acres; section 16 for schools). Read the Northwest Ordinance's provisions.

questions.q: What did the Northwest Ordinance (1787) say about slavery and education?
questions.a: Slavery was banned in the Northwest Territory, and 'schools and the means of education shall forever be encouraged.'

questions.q: How many people did a territory need to apply for statehood?
questions.a: 60,000 free inhabitants.

days.guide: Read Washington's and Jefferson's reactions to Shays' Rebellion.

questions.q: How did Washington and Jefferson react differently?
questions.a: Washington was alarmed and saw the need for a stronger government; Jefferson, in Paris, wrote that 'a little rebellion now and then is a good thing.'

questions.q: Why did Shays' Rebellion lead to the Constitutional Convention?
questions.a: It showed the national government couldn't keep order or respond to crises, convincing leaders the Articles needed replacing.

days.guide: Give the quiz and argument paragraph.

questions.q: What was the Land Ordinance of 1785?
questions.a: A law that surveyed western land into townships and sections for sale, setting aside a section for schools.

weeks.assessment_key: Articles quiz key: weaknesses — no power to tax, no power to regulate interstate/foreign trade, no executive to enforce laws, no national courts, each state one vote, 9 of 13 states to pass laws, unanimous consent to amend, no national army (relied on states), no common currency control; strengths — waged the war, Treaty of Paris (1783), Land Ordinance of 1785, Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Argument paragraph rubric (1–4): clear claim (failure, partial success), two pieces of evidence (e.g., couldn't raise money to pay soldiers/stop Shays' Rebellion vs. Northwest Ordinance's lasting success), reasoning, counterclaim acknowledged.

weeks.prep: Constitution transcript; make delegate profile cards (Madison, Washington, Franklin, Sherman, Gouverneur Morris, James Wilson).
misconceptions: Thinking the Three-Fifths Clause meant enslaved people were 'three-fifths of a person' with rights. It was a formula for counting population for representation and direct taxes; enslaved people had no rights under it and gained power for their enslavers.
Believing all delegates agreed. The Convention was full of debate and compromise; some delegates refused to sign.

days.guide: Create profile cards for six delegates.

questions.q: Why is Madison called the 'Father of the Constitution'?
questions.a: He drafted the Virginia Plan, took detailed notes of the debates and later championed ratification and the Bill of Rights.

questions.q: What role did Gouverneur Morris play?
questions.a: He wrote the final wording of the Constitution, including the Preamble 'We the People of the United States.'

days.guide: Role-play Virginia vs New Jersey Plan; write the Great Compromise.

questions.q: Explain the Great Compromise.
questions.a: Congress has two houses: the House of Representatives based on population and the Senate with equal representation (two per state).

questions.q: Who proposed it?
questions.a: Roger Sherman (and Oliver Ellsworth) of Connecticut.

days.guide: Analyze the Three-Fifths, slave-trade and fugitive-slave clauses and how they contradicted the Declaration.

questions.q: How did the Three-Fifths Clause benefit slaveholding states?
questions.a: Counting enslaved people (who couldn't vote) increased Southern seats in the House and electoral votes.

questions.q: How did these clauses contradict the Declaration?
questions.a: The Declaration said all men are created equal with the right to liberty, yet the Constitution protected slavery.

days.guide: Examine debates on the executive, commerce and Native nations.

questions.q: Why did delegates create a single executive?
questions.a: To provide energy and accountability (Wilson argued for it), while limiting power with checks; others feared a single executive would resemble a king.

questions.q: How does the Constitution treat Indian nations?
questions.a: The commerce clause gives Congress power to regulate commerce 'with the Indian tribes,' treating them as separate nations dealt with by the federal government.

days.guide: Give the compromise quiz.

questions.q: What did the Electoral College compromise resolve?
questions.a: How to choose the president — not directly by Congress nor purely by popular vote, but by electors chosen by the states.

weeks.assessment_key: Compromise quiz key: Virginia Plan (Madison) — bicameral legislature, representation by population (favored large states); New Jersey Plan (Paterson) — one house, equal votes per state (small states); Great (Connecticut) Compromise (Roger Sherman) — House by population, Senate with two senators per state; Three-Fifths Compromise — three-fifths of enslaved people counted for representation and direct taxes; slave trade clause — Congress could not ban importation of enslaved people before 1808; fugitive slave clause — escaped enslaved people had to be returned; Electoral College — compromise between election by Congress and direct popular vote; commerce clause — Congress regulates trade with foreign nations, among the states and with Indian tribes.

weeks.prep: Excerpts of Federalist No. 10, No. 51, Brutus No. 1, Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom; Bill of Rights transcript. Write 10 modern scenarios for the quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking the Bill of Rights was part of the original Constitution. It was added in 1791 after Anti-Federalists demanded it during ratification.
Believing the First Amendment protects you from private companies or parents. It limits government action.

days.guide: Read Federalist No. 10 and Brutus No. 1; chart arguments.

questions.q: What was Madison's solution to faction in Federalist No. 10?
questions.a: A large republic with many competing interests makes it hard for any single faction to dominate.

questions.q: What did Brutus fear?
questions.a: That a large republic could not represent the people, and that the necessary-and-proper and supremacy clauses would let the national government swallow the states and threaten liberty; he also wanted a bill of rights.

days.guide: Analyze Federalist No. 51.

questions.q: Explain 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary.'
questions.a: People aren't perfect, so we need government — but government is run by people too, so it must be checked.

questions.q: What does 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition' mean?
questions.a: Each branch should have the power and motive to check the others.

days.guide: Read Jefferson's Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom; connect to the First Amendment.

questions.q: What did the Virginia Statute (1786) establish?
questions.a: No one could be forced to attend or support any church or be punished for religious beliefs — the basis for the First Amendment's religion clauses.

questions.q: What are the two religion clauses of the First Amendment?
questions.a: The establishment clause (no official national religion) and the free exercise clause.

days.guide: Illustrate each amendment with a modern scenario.

questions.q: Which amendment protects you from being tried twice for the same crime?
questions.a: The 5th (double jeopardy).

days.guide: Give the scenario quiz.

questions.q: What does the 10th Amendment say?
questions.a: Powers not delegated to the federal government nor prohibited to the states are reserved to the states or the people.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario quiz key (Bill of Rights): 1st — religion, speech, press, assembly, petition; 2nd — keep and bear arms; 3rd — no quartering of soldiers in peacetime without consent; 4th — no unreasonable searches and seizures, warrants need probable cause; 5th — grand jury, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination, due process, just compensation for takings; 6th — speedy public trial, impartial jury, lawyer, confront witnesses; 7th — jury in civil cases; 8th — no excessive bail or cruel and unusual punishment; 9th — rights not listed are still retained by the people; 10th — powers not delegated to the U.S. are reserved to the states or the people. Example scenarios: police search a locker without a warrant (4th); a newspaper is shut down for criticizing the mayor (1st); a suspect refuses to testify against himself (5th).

weeks.prep: Constitution transcript; congress.gov; two news articles on one current bill from different outlets. Write the unit 2 test.
misconceptions: Thinking the president makes laws. Congress makes laws; the president signs or vetoes and enforces them.
Believing judicial review is written in the Constitution. It was established by Marbury v. Madison (1803).

days.guide: Scavenger hunt through Articles I–VII.

questions.q: Which article creates Congress? Which the presidency? Which the courts?
questions.a: Article I; Article II; Article III.

questions.q: How many states were needed to ratify the Constitution?
questions.a: Nine (Article VII).

days.guide: Diagram checks and balances with examples.

questions.q: How can Congress check the president?
questions.a: Override vetoes (2/3), reject appointments and treaties (Senate), control funding, impeach and remove.

questions.q: How can courts check Congress?
questions.a: By declaring laws unconstitutional (judicial review).

days.guide: Sort powers into federal, state and shared; discuss enumerated vs implied powers.

questions.q: Is printing money a federal or state power?
questions.a: Federal.

questions.q: What is an implied power?
questions.a: A power not listed but reasonably needed to carry out enumerated powers, justified by the necessary and proper (elastic) clause — e.g., creating a national bank.

days.guide: Trace a current bill on congress.gov; compare two news articles.

questions.q: List the main steps of how a bill becomes law.
questions.a: Introduced → committee → passes House and Senate in identical form (conference if needed) → president signs (or vetoes; Congress can override with 2/3).

questions.q: Why is a free press important to democracy?
questions.a: It informs citizens and holds officials accountable; comparing outlets helps detect bias.

days.guide: Give the unit 2 test.

questions.q: What does the supremacy clause say?
questions.a: The Constitution, federal laws and treaties are the supreme law of the land, above state laws.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test (suggested): Article I — legislative (Congress); II — executive (president); III — judicial (Supreme Court); IV — states' relations; V — amendment process (2/3 of Congress proposes, 3/4 of states ratify); VI — supremacy clause; VII — ratification by 9 states. Checks: president vetoes bills; Congress overrides with 2/3 of both houses; Senate confirms appointments and ratifies treaties (2/3); courts declare laws unconstitutional; Congress can impeach (House) and remove (Senate 2/3). Federalism: federal — coin money, declare war, foreign treaties, regulate interstate commerce; state — schools, local governments, driver's licenses, elections; shared (concurrent) — tax, borrow, make courts, enforce laws. Enumerated powers are listed; implied powers come from the necessary and proper clause. Federalist/Anti-Federalist arguments; Bill of Rights.

weeks.prep: Washington's Farewell Address excerpts (1796); background on Hamilton's financial plan and Jefferson's objections; Whiskey Rebellion summary.
misconceptions: Thinking political parties were planned in the Constitution. Parties formed in the 1790s around Hamilton's and Jefferson's opposing visions.
Assuming Washington wanted the U.S. isolated from all foreign contact. He warned against permanent alliances, while supporting commerce.

days.guide: List Washington's precedents and their effects.

questions.q: Name two precedents Washington set.
questions.a: Creating a cabinet; serving only two terms; being called 'Mr. President'; giving an inaugural address.

days.guide: Debate the National Bank and assumption; T-chart of the two visions.

questions.q: Why did Jefferson oppose the National Bank?
questions.a: He argued the Constitution didn't give Congress power to create a bank (strict construction) and it favored Northern merchants and bankers over farmers.

questions.q: What was assumption?
questions.a: Hamilton's plan for the federal government to take over (assume) the states' Revolutionary War debts.

days.guide: Compare the federal response to the Whiskey Rebellion with Shays' Rebellion.

questions.q: How did the response to the Whiskey Rebellion (1794) differ from Shays' Rebellion?
questions.a: Under the Constitution, Washington called up about 13,000 militia and the rebellion collapsed, proving federal authority; under the Articles, Congress couldn't respond to Shays and Massachusetts relied on a privately funded militia.

days.guide: Read Farewell Address excerpts; identify warnings.

questions.q: What two dangers did Washington warn against?
questions.a: Political parties (factions) and permanent alliances with foreign nations (also sectionalism).

days.guide: Give the quiz and Farewell Address analysis.

questions.q: Name the two first political parties and a leader of each.
questions.a: Federalists (Hamilton, Adams); Democratic-Republicans (Jefferson, Madison).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: precedents — cabinet of advisers, two-term limit (followed until FDR; then 22nd Amendment), title 'Mr. President', inaugural address; first cabinet — Jefferson (State), Hamilton (Treasury), Knox (War), Randolph (Attorney General); Hamilton — national bank, assumption of state debts, tariffs, loose construction, strong central government, manufacturing; Jefferson — strict construction, states' rights, agrarian economy, opposed the bank; Federalist Party (Hamilton, Adams) vs Democratic-Republican Party (Jefferson, Madison); Whiskey Rebellion 1794 — Washington led about 13,000 militia, rebellion collapsed, showing the new government could enforce its laws (unlike Shays' Rebellion under the Articles); Proclamation of Neutrality 1793. Farewell Address analysis: warns against the 'baneful effects of the spirit of party', sectionalism and 'permanent alliances' with foreign nations.

weeks.prep: Sedition Act text (1798); Jefferson's First Inaugural excerpt (1801); Marbury v. Madison summary; U.S. map; Lewis and Clark journal excerpts.
misconceptions: Thinking Marbury got his commission. The Court ruled he deserved it but that the law giving the Court power to issue the writ was unconstitutional — so he didn't get it, and the Court gained judicial review.
Thinking the Louisiana Purchase was just the state of Louisiana. It covered about 828,000 square miles from the Mississippi to the Rocky Mountains, doubling the nation's size.

days.guide: Read the Sedition Act; argue whether it violated the First Amendment.

questions.q: What did the Sedition Act (1798) make a crime?
questions.a: Writing or publishing 'false, scandalous and malicious' statements against the government, Congress or the president.

questions.q: How did Jefferson and Madison respond?
questions.a: With the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, arguing states could judge the acts unconstitutional.

days.guide: Read Jefferson's 1801 Inaugural excerpt.

questions.q: What did Jefferson mean by 'We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists'?
questions.a: Despite party differences, Americans share basic principles; he called for unity after the bitter 1800 election and the first peaceful transfer of power between parties.

days.guide: Summarize Marbury v. Madison (1803).

questions.q: What is judicial review?
questions.a: The power of courts to declare laws or government actions unconstitutional.

questions.q: Who wrote the Marbury opinion?
questions.a: Chief Justice John Marshall.

days.guide: Map the purchase and route; read journal entries.

questions.q: Why did Jefferson hesitate to buy Louisiana?
questions.a: The Constitution didn't explicitly allow buying territory, conflicting with his strict construction view; he went ahead anyway.

questions.q: Why did Napoleon sell Louisiana?
questions.a: He needed money for war in Europe and had lost his army in Haiti (Saint-Domingue), ending plans for an American empire.

days.guide: Give the map quiz and short answer.

questions.q: What were Lewis and Clark's goals?
questions.a: Explore the new territory, find a water route to the Pacific, map the land, record plants and animals, and establish relations with Native nations.

weeks.assessment_key: Map quiz key: Louisiana Purchase (1803, from France/Napoleon, about $15 million) between the Mississippi River and the Rockies; New Orleans; Lewis and Clark route (1804–1806) from near St. Louis up the Missouri River, across the Rockies (Lemhi Pass), down the Snake and Columbia Rivers to the Pacific (Fort Clatsop) and back. Short answer: Sacagawea, a Lemhi Shoshone woman, served as interpreter and guide, helped obtain horses from her brother Cameahwait's band, and her presence signaled the group's peaceful intent.

weeks.prep: Summaries of McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) and Gibbons v. Ogden (1824); Treaty of Greenville (1795) summary and map; 'Rip Van Winkle' (Project Gutenberg); images of Gilbert Stuart's Washington portraits and Charles Willson Peale portraits; recordings of 'Yankee Doodle' and 'Hail, Columbia.' Write the unit 3 test.
misconceptions: Thinking treaties with Native nations were equal agreements freely made. Many, like Greenville, followed military defeat and pressured nations to cede land.
Reading 'Rip Van Winkle' as just a funny tale. It comments on how much changed with the Revolution — and how much stayed the same.

days.guide: Examine McCulloch and Gibbons and how they strengthened national markets.

questions.q: What did McCulloch v. Maryland decide?
questions.a: Congress had implied power to create a national bank, and Maryland could not tax it — federal law is supreme over state law.

questions.q: What did Gibbons v. Ogden decide?
questions.a: Congress, not states, regulates interstate commerce, so New York's steamboat monopoly was invalid — opening national trade.

days.guide: Analyze the Treaty of Greenville and its outcomes for Native nations.

questions.q: What led to the Treaty of Greenville?
questions.a: The U.S. victory under Anthony Wayne at Fallen Timbers (1794) over a Native confederacy; in 1795 nations including the Shawnee, Miami and Delaware ceded most of Ohio.

days.guide: Read 'Rip Van Winkle'; discuss what it says about the new nation.

questions.q: What changes does Rip notice when he returns?
questions.a: The inn's sign now shows George Washington instead of King George III, people argue about elections and 'rights of citizens', and he is suspected of being a Tory when he says he's a loyal subject of the king.

questions.q: What does the story suggest about the Revolution?
questions.a: Big political changes happened, but daily village life and human nature stayed much the same.

days.guide: Analyze portraits and early songs.

questions.q: How did Gilbert Stuart's portraits shape the image of Washington?
questions.a: His dignified portraits (one appears on the $1 bill) presented Washington as a calm, republican leader and became the standard national image.

days.guide: Give the unit 3 test.

questions.q: What is the 'necessary and proper' clause used for in McCulloch?
questions.a: To justify Congress creating a bank as a means to carry out its enumerated powers (taxing, borrowing, regulating currency).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test (suggested): Washington's precedents; Hamilton vs Jefferson; Whiskey Rebellion; Farewell Address warnings; Alien and Sedition Acts; Marbury v. Madison (judicial review); Louisiana Purchase 1803; Lewis and Clark; McCulloch v. Maryland — Congress could create a national bank (implied powers) and states could not tax it ('the power to tax involves the power to destroy'); Gibbons v. Ogden — only Congress regulates interstate commerce (struck down New York's steamboat monopoly); Treaty of Greenville — after the Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794), Native nations ceded most of present-day Ohio; Rip Van Winkle sleeps 20 years through the Revolution.

weeks.prep: Text of 'The Star-Spangled Banner' (all four stanzas); War of 1812 map; Monroe Doctrine key passage (1823).
misconceptions: Thinking the Battle of New Orleans decided the war. It was fought on January 8, 1815, after the Treaty of Ghent was signed (December 24, 1814), though it boosted nationalism and Jackson's fame.
Thinking the Monroe Doctrine was enforced by U.S. power in 1823. It was a statement of policy; Britain's navy effectively backed it at first.

days.guide: Read about impressment and Tecumseh; chart causes.

questions.q: What was impressment?
questions.a: The British practice of seizing sailors from American ships and forcing them into the Royal Navy.

questions.q: What was Tecumseh's goal?
questions.a: To unite Native nations in a confederacy to resist American expansion and land cessions; he allied with Britain.

days.guide: Map major battles.

questions.q: What happened to Washington, D.C., in August 1814?
questions.a: British troops burned the Capitol and the White House.

days.guide: Read Key's full poem; explain its context.

questions.q: What event inspired 'The Star-Spangled Banner'?
questions.a: The British bombardment of Fort McHenry in Baltimore Harbor in September 1814; Key saw the flag still flying at dawn.

questions.q: When did it become the national anthem?

days.guide: Read the Monroe Doctrine's key passage.

questions.q: What was the Monroe Doctrine's message to Europe?
questions.a: The Americas are closed to new European colonization; European interference would be seen as hostile; the U.S. would not interfere in Europe.

days.guide: Give the foreign policy quiz.

questions.q: What did the Treaty of Ghent do?
questions.a: Ended the War of 1812 and restored prewar boundaries (status quo).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: causes — British impressment of American sailors, trade restrictions and seizure of ships, British support for Native resistance (Tecumseh's confederacy), War Hawks (Henry Clay, John C. Calhoun) wanting expansion and national honor; battles — British burned Washington, D.C. (August 1814); Fort McHenry withstood bombardment in Baltimore (September 1814), inspiring Francis Scott Key; Battle of New Orleans (January 1815) won by Andrew Jackson; Treaty of Ghent restored prewar borders; results — nationalism, end of Native confederacy resistance in the Old Northwest (Tecumseh killed 1813 at the Thames), Era of Good Feelings. Monroe Doctrine: Western Hemisphere closed to new European colonization and interference; U.S. would stay out of European affairs.

weeks.prep: Excerpts from Harriet Hanson Robinson's 'Loom and Spindle' or Lowell Offering letters; Erie Canal and National Road map; immigration data 1820–1860 and a nativist cartoon.
misconceptions: Thinking Whitney's cotton gin only affected the South. It also fueled Northern textile mills, shipping and banking.
Thinking all immigrants were welcomed. Irish Catholics and Germans faced nativist hostility (e.g., the Know-Nothing Party).

days.guide: Read Lowell letters; describe conditions.

questions.q: Who worked in the Lowell mills and what were conditions like?
questions.a: Mostly young unmarried New England farm women; long (12–14 hour) days, noisy machines, strict rules, boardinghouses, but cash wages.

questions.q: What did Harriet Robinson describe about the 1836 strike?
questions.a: As an 11-year-old she led her room out in a 'turn-out' protesting higher board charges/wage cuts.

days.guide: Map the Erie Canal and National Road; explain the American System.

questions.q: Why was the Erie Canal important?
questions.a: It connected the Great Lakes to the Atlantic via the Hudson, lowering shipping costs and making New York City the nation's leading port.

questions.q: What were the three parts of Clay's American System?
questions.a: A protective tariff, a national bank and federally funded internal improvements (roads, canals).

days.guide: Chart inventions and effects.

questions.q: How did the steel plow change farming?
questions.a: It cut through tough prairie soil, opening the Midwest to large-scale farming.

questions.q: What did the telegraph do?
questions.a: Sent messages almost instantly over wires using Morse code (first public line 1844).

days.guide: Analyze immigration data and a nativist cartoon.

questions.q: What caused the surge in Irish immigration in the late 1840s?
questions.a: The potato famine (blight), which caused mass starvation in Ireland.

questions.q: What is nativism?
questions.a: Favoring native-born people and opposing immigrants.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What are interchangeable parts?
questions.a: Identical, standardized parts that can replace each other, allowing mass production and easy repair.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Lowell mills — young New England women worked about 12–14-hour days, lived in boardinghouses, organized 'turn-outs' (strikes) in 1834 and 1836; Erie Canal (completed 1825) linked the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo, cutting freight costs dramatically and making New York City a leading port; National Road began at Cumberland, Maryland; Clay's American System — protective tariff, national bank, internal improvements; inventions — cotton gin (Whitney, 1793), steamboat (Fulton's Clermont, 1807), steel plow (John Deere, 1837), telegraph (Morse, 1844), interchangeable parts (Whitney and others); Irish immigration surged after the potato famine (1845–1852); German immigrants often settled in the Midwest; nativism = hostility to immigrants.

weeks.prep: Readings on Richard Allen and the AME Church, Horace Mann's arguments (12th Annual Report, 1848), the Declaration of Sentiments (1848), Thoreau's Walden and Emerson's 'Self-Reliance' excerpts. Write the unit 4 test.
misconceptions: Thinking Seneca Falls immediately won women the vote. It began the organized movement; national women's suffrage came with the 19th Amendment (1920).
Assuming Northern free Black people had equal rights. They faced segregation, voting limits and discrimination, and built their own institutions.

days.guide: Read about Richard Allen and free Black institutions in the North.

questions.q: Why did Richard Allen found the AME Church?
questions.a: Black worshippers were forced into segregated seating and pulled from prayer at St. George's Methodist Church in Philadelphia, so Allen created an independent Black church (Bethel, 1794; AME denomination 1816).

days.guide: Read Horace Mann's arguments.

questions.q: What did Horace Mann argue public schools would do?
questions.a: Create informed citizens and equal opportunity — education as 'the great equalizer' — funded by taxes and open to all children.

days.guide: Compare the Declaration of Sentiments with the Declaration of Independence.

questions.q: How did the Declaration of Sentiments change Jefferson's words?
questions.a: 'We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men and women are created equal.'

questions.q: Name one grievance in the Declaration of Sentiments.
questions.a: Women were denied the right to vote; married women lost property rights; women were barred from most colleges and professions.

days.guide: Read Walden and 'Self-Reliance' excerpts; discuss individualism.

questions.q: What did Thoreau seek at Walden Pond?
questions.a: To 'live deliberately,' simply and close to nature, to discover what truly matters.

questions.q: What is Emerson's main message in 'Self-Reliance'?
questions.a: Trust yourself and your own judgment rather than conforming to society.

days.guide: Give the unit 4 test.

questions.q: Who organized the Seneca Falls Convention?
questions.a: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test (suggested): War of 1812 causes and outcome; Monroe Doctrine; Lowell mills; Erie Canal; American System; inventions; Irish/German immigration and nativism; Richard Allen founded the African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church (independent denomination 1816) after Black worshippers were mistreated at St. George's Methodist Church; Horace Mann — Massachusetts education leader who argued for free, tax-supported common schools to create good citizens and equal opportunity ('the great equalizer'); Seneca Falls Convention (July 1848), Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott, Declaration of Sentiments: 'all men and women are created equal' and demanded rights including voting; transcendentalism — truth found through nature, intuition and individual conscience (Emerson's 'Trust thyself'; Thoreau lived at Walden Pond 1845–47).

weeks.prep: Blank map of the South; data on cotton bales and enslaved population 1790–1860 (U.S. Census; e.g., about 700,000 enslaved people in 1790 and about 3.95 million in 1860; cotton output grew from a few thousand bales around 1790 to roughly 4 million bales by 1860); graph paper.
misconceptions: Thinking most white Southerners owned enslaved people. In 1860 roughly one-quarter of white Southern families did; most were yeoman farmers, but slavery shaped the whole society and economy.
Believing the cotton gin reduced slavery by saving labor. It made short-staple cotton profitable, so demand for enslaved labor and land grew.

days.guide: Label cotton states, rivers and ports; explain climate and soil.

questions.q: Why did cotton grow well in the Deep South?
