questions.a: Long, warm growing season, ample rain and rich soil (like Alabama and Mississippi's Black Belt).

questions.q: Why were rivers and ports important to the cotton economy?
questions.a: They moved bales cheaply to ports like New Orleans for shipment to Northern and British mills.

days.guide: Graph cotton production and enslaved population 1790–1860; write the relationship.

questions.q: What relationship does the graph show?
questions.a: Both rose sharply together after the 1793 cotton gin made cotton profitable, increasing demand for enslaved labor.

questions.q: About how many enslaved people lived in the U.S. in 1860?
questions.a: Nearly 4 million.

days.guide: Build a social pyramid using census statistics.

questions.q: Which group made up the majority of white Southerners?
questions.a: Yeoman farmers who owned small farms and few or no enslaved people.

days.guide: Trace a bale of cotton from Mississippi to Lowell/Manchester.

questions.q: How did the North profit from slavery?
questions.a: Northern mills processed cotton; Northern banks, insurers and shippers financed and carried the trade.

days.guide: Give the quiz and comparison response.

questions.q: Why was cotton called 'King'?
questions.a: It was the South's dominant crop and the nation's leading export, central to the economy.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: cotton grew best in the Deep South's long growing season, warm climate and rich soil (Black Belt); major rivers (Mississippi, Alabama, Tennessee, Red) and ports (New Orleans, Mobile, Savannah, Charleston) moved cotton; Whitney's 1793 gin separated seeds from short-staple cotton quickly; by 1860 cotton was the largest U.S. export ('King Cotton'); society — a small planter elite (20+ enslaved people), yeoman farmers (majority of whites), poor whites, about 260,000 free Black people in the South, nearly 4 million enslaved people; the South depended on Northern shipping, banking and manufactured goods and British/Northern mills. North–South comparison rubric: North — industry, cities, immigrant wage labor, railroads; South — agriculture, cash crops, enslaved labor, fewer cities and factories; uses specific evidence.

weeks.prep: Parent preview: these sources describe violence and family separation; read them first. WPA Slave Narratives (Library of Congress 'Born in Slavery'), Harriet Jacobs's 'Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl' excerpt, The Confessions of Nat Turner excerpt, readings on Denmark Vesey, recordings of 'Wade in the Water' and 'Follow the Drinking Gourd.' Write the unit 5 test.
misconceptions: Thinking enslaved people passively accepted slavery. They resisted daily (work slowdowns, sabotage, learning to read, keeping family and culture), escaped and occasionally rebelled.

Treating 'secret codes' in every spiritual as proven fact. Some songs may have carried hidden meanings; historians debate specific claims (the 'Drinking Gourd' lyrics as we know them were published in 1928).

days.guide: Read two WPA narratives and the Jacobs excerpt; note family, labor and punishment details.

questions.q: What should you consider when sourcing a WPA narrative?
questions.a: Interviews were in the 1930s with elderly people who were children under slavery; interviewers were often white Southerners, which may have influenced what people said.

questions.q: How did Harriet Jacobs escape slavery?
questions.a: She hid for nearly seven years in a cramped attic space in her grandmother's house before escaping north by boat (1842).

days.guide: Read Nat Turner and Vesey accounts; list Southern legal responses.

questions.q: What happened in Nat Turner's Rebellion?
questions.a: In 1831 in Southampton County, Virginia, Turner led enslaved people who killed about 55–60 white people; the militia crushed it, and Turner and many others (including innocent Black people) were executed or killed.

questions.q: How did Southern states respond?
questions.a: Tightened slave codes — banning teaching enslaved people to read and write, limiting gatherings and Black preachers, increasing patrols.

days.guide: Listen to the spirituals; analyze possible double meanings.

questions.q: What might 'Wade in the Water' have meant to freedom seekers?
questions.a: A possible hint to travel through water to throw tracking dogs off the scent; it also has biblical meaning (deliverance). Historians debate the code interpretation.

days.guide: T-chart free Black life in Philadelphia and New Orleans.

questions.q: Name one right and one restriction for free Black people in the North.
questions.a: Rights: own property, found churches and schools; restrictions: segregation, exclusion from many jobs, and voting bans in most states (Pennsylvania removed Black voting in 1838).

days.guide: Give the unit 5 test.

questions.q: Name two forms of everyday resistance.
questions.a: Slowing work, breaking tools, pretending illness, secretly learning to read, running away, preserving culture and family.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test (suggested): cotton gin; Cotton Kingdom; Southern social structure; WPA narratives — interviews in the 1930s with formerly enslaved people (consider age and white interviewers when sourcing); Harriet Jacobs hid nearly seven years in her grandmother's tiny attic crawlspace before escaping north; Nat Turner's Rebellion (August 1831, Southampton County, Virginia) killed about 55–60 white people; Southern responses — laws banning teaching enslaved people to read, restricting gatherings and Black preachers, harsher patrols; Denmark Vesey (Charleston, 1822) planned a revolt, was betrayed and executed with about 34 others; responses — the AME church was destroyed and Negro Seamen Act restricted Black sailors; free Black communities (Philadelphia — churches, schools, some property, but no vote after 1838; New Orleans — larger free population of color with property and trades but legal restrictions). Document-based short answer graded on claim, evidence, sourcing.

weeks.prep: Voter turnout data (1824: about 27% of eligible voters; 1828: about 58%); Jackson's 1832 Bank veto message; the Cherokee Memorial (1830); Jackson's Second Annual Message (1830); removal routes map; Private John Burnett's account (written 1890); Worcester v. Georgia summary.
misconceptions: Thinking Jacksonian democracy meant everyone could vote. It expanded voting to most white men; women, most free Black men and Native Americans were excluded.
Believing the Supreme Court approved removal. In Worcester v. Georgia (1832) the Court ruled Georgia had no authority over Cherokee land; Jackson did not enforce it.

days.guide: Compare 1824 and 1828 turnout; explain expanded white male suffrage.

questions.q: Why did turnout jump in 1828?
questions.a: Most states dropped property requirements for white men, and more states let voters (not legislatures) choose electors; parties organized rallies.

questions.q: What was the 'spoils system'?
questions.a: Rewarding political supporters with government jobs.

days.guide: Read Jackson's 1832 veto; summarize his argument.

questions.q: Why did Jackson veto the Second Bank's recharter?
questions.a: He argued it was unconstitutional, a monopoly that served the rich and foreign investors at the expense of ordinary people.

days.guide: Compare the Cherokee Memorial with Jackson's 1830 message using a sourcing chart.

questions.q: What did the Cherokee argue in their memorial?
questions.a: They had treaty rights to their homeland, had adopted a constitution, schools and farming, and wished to stay on the land of their ancestors.

questions.q: How did Jackson justify removal?
questions.a: He claimed it would benefit both whites and Native people, open land for settlement and protect Native nations from destruction by moving them west.

days.guide: Map removal routes; read Burnett's account.

questions.q: Which five nations were removed from the Southeast?
questions.a: Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), Chickasaw and Seminole.

questions.q: About how many Cherokee died on the Trail of Tears (1838–39)?
questions.a: About 4,000 (roughly a quarter of the nation).

days.guide: Write the document-based paragraph.

questions.q: What did Worcester v. Georgia (1832) decide?
questions.a: Georgia had no authority over the Cherokee Nation; only the federal government could deal with it under treaties.

weeks.assessment_key: Document-based paragraph rubric (1–4): claim (e.g., removal was inconsistent with the Constitution as interpreted by the Supreme Court); evidence — Worcester v. Georgia (1832) held that the Cherokee Nation was a distinct community where Georgia law had no force and only the federal government could deal with it; federal treaties (supreme law under Article VI) guaranteed Cherokee land; Jackson's message argued removal was benevolent and would protect Native people; the Treaty of New Echota (1835) was signed by a minority faction, not the elected Cherokee government; Burnett's account of suffering (about 4,000 of roughly 16,000 Cherokee died); sourcing of each document; counterclaim addressed.

weeks.prep: Image of John Gast's 'American Progress' (1872); O'Sullivan's 1845 excerpt; trail map with distances (Oregon Trail about 2,000 miles from Independence, Missouri; Santa Fe Trail about 900 miles; Mormon Trail about 1,300 miles from Nauvoo, Illinois); Oregon Trail women's diaries; Annie Bidwell biography.
misconceptions: Thinking the West was empty. Native nations, Mexicans and others already lived there.
Believing most pioneers died from Native attacks. Disease (especially cholera), accidents and drownings caused far more deaths.

days.guide: Analyze Gast's painting and O'Sullivan's essay; list who is shown and missing.

questions.q: What does the floating woman (Columbia) carry, and what does it symbolize?
questions.a: A schoolbook and telegraph wire — 'civilization,' education and technology spreading west.

questions.q: How are Native Americans shown?
questions.a: Fleeing west into darkness with the bison, suggesting they must give way to 'progress' — a one-sided view.

days.guide: Map four trails; calculate travel times at 15 miles per day.

questions.q: At 15 miles per day, how long did the 2,000-mile Oregon Trail take?
questions.a: About 133 days (roughly 4–5 months).

questions.q: At 15 miles/day, how long for the ~900-mile Santa Fe Trail?
questions.a: About 60 days.

days.guide: Read women's diaries and about Annie Bidwell; explain Wyoming suffrage (1869).

questions.q: Why did Wyoming grant women the vote in 1869?
questions.a: To attract more women settlers to a mostly male territory, gain publicity, and recognize pioneer women's contributions.

questions.q: Who was Annie Bidwell?
questions.a: A Chico, California, reformer (wife of John Bidwell) who supported women's suffrage, temperance and education and worked with the Mechoopda Maidu community.

days.guide: Examine the rivers and early water-rights conflicts.

questions.q: What is 'first in time, first in right'?
questions.a: The prior-appropriation rule: whoever first used water for a beneficial purpose has the senior right to it — common in the dry West.

days.guide: Give the quiz and painting analysis.

questions.q: What was the leading cause of death on the Oregon Trail?
questions.a: Disease, especially cholera.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Manifest Destiny — belief (John O'Sullivan, 1845) that the U.S. was destined by God to spread across the continent; trails — Oregon (Independence, MO to Oregon City, about 2,000 miles), California (branch to Sacramento Valley), Mormon (Nauvoo, IL to Salt Lake Valley, 1846–47, led by Brigham Young), Santa Fe (trade route, Missouri to Santa Fe); dangers — cholera, river crossings, accidents, weather; Wyoming Territory granted women suffrage in 1869 (to attract women settlers, reward pioneer women's contributions, gain publicity, and as a political gamble); Western water — rivers like the Mississippi, Missouri and Colorado carried trade and irrigation; 'first in time, first in right' (prior appropriation) water-rights conflicts. Painting analysis rubric: describes Columbia carrying a schoolbook and stringing telegraph wire westward, settlers, farmers and railroads following, Native Americans and bison fleeing into darkness; interprets purpose (glorify expansion as progress); notes who's missing or shown negatively.

weeks.prep: Calisphere images of ranchos, Californios and diseños; accounts of the Alamo including José Enrique de la Peña's diary; review materials for units 1–6. Write the semester exam.
misconceptions: Thinking the Texas Revolution was only about liberty. Causes included Mexico's centralization under Santa Anna, cultural differences, and Anglo settlers' insistence on slavery, which Mexico had abolished (1829).
Treating the Alamo as the end of the revolution. Texas won independence at San Jacinto (April 21, 1836).

days.guide: Use Calisphere photos and diseños to describe rancho life.

questions.q: What was the hide-and-tallow trade?
questions.a: Californio ranchos raised cattle and traded hides (for leather) and tallow (fat for candles and soap) with ships, mostly from New England; hides were called 'California banknotes.'

questions.q: What was a diseño?
questions.a: A hand-drawn map showing the boundaries of a Mexican land grant, using landmarks like rivers, hills and trees.

days.guide: Compare Texan and Mexican accounts of the Alamo.

questions.q: How did de la Peña's account differ from the Texan legend?
questions.a: He described defenders, possibly including Davy Crockett, being captured and executed after the battle on Santa Anna's orders, rather than all dying fighting; he wrote from the Mexican army's point of view and criticized Santa Anna.

questions.q: Where did Texas win its independence?
questions.a: At San Jacinto (April 21, 1836), where Sam Houston defeated and captured Santa Anna.

days.guide: Review units 1–3 with a timeline sort and document questions.

questions.q: Put in order: Constitution signed, Declaration, Treaty of Paris, Articles ratified.
questions.a: Declaration (1776), Articles ratified (1781), Treaty of Paris (1783), Constitution signed (1787).

days.guide: Review units 4–6 with vocabulary matching and a DBQ outline.

questions.q: Match: Seneca Falls, Erie Canal, Worcester v. Georgia.
questions.a: Seneca Falls — women's rights convention (1848); Erie Canal — Hudson to Lake Erie (1825); Worcester v. Georgia — Cherokee sovereignty ruling (1832).

days.guide: Give the semester 1 exam.

questions.q: Why did Mexico's 1829 abolition of slavery matter in Texas?
questions.a: Many Anglo settlers held enslaved people and resisted Mexican antislavery laws, one cause of the Texas Revolution.

weeks.assessment_key: Semester 1 exam (suggested cumulative): English/Enlightenment roots; causes of the Revolution; Declaration; Articles and their weaknesses; Constitutional compromises; Federalists vs Anti-Federalists; Bill of Rights; Washington through Monroe; Marbury, McCulloch, Gibbons; War of 1812; Monroe Doctrine; industrialization; reform; Southern economy and slavery; Jackson and Indian Removal; Manifest Destiny; Mexican California (ranchos, hide-and-tallow trade, mission secularization 1833–34, Mexico abolished slavery 1829); Texas (Alamo Feb–March 1836, San Jacinto April 1836, Republic of Texas 1836–1845, annexed 1845). DBQ items scored for claim, evidence, sourcing.

weeks.prep: Polk's war message (May 1846) excerpt; Lincoln's 'spot resolutions' (December 1847); Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo Articles 8–9; Calisphere Gold Rush photos; a forty-niner's letter; a short article on the war's legacy for Mexican Americans. Write the unit 6 test.
misconceptions: Thinking the border was clearly the Rio Grande. Mexico considered the Nueces River the boundary; the land between was disputed, which is why Lincoln demanded the 'spot.'
Assuming treaty promises to Mexican residents were fully kept. Many Californios lost land through the 1851 Land Act's costly title challenges, squatters and debt.

days.guide: Compare Polk's war message and Lincoln's spot resolutions.

questions.q: What was Polk's claim?
questions.a: Mexico had 'invaded our territory and shed American blood upon the American soil.'

questions.q: What did Lincoln demand?
questions.a: That Polk identify the exact 'spot' where blood was shed, implying it was Mexican or disputed land, not U.S. soil.

days.guide: Read Articles 8 and 9; evaluate whether promises were kept.

questions.q: What did Article 8 promise?
questions.a: Mexicans living in the ceded lands could stay or leave, keep their property ('inviolably respected'), and choose U.S. citizenship.

questions.q: Were these promises kept in California?
questions.a: Only partly — the Land Act of 1851 forced Californios to prove titles in long, expensive court cases; many lost land to lawyers' fees, squatters and debt.

days.guide: Read a forty-niner's letter; examine photos; chart impacts on Native Californians, Californios and Chinese miners.

questions.q: How did the Gold Rush affect Native Californians?
questions.a: Their population collapsed from disease, starvation, displacement and state-sponsored violence; many were forced into labor.

questions.q: How did the Foreign Miners' Tax affect Chinese miners?
questions.a: It charged foreign miners monthly fees (1852 version aimed at Chinese), pushing them out of mining or into poorer claims.

days.guide: Read about the war's legacy for Mexican Americans; reflect.

questions.q: What does the saying 'We didn't cross the border; the border crossed us' mean?
questions.a: Many Mexican families became U.S. residents in 1848 because the border moved, not because they migrated.

days.guide: Give the unit 6 test.

questions.q: What was the Gadsden Purchase?
questions.a: The 1853 U.S. purchase of land in southern Arizona and New Mexico from Mexico, for a southern railroad route.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test (suggested): Jacksonian democracy and spoils; Bank War; Indian Removal Act (1830); Worcester v. Georgia; Trail of Tears; Manifest Destiny; trails; Mexican California; Texas independence and annexation (1845); Mexican-American War (1846–1848): Polk claimed Mexico 'shed American blood upon the American soil'; Lincoln's spot resolutions challenged that; Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) — Mexico ceded about half its territory (California, Nevada, Utah, most of Arizona and New Mexico, parts of Colorado and Wyoming) for $15 million, Rio Grande border; Articles 8–9 promised Mexicans could stay, keep property, become U.S. citizens; Gadsden Purchase (1853); gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, Coloma (January 1848); Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, $20/month; 1852 version targeted Chinese miners); California's Native population fell from about 150,000 to about 30,000 by 1870 due to disease, starvation and violence; statehood 1850.

weeks.prep: Pennsylvania Gradual Abolition Act (1780) excerpt; Northwest Ordinance Article 6; Garrison's 'To the Public' (The Liberator, January 1, 1831); Douglass's 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?' (July 5, 1852) excerpt; Underground Railroad map; readings on Harriet Tubman, William Still, Ohio's 1804 Black Laws and James Forten.
misconceptions: Thinking the Underground Railroad was an actual railroad with tunnels. It was a secret network of people and safe houses; most freedom seekers relied on themselves and Black communities.
Assuming all abolitionists agreed. Some sought gradual emancipation or colonization; Garrison demanded immediate abolition and moral persuasion; Douglass later supported political action.

days.guide: Read the 1780 Act and Article 6; map Northern abolition dates.

questions.q: Did Pennsylvania's 1780 act free all enslaved people immediately?
questions.a: No — it was gradual: those already enslaved stayed enslaved; children born after it were free after serving until age 28.

questions.q: Which was the first state (as a republic) to ban adult slavery outright?
questions.a: Vermont, in its 1777 constitution.

days.guide: Read Garrison and Douglass; compare tone and strategy.

questions.q: Quote or paraphrase Garrison's promise in 'To the Public.'
questions.a: 'I will be as harsh as truth… I will not equivocate — I will not excuse — I will not retreat a single inch — AND I WILL BE HEARD.'

questions.q: What was Douglass's main point in 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?'
questions.a: Independence Day celebrations of liberty were hypocrisy to enslaved people, revealing the nation's injustice.

days.guide: Map routes; read about Tubman and Still.

questions.q: Why was Harriet Tubman called 'Moses'?
questions.a: She led enslaved people to freedom, returning to Maryland about 13 times and guiding about 70 people.

questions.q: Why are William Still's records valuable?
questions.a: He interviewed and recorded hundreds of freedom seekers, preserving their names and stories.

days.guide: Read about Northern Black laws and James Forten.

questions.q: What did Ohio's Black Laws require?
questions.a: Black residents had to show certificates of freedom and register; an 1807 law required a $500 bond, discouraging Black settlement.

days.guide: Give the abolition quiz.

questions.q: Name two abolitionist strategies.
questions.a: Newspapers and speeches (moral persuasion), petitions, the Underground Railroad, political parties, slave narratives.

weeks.assessment_key: Abolition quiz key: Pennsylvania's 1780 act was gradual — it freed no one immediately; children born to enslaved mothers after it were free but bound to serve until age 28; Northwest Ordinance Article 6 banned slavery in the territory; Northern abolition dates — Vermont 1777, Pennsylvania 1780 (gradual), Massachusetts 1783 (court rulings), Connecticut and Rhode Island 1784 (gradual), New York 1799 (gradual; complete 1827), New Jersey 1804 (gradual); Garrison — The Liberator, immediate abolition ('I will be heard'); Douglass — escaped slavery 1838, orator, North Star newspaper; Tubman — escaped 1849, about 13 trips rescuing about 70 people; William Still — Philadelphia Vigilance Committee, recorded hundreds of freedom seekers' stories (published 1872); Ohio Black Laws (1804, 1807) required proof of freedom and later a $500 bond; James Forten — wealthy Black Philadelphia sailmaker who funded abolitionism.

weeks.prep: Maps of free and slave states in 1820 and 1850; Henry Clay speech excerpt (1850); Wilmot Proviso text; account of the Anthony Burns case (1854).
misconceptions: Thinking the Missouri Compromise banned slavery everywhere north of 36°30'. It applied to the Louisiana Purchase territory (except Missouri).
Believing the Compromise of 1850 settled the issue. Its stronger Fugitive Slave Act enraged Northerners and deepened sectional conflict.

days.guide: Color the 1820 map with the 36°30' line; explain Clay's role.

questions.q: What did the Missouri Compromise do?
questions.a: Admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as free, keeping the Senate balanced, and banned slavery in the Louisiana Territory north of 36°30' (except Missouri).

questions.q: Why was Henry Clay called the 'Great Compromiser'?
questions.a: He brokered the Missouri Compromise, the 1833 tariff compromise and the Compromise of 1850.

days.guide: Read the Wilmot Proviso; explain the sectional split.

questions.q: Why did the Wilmot Proviso divide Congress by section rather than party?
questions.a: Northern Democrats and Whigs voted for banning slavery in the Mexican Cession while Southerners of both parties opposed, showing slavery outweighed party loyalty.

days.guide: Chart the Compromise of 1850; score which side gained more.

questions.q: What did the North gain in 1850?
questions.a: California admitted as a free state; slave trade ended in Washington, D.C.

questions.q: What did the South gain?
questions.a: A stronger Fugitive Slave Act; possibility of slavery in New Mexico and Utah by popular sovereignty.

days.guide: Read about Anthony Burns; explain how the Act radicalized Northerners.

questions.q: What happened in the Anthony Burns case (1854)?
questions.a: Burns, who had escaped from Virginia, was arrested in Boston; despite protests and a rescue attempt, federal troops marched him to a ship back to slavery while thousands watched — turning many Northerners against the law.

days.guide: Give the quiz and map task.

questions.q: What is popular sovereignty?
questions.a: Letting settlers of a territory vote on whether to allow slavery.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Missouri Compromise (1820, Henry Clay) — Missouri admitted as a slave state, Maine as free (12–12 balance), slavery banned in the rest of the Louisiana Territory north of 36°30'; Wilmot Proviso (1846) — would have banned slavery in any land acquired from Mexico; passed the House, failed in the Senate; voting split North vs South rather than by party; Compromise of 1850 — California admitted free, slave trade (not slavery) banned in D.C., New Mexico and Utah territories decide by popular sovereignty, Texas–New Mexico boundary settled and Texas debt assumed, stronger Fugitive Slave Act (to South). Fugitive Slave Act — federal officials must help capture freedom seekers, no jury trial, citizens could be fined for helping. Map: free vs slave states labeled correctly for 1820 and 1850.

weeks.prep: Map of the Kansas-Nebraska Act; Dred Scott decision excerpts (Chief Justice Taney, 1857); Lincoln's 'House Divided' speech (June 1858); Lincoln–Douglas debate excerpts.
misconceptions: Thinking Lincoln was an abolitionist in 1858. He opposed slavery's expansion into the territories, not immediate abolition where it existed.
Thinking Dred Scott only affected one man. It declared the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional and said Black Americans could not be citizens.

days.guide: Map the Kansas-Nebraska Act; explain how popular sovereignty undid the Missouri Compromise.

questions.q: Why did the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) cause violence?
questions.a: It let settlers vote on slavery in territories north of 36°30', so proslavery and antislavery settlers rushed into Kansas and fought ('Bleeding Kansas').

questions.q: Who sponsored the act?
questions.a: Senator Stephen Douglas of Illinois.

days.guide: Read Taney's opinion; list three holdings and effects.

questions.q: What were the Dred Scott decision's three main holdings?
questions.a: 1) Black Americans, free or enslaved, were not citizens and could not sue in federal court; 2) Congress could not ban slavery in the territories, so the Missouri Compromise was unconstitutional; 3) living in free territory did not make Scott free — enslaved people were property protected by the Fifth Amendment.

questions.q: How did Northerners react?
questions.a: With outrage; it strengthened the new Republican Party.

days.guide: Close-read 'A House Divided'; explain its metaphor.

questions.q: Explain 'A house divided against itself cannot stand.'
questions.a: The nation could not last half slave and half free; it would eventually become all one or all the other.

days.guide: T-chart Lincoln's and Douglas's positions.

questions.q: What was Douglas's Freeport Doctrine?
questions.a: Territories could keep slavery out by refusing to pass local laws protecting it, despite Dred Scott.

questions.q: Who won the 1858 Senate race?
questions.a: Douglas (chosen by the Illinois legislature), but Lincoln gained national fame.

days.guide: Write the DBQ paragraph.

questions.q: What was the Republican Party's main goal in the 1850s?
questions.a: To stop the spread of slavery into the western territories.

weeks.assessment_key: DBQ paragraph rubric (1–4): claim (e.g., 'By 1858 compromise had largely failed, making war very likely but not yet certain'); evidence from at least 3 documents — Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) repealed the Missouri line and led to Bleeding Kansas (sack of Lawrence, Pottawatomie killings, 1856); Dred Scott (1857); 'A House Divided' (1858); Lincoln–Douglas debates; analysis of how each pushed the sections apart; counterclaim (Douglas's popular sovereignty and the Freeport Doctrine still offered compromise; secession was not inevitable until 1860).

weeks.prep: Webster's Second Reply to Hayne (1830) excerpt; Calhoun's nullification arguments (South Carolina Exposition and Protest, 1828); John Brown's last courtroom speech (November 2, 1859) and newspaper reactions; 1860 electoral map and popular vote; South Carolina's Declaration of the Causes of Secession (December 24, 1860). Write the unit 7 test.
misconceptions: Thinking secession declarations focused only on 'states' rights' in general. South Carolina's declaration repeatedly names the protection of slavery and Northern hostility to it as the cause.
Thinking Lincoln won a majority of the popular vote in 1860. He won about 40% in a four-way race, but a clear Electoral College majority (180 of 303) entirely from free states.

days.guide: Compare Webster and Calhoun.

questions.q: What is nullification?
questions.a: The theory that a state can declare a federal law void within its borders.

questions.q: What was Webster's famous line?
questions.a: 'Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable!'

days.guide: Read John Brown's speech and contrasting newspaper reactions.

questions.q: What did John Brown attempt at Harpers Ferry (1859)?
questions.a: To seize the federal arsenal and spark an armed uprising of enslaved people; he was captured and hanged.

questions.q: How did reactions differ North and South?
questions.a: Many Northerners (e.g., Emerson, Thoreau) saw him as a martyr; Southerners saw proof that Northerners wanted to incite slave rebellion.

days.guide: Analyze the 1860 electoral map and popular vote.

questions.q: How did Lincoln win without Southern votes?
questions.a: He carried nearly all the populous free states, giving him an Electoral College majority (180 votes) with about 40% of the popular vote.

questions.q: Name Lincoln's three opponents.
questions.a: Stephen Douglas, John C. Breckinridge and John Bell.

days.guide: Read South Carolina's declaration; identify its main reason.

questions.q: What main reason does South Carolina give for seceding?
questions.a: Northern states' hostility to slavery — refusing to enforce the Fugitive Slave Act and electing a president whose 'opinions and purposes are hostile to slavery.'

days.guide: Give the unit 7 test.

questions.q: When did South Carolina secede?
questions.a: December 20, 1860.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test (suggested): abolition leaders and strategies; Missouri Compromise; Wilmot Proviso; Compromise of 1850; Fugitive Slave Act; Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852); Kansas-Nebraska Act; Dred Scott; Lincoln–Douglas; nullification — Calhoun argued a state could void a federal law (Tariff of 1828/1832); Webster: 'Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable!'; crisis resolved 1833 with Force Bill and compromise tariff; John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry (October 1859), hanged December 1859 — martyr in the North, proof of Northern aggression in the South; election of 1860 — Lincoln (Republican), Douglas (Northern Democrat), Breckinridge (Southern Democrat), Bell (Constitutional Union); Lincoln not on the ballot in most Southern states; South Carolina seceded December 20, 1860, citing Northern hostility to slavery, nonenforcement of the Fugitive Slave Act and election of a president opposed to slavery.

weeks.prep: Lincoln's First Inaugural Address (March 4, 1861) closing paragraphs; 1860 resource statistics (approx.: population North ~22 million vs South ~9 million, including ~3.5 million enslaved; railroad miles ~22,000 vs ~9,000; the North had the large majority of factories and industrial workers); American Battlefield Trust maps.
misconceptions: Thinking the North's victory was guaranteed. The South had skilled officers, interior lines and only needed to defend, not conquer.
Calling Antietam a decisive Union battlefield victory. It was tactically a draw but strategically a Union success: Lee retreated, and Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation.

days.guide: Read the First Inaugural's closing; explain his message.

questions.q: What did Lincoln mean by 'the better angels of our nature'?
questions.a: He appealed to Southerners' shared memories and goodness, hoping they would choose union and peace: 'We are not enemies, but friends.'

questions.q: Did Lincoln promise to end slavery in the South in 1861?
questions.a: No — he said he had no intention to interfere with slavery where it existed, but secession was illegal and he would hold federal property.

days.guide: Graph 1860 resources; predict the advantage.

questions.q: Which side had the advantage in resources, and why?
questions.a: The North — more than twice the population, far more railroads and most of the factories to produce weapons and supplies.

days.guide: Compare the Anaconda Plan with Confederate strategy on a map.

questions.q: What were the two main parts of the Anaconda Plan?
questions.a: Blockade Southern ports and take control of the Mississippi River.

days.guide: Map Fort Sumter, First Bull Run, Antietam; summarize outcomes.

questions.q: Why was Antietam important?
questions.a: Lee's invasion of Maryland was stopped, giving Lincoln the opportunity to issue the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation and discouraging European recognition of the Confederacy.

days.guide: Give the quiz and graph question.

questions.q: What were the border states, and why did they matter?
questions.a: Slave states that stayed in the Union (DE, MD, KY, MO); they had key resources and locations (Maryland surrounds Washington, D.C.).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Fort Sumter (April 12, 1861) — Confederates fired on the fort in Charleston Harbor, starting the war; four more states seceded (Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina, Tennessee); border states (Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri; later West Virginia) stayed in the Union; Anaconda Plan — blockade Southern ports and seize the Mississippi to split the Confederacy; Confederate strategy — defend, wear down Northern will, hope for British/French recognition ('King Cotton diplomacy'); First Bull Run (July 1861) — Confederate victory, showed the war would be long; Antietam (September 17, 1862) — bloodiest single day (about 23,000 casualties), Lee's invasion stopped. Graph interpretation: North's advantages in population, railroads and factories.

weeks.prep: Emancipation Proclamation transcript; USCT photographs (Library of Congress); Corporal James Henry Gooding's letter to Lincoln (September 1863); Douglass's 'Men of Color, To Arms!' (March 1863); biographies of Grant, Lee and Davis; Union and Confederate soldier letters.
misconceptions: Thinking the Emancipation Proclamation freed all enslaved people. It applied only to areas in rebellion; it did not cover the loyal border states or Union-held areas; the 13th Amendment (1865) ended slavery nationwide.
Thinking Black soldiers only appeared late and in small numbers. About 180,000 served in the U.S. Colored Troops — roughly 10% of the Union Army — plus thousands in the Navy.

days.guide: Read the Proclamation; determine exactly who it freed and why it was a war measure.

questions.q: Which enslaved people did the Emancipation Proclamation free?
questions.a: Those in areas still in rebellion against the United States on January 1, 1863 — not those in the loyal border states or Union-controlled areas.

questions.q: Why did Lincoln frame it as a war measure?
questions.a: As commander in chief he could seize enemy resources during war; this gave it a constitutional basis and kept border states loyal.

days.guide: Read Gooding's letter and Douglass's 'Men of Color, To Arms!'

questions.q: What did Corporal Gooding ask Lincoln?
questions.a: For equal pay — Black soldiers were paid $10 (minus $3 for clothing) while white privates received $13.

questions.q: Why did Douglass urge Black men to enlist?
questions.a: Fighting would help end slavery and earn a claim to citizenship and equal rights.

days.guide: Compare Grant, Lee and Davis on a character chart.

questions.q: Give one strength of Grant as a general.
questions.a: Persistence and aggressiveness — he kept attacking and coordinated a war of attrition using Union resources.

days.guide: Compare a Union and a Confederate soldier's reasons for fighting.

questions.q: Name a common reason Union soldiers gave for fighting.
questions.a: To preserve the Union (and, for many, to end slavery).

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: About how many Black soldiers served in the U.S. Colored Troops?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Emancipation Proclamation (issued January 1, 1863) — freed enslaved people in Confederate-held areas, as a military measure under the president's war powers; exempted border states and Union-occupied areas such as Tennessee and parts of Louisiana and Virginia; allowed Black men to enlist; changed war aims to include ending slavery and discouraged Britain and France from aiding the Confederacy; 'contraband' — Union term for people who escaped to Union lines; 54th Massachusetts — famous Black regiment, assault on Fort Wagner (July 1863); Gooding protested being paid $10 a month (minus $3 for clothing) versus $13 for white privates — Congress equalized pay in 1864; Grant — persistent Union general who won at Vicksburg; Lee — Confederate commander of the Army of Northern Virginia; Davis — Confederate president. Soldier comparison: Union soldiers often cited preserving the Union (and increasingly ending slavery); Confederates often cited defending home, independence and slavery.

weeks.prep: Maps of Gettysburg and Vicksburg (1863); Gettysburg Address text (November 19, 1863); readings on Clara Barton and the New York draft riots (July 1863); Brady and Gardner photographs.
misconceptions: Thinking photographs were taken during combat. Long exposure times meant photos showed camps, portraits and aftermath; some (like Gardner's 'Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter') were staged.
Thinking the Gettysburg Address was a long speech. It was about 270 words and took about two minutes.

days.guide: Map both 1863 campaigns; explain their effect.

questions.q: Why were Gettysburg and Vicksburg turning points?
questions.a: Gettysburg ended Lee's last major invasion of the North; Vicksburg gave the Union control of the Mississippi River, splitting the Confederacy in two.

questions.q: When did Vicksburg surrender?

days.guide: Close-read the Gettysburg Address; connect to the Declaration.

questions.q: What year does 'four score and seven years ago' refer to?
questions.a: 1776 (87 years before 1863) — the Declaration of Independence.

questions.q: What did Lincoln mean by 'a new birth of freedom'?
questions.a: The war would renew the nation's commitment to the Declaration's ideal of equality, now including ending slavery.

days.guide: Read about Clara Barton and the draft riots; compare civilian hardships.

questions.q: Why did the New York draft riots break out?
questions.a: Anger at the draft, especially the $300 fee that let wealthier men avoid service, mixed with racism; rioters attacked Black New Yorkers.

questions.q: What hardship did Southern civilians face?
questions.a: Food shortages, high inflation, the Union blockade and bread riots.

days.guide: Analyze Brady and Gardner photographs; list new technologies.

questions.q: How did battlefield photographs change public views of war?
questions.a: They showed the dead on battlefields to civilians for the first time, making the war's cost real.

questions.q: Name two new military technologies.
questions.a: Rifled muskets with Minié balls, ironclad warships, telegraph, railroads, observation balloons.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: Who was Clara Barton?
questions.a: A Civil War nurse who later founded the American Red Cross.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Gettysburg (July 1–3, 1863) — Lee's invasion of the North defeated (Pickett's Charge failed); Vicksburg surrendered to Grant on July 4, 1863, giving the Union control of the Mississippi and splitting the Confederacy; Gettysburg Address — 'Four score and seven years ago' (87 years earlier = 1776, linking to the Declaration), 'a new birth of freedom', 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'; home fronts — Northern draft (1863 Enrollment Act; $300 commutation fee) sparked New York draft riots in which mobs attacked Black residents and burned the Colored Orphan Asylum; Southern shortages, inflation and bread riots (Richmond, 1863); Clara Barton nursed soldiers ('Angel of the Battlefield') and later founded the American Red Cross (1881); new technology — rifled muskets and Minié balls, ironclads (Monitor vs Virginia, March 1862), telegraph, railroads, photography.

weeks.prep: Map of Sherman's March; Lincoln's Second Inaugural Address (March 4, 1865); accounts of Appomattox (April 9, 1865) including Grant's terms; casualty statistics (traditional estimate about 620,000 deaths; recent research about 750,000). Write the unit 8 test.
misconceptions: Thinking the war ended the moment Lee surrendered. Other Confederate forces surrendered over the following weeks.
Believing Lincoln planned harsh punishment for the South. His Second Inaugural called for 'malice toward none' and binding up the nation's wounds.

days.guide: Map Sherman's march; debate total war.

questions.q: What is total war?
questions.a: Warfare aimed at destroying the enemy's ability and will to fight, including civilian resources like farms, railroads and supplies.

questions.q: What did Sherman's March accomplish?
questions.a: It destroyed Confederate resources in Georgia, captured Savannah (December 1864) and undermined Southern morale.

days.guide: Read the Second Inaugural; analyze 'with malice toward none.'

questions.q: What did Lincoln mean by 'with malice toward none, with charity for all'?
questions.a: The nation should reunite without revenge, healing and caring for all who suffered.

questions.q: What did Lincoln say was the cause of the war?
questions.a: Slavery — enslaved people were 'somehow the cause of the war.'

days.guide: Read accounts of Appomattox and Grant's terms.

questions.q: What terms did Grant offer Lee's army?
questions.a: Soldiers could go home on parole and not be prosecuted, officers kept sidearms, men kept their horses, and the Union gave rations to the hungry Confederates.

days.guide: Graph casualties; chart consequences.

questions.q: Name one political and one economic consequence.
questions.a: Political: Union preserved, slavery abolished, stronger federal government. Economic: Southern economy devastated; Northern industry expanded.

days.guide: Give the unit 8 test.

questions.q: Who assassinated Lincoln and when?
questions.a: John Wilkes Booth, on April 14, 1865, at Ford's Theatre (Lincoln died April 15).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test (suggested): Fort Sumter; border states; Anaconda Plan; Bull Run; Antietam; Emancipation Proclamation; USCT and 54th Massachusetts; Gettysburg and Vicksburg; Gettysburg Address; draft riots; Sherman's March to the Sea (November–December 1864, Atlanta to Savannah, total war destroying railroads, farms and supplies); Second Inaugural ('With malice toward none, with charity for all'); Appomattox Court House — Lee surrendered to Grant April 9, 1865; terms let Confederate soldiers go home on parole, officers keep sidearms, men keep horses, and Grant provided rations; Lincoln assassinated by John Wilkes Booth April 14, 1865 (died April 15); consequences — slavery ended (13th Amendment), Union preserved, federal power grew, South's economy devastated, about 620,000–750,000 dead.

weeks.prep: 13th Amendment text; Mississippi Black Codes (1865) excerpt; summaries of the Ten Percent Plan, Johnson's plan, the Radical Republican plan, the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and Johnson's impeachment.
misconceptions: Thinking the 13th Amendment ended all forced labor. Its exception 'as a punishment for crime' allowed convict leasing that re-enslaved many Black Southerners.
Believing Johnson was removed from office. The House impeached him (1868), but the Senate acquitted him by one vote.

days.guide: Chart the three plans.

questions.q: What did the Ten Percent Plan require?
questions.a: 10% of a state's 1860 voters to take a loyalty oath and accept the end of slavery before forming a new government.

questions.q: What did Radical Republicans want?
questions.a: Congressional control, punishment of Confederate leaders, and protection of freedpeople's civil and voting rights.

days.guide: Read the 13th Amendment; discuss the exception clause.

questions.q: What does the 13th Amendment's exception allow?
questions.a: Involuntary servitude 'as a punishment for crime' — used to justify convict leasing and forced prison labor.

days.guide: Read the Mississippi Black Codes; explain restrictions.

questions.q: Give two ways Black Codes restricted freedpeople.
questions.a: Required yearly labor contracts, arrested unemployed people as 'vagrants' and leased them out, barred renting land in some areas, forced apprenticeships of children, limited gun ownership.

days.guide: Explain the Civil Rights Act of 1866, Johnson's vetoes and impeachment.

questions.q: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1866 do?
questions.a: Declared all persons born in the U.S. citizens (except untaxed Native Americans) with equal rights to make contracts, own property and sue; Congress passed it over Johnson's veto.

questions.q: Why was Johnson impeached?
questions.a: Officially for violating the Tenure of Office Act by firing Secretary of War Stanton; really over his clash with Congress on Reconstruction.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What was the result of Johnson's Senate trial?
questions.a: Acquitted by one vote (35–19, one short of two-thirds).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Ten Percent Plan (Lincoln, 1863) — a state could rejoin when 10% of 1860 voters swore loyalty and accepted emancipation; Johnson's plan — pardons for most Confederates who swore loyalty, states had to ratify the 13th Amendment and repudiate secession and Confederate debts; allowed former Confederates back into power; Radical Republicans (Thaddeus Stevens, Charles Sumner) — Congress should control Reconstruction, protect freedpeople's rights, Reconstruction Acts (1867) divided the South into five military districts and required states to ratify the 14th Amendment and allow Black male suffrage; 13th Amendment (ratified December 1865) abolished slavery 'except as a punishment for crime'; Mississippi Black Codes — required annual labor contracts, punished 'vagrancy', limited land rental, allowed apprenticing Black children; Civil Rights Act of 1866 — declared citizenship and equal legal rights, passed over Johnson's veto; impeachment — for violating the Tenure of Office Act (firing Stanton); acquitted 35–19, one vote short.

weeks.prep: Freedmen's Bureau letters (National Archives 'Freedmen's Bureau records'); 14th and 15th Amendment texts; biographies of Hiram Revels and Robert Smalls; readings on the Exodusters and Buffalo Soldiers.
misconceptions: Thinking the 15th Amendment gave everyone the vote. It barred denial based on race, color or previous servitude, but not sex; women were excluded, and states later used poll taxes and literacy tests.
Believing freedpeople received land. 'Forty acres and a mule' (Sherman's Field Order No. 15) was largely reversed by Johnson; most became sharecroppers.

days.guide: Read letters to the Freedmen's Bureau.

questions.q: What did freedpeople most often seek from the Bureau?
questions.a: Reuniting with family members sold away, schools for their children, and fair wages and contracts.

days.guide: Paraphrase the 14th and 15th Amendments; who was protected and left out.

questions.q: Paraphrase the 14th Amendment's equal protection clause.
questions.a: States must treat all people equally under the law.

questions.q: Who was left out of the 15th Amendment?
questions.a: Women of all races; also most Native Americans and Asian immigrants could not vote because they were not citizens.

days.guide: Research Revels and Smalls; write biography cards.

questions.q: What 'first' did Hiram Revels achieve?
questions.a: First African American U.S. senator (1870, Mississippi).

questions.q: How did Robert Smalls gain freedom?
questions.a: In 1862 he piloted the Confederate ship Planter out of Charleston Harbor and delivered it to the Union navy with his family and others aboard.

days.guide: Read about the Exodusters and Buffalo Soldiers; list push and pull factors.

questions.q: Give one push and one pull factor for the Exodusters.
questions.a: Push: violence and debt in the South after Reconstruction; pull: cheap land and freedom in Kansas.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What was sharecropping?
questions.a: A system where families farmed a landowner's land in exchange for a share of the crop, often leaving them in debt.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Freedmen's Bureau (1865) — provided food, medical care, schools (helped found Howard, Fisk and others), negotiated labor contracts, helped reunite families; 14th Amendment (1868) — all persons born or naturalized in the U.S. are citizens; no state may deny due process or equal protection; 15th Amendment (1870) — right to vote can't be denied because of race, color or previous condition of servitude; left out women, most Native Americans (not citizens until 1924), Chinese immigrants (barred from naturalization); sharecropping — farming land for a share of the crop, often trapped in debt; Hiram Revels — first Black U.S. senator (Mississippi, 1870); Robert Smalls — escaped slavery by commandeering the Confederate ship Planter (1862), later congressman from South Carolina; Exodusters — about 6,000 or more Black Southerners who moved to Kansas in 1879 (push: violence, sharecropping debt, end of Reconstruction; pull: land, freedom); Buffalo Soldiers — Black regiments (9th and 10th Cavalry, 24th and 25th Infantry) formed 1866 serving in the West.

weeks.prep: Parent preview: congressional testimony on Klan violence is disturbing. Thomas Nast cartoons; 1871 testimony excerpts; information on the 1876 election; examples of Jim Crow laws; voter registration data (e.g., Louisiana registered Black voters fell from about 130,000 in 1896 to about 1,300 in 1904). Prepare at least 4 DBQ documents. Write the unit 9 test.
misconceptions: Thinking Reconstruction achieved nothing. It produced the 13th–15th Amendments, Black officeholders, public schools and churches, even though many gains were rolled back.
Thinking Jim Crow laws existed only in the South. Segregation and discrimination existed nationwide, though Southern laws were most systematic.

days.guide: Read 1871 Klan testimony; explain the Enforcement Acts.

questions.q: What was the purpose of the KKK during Reconstruction?
questions.a: To restore white supremacy by terrorizing Black people and white Republicans, especially to stop Black voting.

questions.q: What did the Enforcement Acts do?
questions.a: Made it a federal crime to interfere with voting and allowed the president to use troops and suspend habeas corpus against the Klan.

days.guide: Explain the 1876 election and Compromise of 1877.

questions.q: What did Democrats get in the Compromise of 1877?
questions.a: The withdrawal of federal troops from the South, ending Reconstruction (Republicans got Hayes as president).

days.guide: Analyze Jim Crow laws, poll taxes and literacy tests with registration data.

questions.q: How did poll taxes and literacy tests limit Black voting without naming race?
questions.a: Many Black citizens were poor or denied schooling, and white officials applied tests unfairly; grandfather clauses exempted most whites.

questions.q: What did Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) decide?
questions.a: Segregation was constitutional if facilities were 'separate but equal.'

days.guide: Write the DBQ essay: Was Reconstruction a success or failure?

questions.q: Give one piece of evidence for 'success.'
questions.a: The 14th and 15th Amendments, Black officeholders like Revels, public schools and new Black colleges.

questions.q: Give one piece of evidence for 'failure.'
questions.a: Klan violence, Black Codes, sharecropping debt, withdrawal of troops in 1877 and Jim Crow disenfranchisement.

days.guide: Give the unit 9 test.

questions.q: What ended Reconstruction?
questions.a: The Compromise of 1877 and the withdrawal of federal troops from the South.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test (suggested): Reconstruction plans; 13th–15th Amendments; Black Codes; Freedmen's Bureau; Revels and Smalls; KKK founded 1865–66, used terror to stop Black voting and Republican government; Enforcement Acts (1870–71, including the Ku Klux Klan Act) let the federal government prosecute Klan violence; Compromise of 1877 — disputed 1876 election (Tilden won the popular vote; 20 electoral votes disputed in Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina and Oregon) resolved by giving Hayes the presidency in exchange for withdrawing federal troops from the South, ending Reconstruction; Jim Crow — segregation laws, poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses; Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) 'separate but equal.' DBQ essay rubric (1–4): thesis taking a position (success, failure, or mixed), uses 4+ documents accurately, outside knowledge, sourcing, counterargument, organization.

weeks.prep: Railroad and land-grant maps; readings on Chinese workers (Central Pacific) and Irish workers (Union Pacific); Homestead Act (1862) text; Chief Joseph's surrender speech (1877); accounts of Little Bighorn (1876) and Wounded Knee (1890) from Lakota and Army perspectives; Dawes Act summary; Carlisle Indian School before-and-after photos (e.g., Tom Torlino). Parent preview: violence and cultural loss.
misconceptions: Thinking Little Bighorn was a 'massacre' of soldiers. It was a battle in which Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors defeated Custer's 7th Cavalry; Wounded Knee (1890) was the massacre of mostly unarmed Lakota, including women and children.

Believing the Dawes Act helped Native Americans by giving them land. It broke up communal reservation land; 'surplus' land was sold to settlers, and Native landholdings fell from about 138 million acres (1887) to about 48 million (1934).

days.guide: Read about railroad workers; map the 1869 route.

questions.q: Where did the two railroads meet, and when?
questions.a: Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869.

questions.q: What role did Chinese workers play?
questions.a: They made up most of the Central Pacific's workforce, blasting tunnels through the Sierra Nevada in dangerous conditions for less pay than white workers.

days.guide: Read the Homestead Act; analyze settlement maps.

questions.q: What did the Homestead Act offer?
questions.a: 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and farmed it for five years (paying a small filing fee).

days.guide: Read Chief Joseph's speech and multiple-perspective accounts of Little Bighorn and Wounded Knee.

questions.q: Quote Chief Joseph's famous line.
questions.a: 'From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever.'

questions.q: Why is Wounded Knee called a massacre?
questions.a: U.S. soldiers killed about 250–300 Lakota, many unarmed women and children, while disarming them.

days.guide: Explain allotment; analyze Carlisle photographs.

questions.q: What was the goal of the Dawes Act?
questions.a: To assimilate Native Americans by breaking up tribal land into individual farms; it led to massive loss of Native land.

questions.q: What do before-and-after Carlisle photos show?
questions.a: Students' traditional clothing and long hair replaced with uniforms and short hair — the schools' goal of erasing Native culture.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What was the transcontinental railroad's effect on Plains nations?
questions.a: It brought settlers and hunters who destroyed the bison herds, splitting and undermining Plains nations' way of life.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Pacific Railway Act (1862); Central Pacific built east from Sacramento with thousands of Chinese workers (most of its workforce), who did dangerous Sierra Nevada tunneling for lower pay; Union Pacific built west from Omaha with many Irish workers and Civil War veterans; joined with the golden spike at Promontory Summit, Utah, May 10, 1869; Homestead Act — 160 acres free to citizens or intending citizens (21+ or heads of household, including women and later freedpeople) who lived on and improved it for 5 years; Little Bighorn (June 1876) — Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse's warriors defeated Custer; Nez Perce — Chief Joseph surrendered October 1877 ('I will fight no more forever'); Wounded Knee (December 29, 1890) — U.S. troops killed about 250–300 Lakota; Dawes Act (1887) — allotted 160 acres to family heads, sold surplus land, aimed at assimilation; boarding schools (Carlisle 1879, Richard Pratt: 'Kill the Indian… save the man') forbade Native languages and cultures.

weeks.prep: Carnegie's 'The Gospel of Wealth' (1889) excerpt; political cartoons of Rockefeller (e.g., Standard Oil as an octopus, 1904); readings on Edison, Bell, Lewis Latimer and the Wright brothers.
misconceptions: Mixing up vertical and horizontal integration. Vertical = owning every stage of production (Carnegie: mines, railroads, mills); horizontal = buying up competitors in one stage (Rockefeller: refineries).
Thinking Edison invented everything alone. He ran a research lab at Menlo Park with teams; Latimer, for example, improved the carbon filament.

days.guide: Diagram vertical and horizontal integration.

questions.q: Define vertical integration with Carnegie's example.
questions.a: Controlling all stages of production — Carnegie owned iron ore mines, coal mines, railroads/ships and steel mills.

questions.q: Define horizontal integration with Rockefeller's example.
questions.a: Buying or merging with competitors in the same business — Standard Oil absorbed rival refineries.

days.guide: Read the Gospel of Wealth and two cartoons; write an argument paragraph.

questions.q: What did Carnegie believe the wealthy should do with their money?
questions.a: Give it away during their lives for the public good (libraries, universities); 'The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.'

questions.q: What does a cartoon showing Standard Oil as an octopus suggest?
questions.a: That the company's tentacles strangled competitors, government and the public — a monopoly abusing power.

days.guide: Chart inventors and how each changed daily life.

questions.q: How did Lewis Latimer contribute to electric lighting?
questions.a: He patented an improved process for making long-lasting carbon filaments, making bulbs cheaper and more practical.

questions.q: When and where did the Wright brothers first fly?
questions.a: December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk (Kill Devil Hills), North Carolina.

days.guide: Explain tariffs, land grants and subsidies.

questions.q: How did protective tariffs help American industry?
questions.a: They taxed imported goods, making foreign products more expensive and protecting U.S. manufacturers from competition.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What is philanthropy?
questions.a: Giving money or effort to promote the welfare of others, such as funding libraries or schools.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: monopoly — one company controls an industry; trust — combination of companies controlled by one board (Standard Oil Trust, 1882; refined about 90% of U.S. oil by 1880); Carnegie Steel — vertical integration, Bessemer process; Gospel of Wealth — the rich have a duty to give their fortunes away for public good during their lifetime ('The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced'); Carnegie funded about 2,500 libraries; 'robber baron' (exploited workers and crushed competitors) vs 'captain of industry' (built the economy, philanthropy); inventors — Bell telephone (1876), Edison phonograph (1877) and practical light bulb (1879), Latimer improved the carbon filament (1881) and drafted Bell's patent drawings, Wright brothers first powered flight at Kitty Hawk (December 17, 1903); government aid — protective tariffs, railroad land grants, subsidies, laissez-faire regulation. Argument paragraph rubric: clear claim, two pieces of evidence, counterclaim.

weeks.prep: Immigration data by region 1870–1910; 'The New Colossus' (Emma Lazarus, 1883); translated Angel Island poems; Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) summary; Jacob Riis photographs from 'How the Other Half Lives' (1890); John Muir Yosemite excerpts.
misconceptions: Thinking Ellis Island and Angel Island were similar. Ellis Island (opened 1892) processed most European immigrants in hours; Angel Island (1910–1940) detained many Chinese immigrants for weeks or months under exclusion laws.

Thinking 'new immigrants' came from the same places as earlier ones. After about 1880 most came from Southern and Eastern Europe (Italy, Russia, Austria-Hungary, Poland), not Northern and Western Europe.

days.guide: Graph immigration by region 1870–1910; read 'The New Colossus.'

questions.q: What shift does the graph show?
questions.a: Immigration shifted from Northern/Western Europe to Southern/Eastern Europe after about 1880.

questions.q: What image of America does 'The New Colossus' present?
questions.a: A welcoming 'Mother of Exiles' offering refuge to the poor and oppressed.

days.guide: Read Angel Island poems and the Chinese Exclusion Act; compare with Ellis Island.

questions.q: What did the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) do?
questions.a: Banned Chinese laborers from immigrating and barred Chinese immigrants from becoming citizens.

questions.q: What feelings do Angel Island poems express?
questions.a: Frustration, loneliness, humiliation and anger at being detained and treated unjustly.

days.guide: Analyze Riis photographs; describe urban conditions.

questions.q: Describe tenement conditions in Riis's photos.
questions.a: Overcrowded, dark, poorly ventilated rooms; families and workers in tiny spaces; little sanitation; children working or sleeping on streets.

questions.q: What was Riis's purpose?
questions.a: To shock middle-class readers into supporting housing reform.

days.guide: Read Muir; explain the start of conservation.

questions.q: What did John Muir advocate?
questions.a: Preserving wilderness like Yosemite for its own sake and public enjoyment; he co-founded the Sierra Club.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: Why did many immigrants settle in cities?
questions.a: Factory jobs, cheap (tenement) housing and existing ethnic communities.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 'old' immigrants (before 1880) mostly from Northern/Western Europe (Ireland, Germany, Britain, Scandinavia); 'new' immigrants mostly from Southern/Eastern Europe, often Catholic, Orthodox or Jewish; Ellis Island (New York Harbor, 1892); Angel Island (San Francisco Bay, 1910); Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) — banned Chinese laborers for 10 years, extended and made permanent, repealed 1943 — first major law barring a group by nationality; 'The New Colossus' — 'Give me your tired, your poor, / Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free' (on the Statue of Liberty's pedestal); tenements — crowded, poorly lit and ventilated apartment buildings; Riis exposed conditions with flash photography; assimilation — adopting the new culture; nativism — opposition to immigrants; John Muir — naturalist who helped make Yosemite a national park (1890) and founded the Sierra Club (1892).

weeks.prep: Lewis Hine child labor photographs (Library of Congress, National Child Labor Committee collection); readings on Gompers and the AFL, the Haymarket Affair (1886) and the Pullman Strike (1894); Omaha Platform (1892) excerpts; Bryan's 'Cross of Gold' (1896) excerpts.
misconceptions: Thinking strikes usually succeeded. Haymarket and Pullman ended in defeat for workers; government often sided with employers using courts and troops.
Thinking the silver debate was about jewelry. 'Free silver' meant coining silver to expand the money supply, raising prices and helping indebted farmers.

days.guide: Analyze 3 Hine photographs with see-think-wonder; write captions.

questions.q: What purpose did Lewis Hine's photographs serve?
questions.a: To document child labor and persuade the public and lawmakers to pass child labor laws.

days.guide: Read about Gompers/AFL; compare Haymarket and Pullman.

questions.q: What were the AFL's goals?
questions.a: Higher wages, shorter hours and better conditions for skilled workers through collective bargaining.

questions.q: How did the Pullman Strike end?
questions.a: The federal government obtained a court injunction and sent troops; the strike collapsed and Debs was jailed.

days.guide: Explain the Grange; read the Omaha Platform.

questions.q: Why were farmers angry in the late 1800s?
questions.a: Falling crop prices, high railroad shipping rates, debt and tight money (deflation).

questions.q: Name two Omaha Platform demands that later became law.
questions.a: Graduated income tax (16th Amendment) and direct election of senators (17th Amendment); also the secret ballot and 8-hour day.

days.guide: Read Bryan's 'Cross of Gold'; explain the silver debate.

questions.q: What did 'free silver' supporters want?
questions.a: Unlimited coinage of silver (at 16 to 1 with gold) to increase the money supply, raise prices and ease farmers' debts.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What is collective bargaining?
questions.a: Workers negotiating as a group with employers over wages and conditions.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: child labor — children worked long hours in mills, mines and factories for low pay; Hine's photos built support for child-labor laws; labor unions use collective bargaining and strikes; AFL (1886, Samuel Gompers) organized skilled workers by craft for 'bread-and-butter' goals — higher wages, shorter hours (8-hour day), safer conditions; Haymarket (Chicago, May 1886) — bomb at a labor rally killed police; anarchists convicted; public turned against unions (Knights of Labor declined); Pullman Strike (1894) — Pullman cut wages without cutting company-town rents; Eugene Debs's American Railway Union boycotted Pullman cars; federal injunction and troops broke the strike; laissez-faire — government stays out of business; Grange (1867) — farmers' cooperatives, pushed for railroad regulation (Granger laws); Populist Omaha Platform — free coinage of silver, graduated income tax, government ownership of railroads and telegraphs, direct election of senators, secret ballot, 8-hour day; Bryan's 'Cross of Gold' (1896) — 'You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold'; Bryan lost to McKinley.

weeks.prep: Library books; Library of Congress and Calisphere sources; poster board or slides; citation format (author/creator, title, date, source/URL). Write the unit 10 test.
misconceptions: Using mainly secondary sources. The exhibit should center on at least 3 primary sources with captions that source them.
Writing a topic, not a thesis. A thesis makes an arguable claim about impact.

days.guide: Choose a topic; locate 3 primary sources.

questions.q: What is the difference between a primary and a secondary source?
questions.a: A primary source was created at the time by someone involved (letter, photo, law); a secondary source analyzes events later (textbook, article).

days.guide: Take cited notes; write a thesis.

questions.q: Turn 'Jacob Riis' into a thesis.
questions.a: Example: 'Jacob Riis's photographs exposed tenement conditions and pushed New York to pass housing reforms, showing the power of photography to drive change.'

days.guide: Build the exhibit with captions.

questions.q: What should a caption include?
questions.a: Creator, date, what the source shows and why it matters to the thesis.

days.guide: Present to family; answer questions.

questions.q: How does your topic connect to the Industrial Age?
questions.a: Open answer — must link to industrialization, immigration, labor or business with evidence.

days.guide: Give the unit 10 test.

questions.q: What was the significance of the Chinese Exclusion Act?
questions.a: It was the first U.S. law to ban immigration based on nationality.

weeks.assessment_key: Exhibit rubric (1–4 each): thesis (arguable claim about the topic's impact on American life), 3+ primary sources correctly identified and cited, captions that source and explain each, historical accuracy and context, presentation and answers to questions. Unit 10 test (suggested): transcontinental railroad, Homestead Act, Plains wars, Dawes Act, boarding schools, vertical/horizontal integration, Gospel of Wealth, inventors, new immigration, Ellis/Angel Island, Chinese Exclusion Act, tenements and Riis, conservation, child labor, AFL, Haymarket, Pullman, Grange, Populists, Cross of Gold.

weeks.prep: Notebook timeline; all course documents. Write the final exam in two parts (Revolution–antebellum; Civil War–Industrial America).
misconceptions: Describing the Declaration's promise as fulfilled by 1900. Many groups gained rights, but women, Black Americans, Native Americans and Asian immigrants still faced major barriers.
Listing events without explaining significance. Each turning point should explain why it changed the course of history.

days.guide: Complete the timeline; mark 10 turning points with explanations.

questions.q: Why is 1863 a turning point?
questions.a: The Emancipation Proclamation made ending slavery a war aim, and Gettysburg and Vicksburg turned the war in the Union's favor.

days.guide: Write the essential question essay.

questions.q: Give one example of progress and one setback in fulfilling the Declaration.
questions.a: Progress: the 13th–15th Amendments; setback: Jim Crow laws and disenfranchisement after 1877 (or Indian Removal, Chinese Exclusion).

days.guide: Give final exam part 1.

questions.q: What compromise created the House and Senate structure?
questions.a: The Great (Connecticut) Compromise.

days.guide: Give final exam part 2.

questions.q: What did the 14th Amendment guarantee?
questions.a: Citizenship for all born or naturalized in the U.S., due process and equal protection of the laws.

days.guide: Write the reflection on the most important person and event.

questions.q: What makes a person or event 'most important'?
questions.a: Its scale of impact, how long its effects lasted and how many people it affected — answer should justify with evidence.

weeks.assessment_key: Essential question essay rubric (1–4): thesis on how Americans struggled to fulfill 'all men are created equal' and unalienable rights (e.g., expanding but incomplete); evidence across the period — Revolution and Constitution's compromises with slavery, Bill of Rights, abolitionists (Douglass, Garrison, Tubman), Seneca Falls, Indian Removal and Worcester, Civil War and Emancipation, 13th–15th Amendments, Reconstruction's rollback and Jim Crow, Chinese Exclusion, labor and Populist movements; analysis of progress and setbacks; organization and conventions. Final exam: part 1 and part 2 drawn from unit tests; 80%+ proficient. Suggested 10 turning points: 1776 Declaration, 1787 Constitution, 1791 Bill of Rights, 1803 Louisiana Purchase/Marbury, 1830 Indian Removal Act, 1848 Mexican Cession/Seneca Falls, 1857 Dred Scott, 1861 Fort Sumter, 1863 Emancipation/Gettysburg, 1865–1870 Reconstruction Amendments, 1869 transcontinental railroad, 1877 end of Reconstruction, 1882 Chinese Exclusion.

MATH.overview: Mathematics 8 follows the Illustrative Mathematics sequence: transformations and similarity, linear relationships, equations and systems, functions and volume, data, exponents, and the Pythagorean theorem. Teach each day by modeling one example, doing one together, then letting the child work independently while you check the first few problems. Emphasize explaining reasoning in words and checking answers by substitution or estimation, and use Desmos to verify graphs.

weeks.prep: Print or copy a 15-problem Grade 7 readiness check (proportions, integers, expressions). Gather tracing paper, graph paper, a protractor, a ruler and a cardboard cutout (e.g., an L-shape or flag) that is not symmetric so flips are visible.
misconceptions: Confusing rotation and reflection. Correct it by tracing the figure: if you must flip the tracing paper over to match, it is a reflection; if you only turn it, it is a rotation.
Describing moves vaguely ('it moved over'). Require precise language: direction and distance for translations, center/angle/direction for rotations, and the line for reflections.

days.guide: Give the readiness check untimed and note which skills (proportions, integer operations, expressions) need review in later warm-ups. Then hand the child the cutout on tracing paper and ask them to slide, turn and flip it, saying aloud exactly what each move did; model one precise sentence such as 'I turned it a quarter turn clockwise around its corner.'

questions.q: Solve 3/4 = x/20.

questions.a: 8 (−7 + 12 = 5, and subtracting −3 adds 3).

questions.q: You flip the cutout over so it faces the other way. Which move is that?
questions.a: A reflection (flip).

days.guide: Model translating a triangle: draw a directed segment (arrow) and move every vertex the same distance in the same direction, labeling A→A', B→B', C→C'. The child draws 4 images; check that every vertex moved by the same arrow and that the image is the same shape facing the same way.

questions.q: Point A(2, 3) is translated 4 units right and 5 units down. What are the coordinates of A'?
Does a translation change which way a figure faces?
questions.a: No. A translation slides every point the same distance and direction, so orientation and size stay the same.

days.guide: Show how to pin tracing paper at the center of rotation with a pencil tip, trace the figure, and turn it 90°, 180° or 270°, using a protractor or the grid corners to measure. Have the child record center, angle and direction (clockwise/counterclockwise) for each; check that a vertex's distance from the center is unchanged.

questions.q: Rotate the point (3, 1) 90° clockwise about the origin.
Is a 270° clockwise rotation the same as some counterclockwise rotation?
questions.a: Yes — 270° clockwise is the same as 90° counterclockwise.

days.guide: Model reflecting across a vertical line by counting each vertex's distance to the line and placing the image the same distance on the other side; repeat for a horizontal line and the diagonal y = x (fold the paper on the line to check). The child completes the 8 mixed practice problems and names each move.

questions.q: Reflect (4, −2) across the x-axis.
Reflect (2, 5) across the line y = x.
questions.a: (5, 2) — the coordinates swap.

questions.q: A reflected point is 3 units left of the mirror line. Where is its image?
questions.a: 3 units right of the line, on a perpendicular to it.

days.guide: Give the 6-item quiz (see assessment key) without help, then have the child correct errors in the notebook in a different color, writing why the original was wrong. Review & check day: have the child redo any missed problem in the notebook and explain the error in one sentence.

questions.q: Describe precisely the move that takes (1, 2) to (−1, −2).
questions.a: A rotation of 180° about the origin (equivalently, a reflection across the x-axis followed by one across the y-axis).

weeks.assessment_key: Use these 6 items on a grid with triangle A(1,2), B(4,2), C(1,4): 1) Translate 3 left, 2 up → A'(-2,4), B'(1,4), C'(-2,6). 2) Reflect over the x-axis → (1,-2),(4,-2),(1,-4). 3) Reflect over the y-axis → (-1,2),(-4,2),(-1,4). 4) Rotate 180° about the origin → (-1,-2),(-4,-2),(-1,-4). 5) Rotate 90° counterclockwise about the origin → (-2,1),(-2,4),(-4,1). 6) Identify a pictured move and describe it precisely (e.g., 'a reflection across the line y = x'). Each item: 1 point for correct image, 1 point for a precise description (type + direction/distance, center/angle/direction, or line). 80% = 10/12.

weeks.prep: Gather graph paper, tracing paper, ruler, protractor; open GeoGebra (free at geogebra.org) and practice drawing a line and using the Rotate tool yourself first.
misconceptions: Mixing up the rotation rules. Have the child test with one point, e.g., (2, 0) rotated 90° counterclockwise must land on the positive y-axis at (0, 2), so the rule is (x, y) → (−y, x).
Writing a translation rule with the wrong sign (moving left as +). Remind: right/up add, left/down subtract.

days.guide: Have the child measure all sides and angles of a quadrilateral, then perform a translation, a rotation and a reflection and measure the images. Ask them to write a conclusion; guide them to 'side lengths and angle measures stay the same.'

questions.q: A triangle has sides 3, 4 and 5 cm and a 90° angle. After a reflection then a rotation, what are the image's measures?
questions.a: The same: sides 3, 4, 5 cm and a 90° angle, because rigid motions preserve lengths and angles.

days.guide: In GeoGebra draw two parallel lines and a point not on them; rotate both lines 180° about the point. Ask the child to explain why the images are parallel to the originals and to each other.

questions.q: Why is a line's image under a 180° rotation parallel to the original line?
questions.a: A 180° rotation sends every direction to its exact opposite, so the image line runs in the same direction (same slope) as the original; and because rigid motions keep lines that never meet from meeting, parallel lines stay parallel.

days.guide: Model one translation on the coordinate plane and build a before/after table of coordinates; ask what was added to x and to y. The child writes the rule (x, y) → (x + a, y + b) for 6 examples.

questions.q: Apply (x, y) → (x − 3, y + 2) to the point (5, 1).
A point moves from (−1, 4) to (3, 0). Write the rule.

days.guide: Have the child plot a triangle, reflect/rotate it with tracing paper, then list original and image coordinates side by side to discover each rule. Summarize on an index card: x-axis (x, −y); y-axis (−x, y); 90° CCW (−y, x); 90° CW (y, −x); 180° (−x, −y).

questions.q: Rotate (2, −5) 90° counterclockwise about the origin.
Reflect (−3, 7) over the y-axis.

days.guide: Child completes the 10-problem worksheet, then is given before-and-after coordinate lists and names the rule. Review & check day: have the child redo any missed problem in the notebook and explain the error in one sentence.

questions.q: Before: (1, 2), (3, 4). After: (−1, 2), (−3, 4). Which transformation?
questions.a: A reflection over the y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y).

weeks.assessment_key: Four rules (1 point each): 1) translation 5 left, 1 up: (x, y) → (x − 5, y + 1); 2) reflection over the x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y); 3) rotation 180° about origin: (x, y) → (−x, −y); 4) rotation 90° counterclockwise about origin: (x, y) → (−y, x). Justification (2 points): rigid motions preserve side lengths, angle measures and parallelism, so the image is congruent to the original; full credit names at least lengths and angles.

weeks.prep: Gather tracing paper, graph paper, cardstock, scissors. Cut 4–6 quadrilaterals from cardstock in advance, including two that are congruent but mirror images and one pair that is close but not congruent.
misconceptions: Saying figures are congruent because they 'look the same.' Require a sequence of rigid motions that maps one exactly onto the other.
Thinking a flipped (mirror-image) figure is not congruent. A reflection is a rigid motion, so mirror images are congruent.

days.guide: Show 8 pairs of figures; for each, the child decides congruent or not and must justify with a move ('a 90° rotation maps one onto the other') or a measurement that breaks congruence.
