days.guide: Stork stand: hands on hips, one foot on the inside of the other knee, eyes closed, time until balance lost. Ruler drop: partner holds the ruler at 0 between the child's thumb and finger and drops without warning; record cm; reaction time t = √(2d ÷ 980) seconds.

questions.q: If the ruler falls 15 cm, what is the reaction time?

days.guide: The child charts all six components and identifies the strongest and weakest.

questions.q: Which component is the weakest, and which drill would improve it?
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., low agility → ladder and cone-cutting drills 2–3 times per week.

weeks.assessment_key: Profile chart: proficient (4) = all six components with a score, test name and unit; strongest and weakest identified with a sport connection and one improvement drill; 3 = one component missing; 2 = scores without analysis; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Fitness journal, a goal sheet, and an optional step counter. Prepare a list of 12 reasons people exercise. Plan a 20-minute jog/walk interval route.
misconceptions: Relying only on outside rewards. Correct: intrinsic motivation (enjoyment, feeling good) keeps people active longer.
Setting a goal without a weekly action. Correct: each goal needs specific weekly steps.

days.guide: Sort reasons (fun, weight, prize, friends, stress relief, parent's request, trophies, feeling strong) into intrinsic vs. extrinsic; child picks top three motivators. Run a 20-minute jog/walk interval (e.g., 2 min jog/1 min walk).

questions.q: Is 'I run because I enjoy the feeling afterward' intrinsic or extrinsic?
questions.a: Intrinsic — the reward comes from the activity itself.

days.guide: The child names three barriers and a strategy for each, then does a 15-minute circuit (squats, push-ups, jumping jacks, plank, lunges; 40 s on/20 s off).

questions.q: Give a strategy for 'too much screen time.'
questions.a: Set an active break every 30 minutes, replace one show with a walk, or exercise during a show.

days.guide: The child writes two SMART goals with weekly action steps.

questions.q: Make this SMART: 'Get better at the PACER.'
questions.a: Example: 'Increase my PACER from 40 to 48 laps by week 19 by running intervals 3 days a week for 25 minutes.'

days.guide: Start a log of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) 4 days a week; do a 30-minute activity outside class.

questions.q: How can you tell activity is moderate vs. vigorous?
questions.a: Talk test: moderate — can talk but not sing; vigorous — can only say a few words without pausing for breath.

days.guide: Review goals together; parent signs. Play an active game.

questions.q: How many minutes of activity do teens need daily?
questions.a: At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity.

weeks.assessment_key: Signed SMART goal sheet: 1 pt each for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound per goal + weekly action steps + signature (proficient = both goals meet all criteria). Activity log: 4 entries with date, activity, minutes and intensity.

weeks.prep: Gather a tarp or old sheet, blindfold, cones, hula hoop, carpet squares or pool noodles. Recruit siblings, friends or co-op members (3+ people). Set boundaries and safety rules: walk only in blind maze, spotters ready.
misconceptions: Leaders talking over others. Correct: good teams listen to all ideas and test them.
Giving up after one failed attempt. Correct: plan, try, debrief, adjust.

days.guide: Group stands on a tarp and flips it without anyone stepping off; debrief: Who led? What worked?

questions.q: What strategy usually works for the tarp flip?
questions.a: Crowd onto one half, fold/roll the open half over, step onto the flipped side, and repeat — communicating each step.

days.guide: Guide a blindfolded partner through a cone maze with words only; switch roles.

questions.q: What makes verbal directions effective?
questions.a: Specific, short, calm cues with distances and directions ('Two small steps left, stop'), and checking that the partner understood.

days.guide: Helium hoop: everyone's fingertips under the hoop; lower it to the ground without losing contact. Try three strategies.

questions.q: Why does the hoop rise?
questions.a: Everyone pushes up slightly to keep contact, so combined upward pressure lifts it; the group must coordinate and slow down together.

days.guide: Cross a 10 m 'river' with four squares as a group; if anyone touches the 'water,' restart.

questions.q: What made your team successful or unsuccessful?
questions.a: Answers vary; strong answers name planning, roles, communication and encouragement.

days.guide: The child writes a debrief reflection.

questions.q: Name two communication behaviors that help a team.
questions.a: Listening to every idea, using encouraging words, clear instructions, checking for agreement, staying calm.

weeks.assessment_key: Debrief reflection rubric: 4 = describes at least two challenges with specific helpful and unhelpful behaviors, explains their effect on the group, and states one personal change; 3 = specific but one example; 2 = general ('we worked together'); 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Cones, balls, a lesson-plan template (warm-up, activity, rules, safety, cool-down). Arrange a group of family or friends for Thursday.
misconceptions: Explaining too long. Correct: explain in under a minute, demonstrate, then play and fix as you go.
Planning games that eliminate players. Correct: choose games where everyone stays active (re-entry rules).

days.guide: Discuss good coaches; list five leadership behaviors (clear instructions, encouragement, fairness, listening, modeling effort).

questions.q: Name three behaviors of a good team captain.
questions.a: Encourages teammates, communicates clearly, shows good sportsmanship, leads by example, includes everyone.

days.guide: Write a 20-minute plan with timing.

questions.q: What three parts should every session have?
questions.a: Warm-up, main activity, cool-down.

days.guide: Write two modifications (larger target, softer ball, walking rule, partner assistance, shorter distance).

questions.q: Give a modification for someone with limited mobility in a tag game.
questions.a: Let them tag with a pool noodle, use a smaller area, or give them a role like 'freer' who can unfreeze players while seated or walking.

days.guide: The child leads the session, explaining rules and safety.

questions.q: What should you check before starting?
questions.a: Space is clear of hazards, boundaries are marked, equipment is safe, everyone knows the rules and stop signal.

days.guide: Collect thumbs up/down; self-evaluate with the rubric.

questions.q: What one thing would you change next time?
questions.a: Answers vary; strong answers are specific (e.g., shorter explanation, bigger boundary).

weeks.assessment_key: Leadership rubric (4 levels): Planning (warm-up, game, cool-down timed); Communication (clear, brief rules with demo); Safety (boundaries, stop signal); Inclusion (modifications used, everyone active); Enthusiasm/feedback. Proficient = 3+ in every row.

weeks.prep: Football (junior size for smaller hands), flag belts or bandanas, cones every 5 and 10 yards. Phone for video on Friday.
misconceptions: Throwing with only the arm. Correct: step toward the target with the opposite foot and rotate hips and shoulders.
Catching against the body. Correct: catch with hands in a diamond or basket shape, then tuck.

days.guide: Teach grip (fingers on laces, gap between ball and palm), side stance, step with opposite foot, elbow at/above shoulder, release with wrist flick and follow-through to opposite hip. 50 throws at 10 yards.

questions.q: Which foot steps when a right-handed player throws?
questions.a: The left foot steps toward the target.

days.guide: Diamond catch (thumbs together) for balls above chest; basket (pinkies together) below chest. 40 throws.

questions.q: Which hand shape for a ball at the knees?
questions.a: Basket — pinkies together, palms up.

days.guide: Run slant, out, post and curl against air; QB throws on time.

questions.q: Describe a slant and a curl.
questions.a: Slant: a few steps upfield then a sharp diagonal cut toward the middle. Curl: run upfield then turn back toward the quarterback.

days.guide: 1-v-1 grid: defender pulls flag; attacker uses juke or spin. Emphasize no contact, no flag guarding.

questions.q: What is flag guarding?
questions.a: Using hands, arms or the ball to block a defender from pulling your flag — it's a penalty.

days.guide: Video a partner's throw and identify one biomechanical fix.

questions.q: Why does a spiral fly farther and more accurately?
questions.a: Spin stabilizes the ball (gyroscopic stability) and reduces air resistance.

weeks.assessment_key: Throw analysis: proficient answer identifies one specific fault from video (e.g., stepping with the same-side foot, low elbow, early release, no follow-through), explains its effect on accuracy or distance, and gives a cue to fix it (e.g., 'step to target with opposite foot').

weeks.prep: Football, flag belts, cones, paper/whiteboard for play cards. Write a rules quiz.
misconceptions: Running in a pack around the ball. Correct: spread out to create passing lanes.
Rushing the quarterback immediately. Correct: rushers must start from the rush line (often 7 yards back) or wait for a count.

days.guide: Draw three plays with routes and a QB.

questions.q: Why give each receiver a different route?
questions.a: To spread the defense and create open passing options at different depths.

days.guide: Walk through, then run plays at speed.

questions.q: Why walk through first?
questions.a: So everyone learns routes and timing before adding speed.

days.guide: Practice person-to-person and zone; compare.

questions.q: Which defense often stops short passes better and why?
questions.a: Person-to-person often stops short passes because each receiver is closely covered; zone can leave gaps underneath.

days.guide: Play a small-sided game with rotating QBs.

questions.q: What is a down?
questions.a: One play; a team gets a set number of downs (often 4) to reach midfield or score.

days.guide: Self-assess; give the rules quiz.

questions.q: How many points is a touchdown?
questions.a: 6 points.

weeks.assessment_key: Rules quiz key (typical recreational flag football): 1) touchdown = 6 2) extra point: 1 point from 5 yards, 2 points from 10–12 yards (league-dependent) 3) safety = 2 4) 4 downs to cross midfield, 4 more to score 5) no contact, no tackling 6) flag guarding is a penalty 7) rusher must start 7 yards from the line of scrimmage 8) ball is dead where the flag is pulled. Play cards: 3 plays with routes drawn and labeled.

weeks.prep: A small soft ball, cones, tape for a 6 m semicircle around a goal (two cones about 3 m apart or a wall target).
misconceptions: Running with the ball. Correct: max 3 steps while holding and 3 seconds holding, or dribble.
Stepping into the goal area. Correct: only the goalkeeper may stand in the 6 m area; shooters can jump in and release before landing.

days.guide: Teach origins (popular in Europe, Olympic sport since 1972 indoors) and rules: 3 seconds, 3 steps, goal area. Play keep-away.

questions.q: What are the 3-second and 3-step rules?
questions.a: A player may hold the ball no more than 3 seconds and take no more than 3 steps while holding it.

days.guide: Practice shoulder, bounce and wrist passes on the move in a triangle.

questions.q: When is a bounce pass useful?
questions.a: To get past a defender's raised arms or to a teammate on the move close by.

days.guide: Step shot and jump shot from outside the arc.

questions.q: Why use a jump shot?
questions.a: It lets the shooter release the ball over defenders and lean into the area while in the air.

days.guide: Goalkeeper ready stance (feet shoulder-width, knees bent, hands up) and blocks.

questions.q: What is the goalkeeper's ready position?
questions.a: Feet shoulder-width, knees slightly bent, weight on balls of feet, hands up and out.

days.guide: Skills check: 10 passes on the move, 5 shots; record.

questions.q: How many players per team on the court in official handball?
questions.a: Seven (six court players and a goalkeeper).

weeks.assessment_key: Skills checklist: passes — step toward target, accurate to chest, on the move (8/10 = proficient); shots — outside 6 m line, step or jump shot form, on target (3/5 = proficient); follows 3-step/3-second rules.

weeks.prep: Handball, cones, pinnies. Recruit at least 3 players for 2-v-1 and 3-v-2 drills.
misconceptions: Standing still after passing. Correct: pass and move (cut) into open space.
Slow transition. Correct: after a save, look long immediately for a fast break.

days.guide: Give-and-go: pass, cut past the defender, receive the return pass.

questions.q: Describe a give-and-go.
questions.a: Pass to a teammate, immediately cut toward the goal, and receive a return pass in space.

days.guide: After a goalkeeper save, three attackers sprint to attack two defenders.

questions.q: Why is a 3-on-2 fast break effective?
questions.a: Attackers outnumber defenders, so one attacker is always open.

days.guide: Set a screen: stand still beside the defender; shooter uses it to get free.

questions.q: What makes a legal screen?
questions.a: The screener is stationary, with arms close to the body, and allows the defender room to see it; moving screens are fouls.

days.guide: Small-sided game, rotating positions every 5 minutes.

questions.q: What should defenders do when the other team scores?
questions.a: Sprint back and set up between attackers and the goal.

days.guide: Write a comparison of handball, soccer and basketball strategies.

questions.q: Name two strategies common to all invasion games.
questions.a: Creating space by spreading out, passing and moving, fast breaks, man-to-man or zone defense, keeping between opponent and goal.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison rubric: 4 = names at least three shared strategies (create space, give-and-go, fast break, defensive positioning) and one difference per sport (e.g., handball 3-step rule, soccer uses feet and offside, basketball shot clock/dribble), with examples; 3 = two shared and differences; 2 = lists rules only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Balls, flag belts, whistle, bracket sheet for a round-robin. Print officiating signals (touchdown: both arms straight up; foul: hand raised/flag; handball free throw).
misconceptions: Officials favoring their own team. Correct: call what you see consistently for both teams.
Arguing calls. Correct: accept the call; good sportsmanship includes respecting officials.

days.guide: Teach hand signals and common fouls: flag guarding, offside, illegal contact (football); 4+ steps, double dribble, entering goal area (handball).

questions.q: In handball, what happens if a court player enters the goal area?
questions.a: The ball is awarded to the goalkeeper (or opponents get a free throw).

days.guide: Round-robin; child officiates one game.

questions.q: What does a good official do?
questions.a: Watches closely, signals clearly, applies rules consistently and stays calm.

days.guide: Second round; team plans strategy.

questions.q: Give a strategy your team used.
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., zone defense against a strong passer.

days.guide: Finals and scoreboard duty.

questions.q: How do you break a tie in round-robin standings?
questions.a: Common methods: head-to-head result, then point differential.

days.guide: Child writes the reflection.

questions.q: How did you handle a conflict?
questions.a: Answers vary; strong answers describe calm communication and accepting decisions.

weeks.assessment_key: Officiating observation (parent checklist): correct signals, consistent calls, clear voice/whistle, calm handling of disputes (3–4 of 4 proficient). Team reflection: 4 = specific teamwork examples, fairness reflection, conflict handled and lesson learned.

weeks.prep: Tennis racket (junior 25–26 inch if needed), 6+ balls, a wall or court, chalk. Phone for Friday video.
misconceptions: Swinging only with the arm. Correct: turn shoulders early, step in, and rotate through the ball.
Hitting late beside or behind the body. Correct: contact slightly in front of the front hip.

days.guide: Eastern forehand grip ('shake hands'); ready position. Rally against a wall 10 minutes.

questions.q: Describe the ready position.
questions.a: Feet shoulder-width, knees bent, weight on balls of feet, racket in front with both hands.

days.guide: Drop-and-hit forehands with low-to-high swing.

questions.q: Why swing low to high?
questions.a: It brushes up the back of the ball, creating topspin that brings it down into the court.

days.guide: Two-hand backhand from tosses.

questions.q: Name one advantage of a two-handed backhand.
questions.a: More stability and power for players with less wrist strength.

days.guide: Overhand serve with trophy position into a target box.

questions.q: What is the trophy position?
questions.a: Tossing arm up, racket arm bent behind with elbow up, knees bent — like a trophy figure, ready to swing up.

days.guide: Self-video a forehand and compare to the checklist.

questions.q: Where should the contact point be?
questions.a: In front of the body, about waist height, beside the front hip.

weeks.assessment_key: Forehand checklist (1 pt each): ready position; early unit turn; eastern grip; step with front foot; contact in front; low-to-high swing; follow-through over opposite shoulder; recovery to ready. 6+/8 proficient.

weeks.prep: Tennis gear, table tennis paddles and balls (or improvised table with a net of books). Scoring sheets.
misconceptions: Thinking tennis points go 1-2-3-4. Correct: love (0), 15, 30, 40, game; at 40-40 (deuce) a player must win by two.
Serving table tennis anywhere. Correct: toss the ball at least 6 inches from an open palm and strike it so it bounces on your side first.

days.guide: Cooperative rallies aiming for 10.

questions.q: Why practice cooperative rallies?
questions.a: To build consistency and control before competitive play.

days.guide: Teach scoring and play a tiebreaker (first to 7, win by 2).

questions.q: Server has 40, receiver has 30. Server wins the point. What's the score?
questions.a: Game to the server.

questions.q: What happens after deuce if the server wins a point?
questions.a: 'Advantage server'; winning the next point wins the game, losing it returns to deuce.

days.guide: Shakehand grip; push and forehand drive.

questions.q: What is the shakehand grip?
questions.a: Hold the paddle as if shaking hands, index finger along the back of the blade, thumb on the front.

days.guide: Experiment with topspin and backspin.

questions.q: How does topspin make the ball behave?
questions.a: It dips down faster and kicks forward after bouncing; backspin floats and slows or checks back.

days.guide: Best-of-three table tennis to 11 and a short tennis set.

questions.q: How does a table tennis game end?
questions.a: First to 11 points, winning by 2; serve alternates every 2 points (every 1 point at 10-10).

weeks.assessment_key: Scoring quiz key: 1) 0-15-30-40-game 2) deuce at 40-40 3) win by two after deuce 4) a set is first to 6 games, win by 2 (tiebreak at 6-6) 5) tiebreak first to 7 by 2 6) table tennis to 11 by 2 7) serve changes every 2 points 8) let = serve touches the net and lands in, replay. Match observation: keeps score correctly, legal serves, good sportsmanship.

weeks.prep: Volleyball (light trainer for beginners), net or rope at about 7'4" (or lower), cones.
misconceptions: Hitting the ball with fists or open palms in bumps. Correct: form a flat platform with forearms, angle toward target.
Running past the ball on the approach. Correct: take off behind the ball so contact is in front of the hitting shoulder.

days.guide: 50 forearm passes and 50 sets with a partner.

questions.q: Where does the ball contact the arms on a forearm pass?
questions.a: On the flat part of the forearms above the wrists, with arms straight and thumbs together.

days.guide: 3-step approach (right-hander: left-right-left), both arms swing back then up, high elbow, contact at the top.

questions.q: Why swing both arms back on the approach?
questions.a: The arm swing adds momentum and height to the jump.

days.guide: Block: shuffle step, jump with hands up and over the net, press hands forward, land on both feet.

questions.q: What should the blocker's hands do?
questions.a: Reach up and over the net, fingers spread, penetrating forward to deflect the ball down.

days.guide: Teach rotation (clockwise when gaining serve) and run pass-set-hit.

questions.q: When does a team rotate?
questions.a: When it wins back the serve (side-out), players rotate one position clockwise.

days.guide: Modified game requiring three contacts.

questions.q: Why require three contacts?
questions.a: It builds the pass-set-attack pattern used in real volleyball.

weeks.assessment_key: Spike approach checklist: correct 3-step footwork (L-R-L for right-handers), arms swing back on the last two steps, two-foot takeoff, high elbow 'bow and arrow' arm, contact at highest reach in front of hitting shoulder, wrist snap, two-foot landing. 5+/7 proficient.

weeks.prep: Rackets, balls, volleyball, practice log. Prepare a 10-question written test.
misconceptions: Thinking blocked practice (same skill repeatedly) is always better because it feels better. Correct: random practice feels harder but leads to better retention and game transfer.
Peer feedback that's only criticism. Correct: use praise-fix-praise.

days.guide: 10 minutes blocked (all forehands), 10 random (forehands/backhands mixed); note difference.

questions.q: Which practice type leads to better long-term learning?
questions.a: Random practice — even though performance during practice is lower, retention and transfer are better.

days.guide: Visualize serves for 2 minutes, then 20 serves; compare to 20 without.

questions.q: What is mental rehearsal?
questions.a: Imagining performing a skill in detail without moving, which strengthens the neural pattern.

days.guide: Coach a partner with praise-fix-praise.

questions.q: Give an example of praise-fix-praise.
questions.a: 'Great toss height. Try stepping in with your front foot. Your follow-through is strong!'

days.guide: Mini-tournament in chosen net game.

questions.q: Name a net-game strategy.
questions.a: Hit to open space, move opponent side to side, return to ready position in the center.

days.guide: Give the written test.

questions.q: What does 'side-out' mean in volleyball?
questions.a: The receiving team wins the rally and gains the serve.

weeks.assessment_key: Written test key: 1) hit to open space 2) return to base position after each shot 3) tennis scoring 0-15-30-40 4) deuce/advantage 5) table tennis to 11 win by 2 6) volleyball rally scoring to 25 win by 2 7) rotate clockwise on side-out 8) blocked vs random practice; random better for retention 9) mental rehearsal improves performance 10) praise-fix-praise feedback. 8/10 proficient.

weeks.prep: Heart-rate monitor or a watch for 15-second pulse counts (×4). Fitness journal. Diagram templates.
misconceptions: Thinking the heart gets bigger only in disease. Correct: training enlarges and strengthens the heart muscle so stroke volume increases and resting heart rate drops.
Believing muscles grow during exercise. Correct: exercise creates the stimulus; muscles repair and grow during recovery.

days.guide: Record HR, breaths/min and skin temperature at rest, after 5 min jogging and after 5 min rest.

questions.q: Why does heart rate rise during exercise?
questions.a: Working muscles need more oxygen and nutrients, and carbon dioxide must be removed faster.

days.guide: Teach stroke volume (blood per beat) and cardiac output = HR × SV. Do a 25-minute interval run.

questions.q: If HR = 70 bpm and SV = 70 mL, what is cardiac output?

days.guide: Explain resistance and impact exercise stimulate muscle protein synthesis and bone remodeling. Plyometric circuit.

questions.q: Why do jumping activities strengthen bones?
questions.a: Impact loads stimulate bone-building cells to add mineral, increasing bone density — especially important during adolescence.

days.guide: Explain practice strengthens nerve pathways (motor learning). Ladder drill.

questions.q: Why do skills feel easier with practice?
questions.a: Neural pathways become more efficient and coordinated, so movements become more automatic.

days.guide: Diagram four systems (cardiovascular, respiratory, muscular, skeletal/nervous) with short-term responses and long-term adaptations.

questions.q: Give a long-term adaptation of the respiratory system.
questions.a: Stronger breathing muscles and more efficient oxygen use, so breathing rate during submaximal exercise is lower.

weeks.assessment_key: Diagram key — Cardiovascular: short-term HR and SV rise; long-term lower resting HR, larger stroke volume. Respiratory: breathing rate/depth rise; long-term stronger diaphragm, better efficiency. Muscular: more blood flow, heat, fatigue; long-term strength, endurance, more mitochondria. Skeletal: loading; long-term higher bone density. Nervous: motor unit recruitment; long-term better coordination. Proficient: 4 systems with one response and one adaptation each.

weeks.prep: Resistance bands, light dumbbells or water jugs, mat, muscle chart. Technique checklist for squat, lunge, glute bridge, push-up, band row, overhead press, plank.
misconceptions: Knees caving in during squats. Correct: push knees out over toes, chest up, weight in heels/mid-foot.
Arching the back during planks or push-ups. Correct: brace core, straight line from head to heels.

days.guide: Label 10 muscles with one exercise each (pectorals – push-up; latissimus dorsi – row; deltoids – overhead press; biceps – curl; triceps – dips; abdominals – plank; quadriceps – squat; hamstrings – glute bridge; gluteus maximus – lunge; gastrocnemius – calf raise).

questions.q: Which muscle does a squat mainly work?
questions.a: Quadriceps and gluteus maximus (also hamstrings).

days.guide: Teach squat, lunge and glute bridge form; 3×10–12.

questions.q: Give two squat cues.
questions.a: Chest up, hips back, knees track over toes, weight through heels, thighs toward parallel.

days.guide: Push-up, band row and overhead press; 3×10–12.

questions.q: Which muscles does a band row work?
questions.a: Upper back (latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, trapezius) and biceps.

days.guide: Plank, side plank, bird dog, dead bug; 3 rounds.

questions.q: Why train the core?
questions.a: It stabilizes the spine, transfers force between upper and lower body and helps prevent back injury.

days.guide: Parent checks six exercises.

questions.q: Why breathe out during the effort phase?
questions.a: Exhaling on exertion helps brace and avoids holding breath, which spikes blood pressure.

weeks.assessment_key: Technique checklist: each exercise scored 0–2 (0 = unsafe form, 1 = minor errors, 2 = correct: neutral spine, controlled tempo, full range, correct joint alignment, breathing). 10+/12 proficient.

weeks.prep: Resistance bands, workout log. Rep-range chart: endurance 15–20 reps, 30–60 s rest; strength/hypertrophy for teens 8–12 reps with good form, 60–90 s rest.
misconceptions: Training only 'mirror muscles.' Correct: balance opposing muscle groups to prevent injury and posture problems.
Adding weight before mastering form. Correct: progress gradually (about 10% or a few reps at a time) only with good form.

days.guide: Compare rep ranges and rest; do an endurance circuit (15–20 reps).

questions.q: Which builds muscular endurance: 3×20 light or 3×8 heavier?
questions.a: 3×20 with light resistance.

days.guide: Plan a full-body workout pairing opposing muscles.

questions.q: Name the opposing muscle for chest and for quadriceps.
questions.a: Chest (pectorals) ↔ upper back (lats/rhomboids); quadriceps ↔ hamstrings.

days.guide: Do the workout; record sets, reps and RPE (1–10).

questions.q: What does an RPE of 7 mean?
questions.a: Hard effort, but could do a few more reps with good form.

days.guide: Adjust exercises using progression.

questions.q: What is the progression principle?
questions.a: Gradually increase the load (reps, resistance, sets) as the body adapts.

days.guide: Submit plan with rationale.

questions.q: Why include a warm-up before strength work?
questions.a: Raises muscle temperature and prepares joints, reducing injury risk.

weeks.assessment_key: Workout plan rubric: 4 = warm-up, 6–8 exercises covering all major muscle groups with opposing pairs, sets/reps/rest matched to goal, progression plan, cool-down, rationale for each; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = unbalanced or missing parameters; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Food labels, water bottle, bathroom scale, sleep log, poster paper.
misconceptions: Skipping carbohydrates before exercise. Correct: carbohydrates are the main fuel for moderate-to-intense exercise.
Waiting until thirsty to drink. Correct: drink regularly before, during and after; thirst lags behind fluid needs.

days.guide: Plan three pre-workout snacks (banana, toast with jam, granola bar) 1–3 hours before; explain carbs fuel muscles as glycogen.

questions.q: Why are carbohydrates the main fuel for exercise?
questions.a: They break down to glucose and are stored as glycogen in muscles and liver, providing quick energy for moderate-to-intense activity.

days.guide: Weigh before and after a 30-minute workout (no drinking or bathroom between if possible). Replace about 16–24 oz of fluid per pound lost.

questions.q: You lost 1.5 lb during practice. How much should you drink?
questions.a: About 24–36 oz (16–24 oz per pound).

days.guide: Plan a post-workout snack with protein and carbs within about an hour (chocolate milk, yogurt with fruit, turkey sandwich).

questions.q: Why include protein after a workout?
questions.a: Protein provides amino acids to repair and rebuild muscle; carbs refill glycogen.

days.guide: Log sleep; compare to 8–10 hours. Yoga cool-down.

questions.q: How does sleep affect performance?
questions.a: Sleep restores energy, supports muscle repair (growth hormone release), reaction time, mood and injury prevention.

days.guide: Create a one-day fuel plan poster.

questions.q: What should a fuel plan include?
questions.a: Balanced meals, pre- and post-exercise snacks, hydration schedule and sleep target.

weeks.assessment_key: Poster rubric: 4 = three balanced meals, pre-workout carbohydrate snack with timing, post-workout carb + protein snack, hydration schedule with amounts, sleep target 8–10 h, avoids energy drinks; 3 = one element missing; 2 = partial; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Fitness journal, stopwatch, mat, week 1 scores and the SMART goal sheet. Prepare the progress-report template.
misconceptions: Thinking a plateau means failure. Correct: plateaus are normal; change the training stimulus (FITT) or allow more recovery.
Believing more training is always better. Correct: without rest, overtraining causes fatigue, injury and worse performance.

days.guide: Retest the two items tied to the SMART goals using the same protocols.

questions.q: Why use the same test protocol each time?
questions.a: So results are comparable and changes reflect fitness, not testing differences.

days.guide: Compare with week 1; classify as progressed, plateaued or declined.

questions.q: Your push-ups went from 15 to 15. What might you change?
questions.a: Increase frequency or intensity (more sets, harder variation), check consistency, sleep and nutrition.

days.guide: List overtraining signs: persistent soreness, fatigue, poor sleep, irritability, declining performance, elevated resting HR, frequent injuries/illness.

questions.q: Name three signs of overtraining.
questions.a: Persistent fatigue and soreness, decreased performance, trouble sleeping, moodiness, elevated resting heart rate, frequent injuries or illness.

days.guide: Revise SMART goals and weekly plan.

questions.q: How do you revise a goal you already met?
questions.a: Set a new, slightly more challenging target with a new date.

days.guide: 40-minute activity combining cardio and strength.

questions.q: Name the FITT parts.
questions.a: Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type.

weeks.assessment_key: Progress report: 4 = both retests recorded with comparison to week 1, classified correctly, reasons explained, revised SMART goals with weekly plan; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = scores without analysis; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Plastic or whiffle golf balls, a putter or broom handle, cups/targets, hula hoops, a frisbee or disc, tape measure. Set up a 6-hole course with par values.
misconceptions: Swinging hard on putts. Correct: putting is a smooth pendulum from the shoulders with the wrists quiet.
Releasing the disc high and flat. Correct: keep the disc level or slightly nose-down and release on a straight line.

days.guide: Putting grip; pendulum stroke from shoulders; putts from 3, 6, 9 feet.

questions.q: What makes a putting stroke consistent?
questions.a: Rocking the shoulders like a pendulum with still wrists and head, and a stroke length matched to distance.

days.guide: Chip into a hoop from 10 and 20 feet.

questions.q: How is a chip different from a full swing?
questions.a: Short, controlled swing with little wrist; the ball flies low then rolls.

days.guide: Backhand drive: reach back, pull across the chest, snap wrist, follow-through; measure distances.

questions.q: Why does reach-back add distance?
questions.a: It lengthens the pull, so the disc accelerates over a longer distance before release.

days.guide: Play a 6-hole round, scoring relative to par.

questions.q: If par is 3 and you take 4 strokes, what's your score on the hole?
questions.a: +1 (a bogey).

days.guide: Explain how angle of release and follow-through affected results.

questions.q: What happens if the disc is released nose-up?
questions.a: It climbs, stalls and drops short.

weeks.assessment_key: Scorecard: all 6 holes scored with total relative to par (correct arithmetic). Written analysis: 4 = explains release angle, follow-through and force with specific examples from the round and one adjustment; 3 = one factor explained; 2 = describes results only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Bean bags, 10 plastic bottles (add a little water/sand), playground ball, target poster with three rings (e.g., 10/5/1 points), tape lines at 3 distances.
misconceptions: Rushing shots under pressure. Correct: a consistent pre-shot routine improves accuracy.
Using too much force for accuracy. Correct: controlled force and follow-through toward the target.

days.guide: Bocce-style toss: underhand, step with opposite foot, follow-through toward the jack.

questions.q: How do you win a bocce frame?
questions.a: The team with the ball(s) closest to the target ball (pallino/jack) scores a point for each ball closer than the opponent's closest.

days.guide: Bowl at pins: 4-step approach, swing arm like a pendulum, release at the ankle, follow-through.

questions.q: How is a strike recorded and scored?
questions.a: X; 10 plus the pins from the next two balls.

days.guide: Target throws from three distances; record scores.

questions.q: Why might accuracy drop at longer distances?
questions.a: More force is needed, small errors in release angle grow, and control decreases.

days.guide: Design a pre-shot routine (breath, look, picture, go); compare scores with and without.

questions.q: Why use a pre-shot routine?
questions.a: It focuses attention, calms nerves and makes each attempt more consistent.

days.guide: Target triathlon: record totals.

questions.q: What do all target games have in common?
questions.a: Accuracy toward a target with controlled force, aim and follow-through.

weeks.assessment_key: Triathlon score sheet: totals correct for bowling (frame scoring), bocce (points per frame) and target throw (sum of ring values). Proficient: correct scoring, uses routine on every attempt, and a brief note on which game was strongest.

weeks.prep: Flat bat or paddle, tennis ball, cones/bucket as a wicket, kickball. Print simple cricket rules.
misconceptions: Bending the elbow when bowling in cricket. Correct: the arm must stay straight (that's a 'throw' if bent).
Thinking cricket batters must run on every hit. Correct: they run only when it's safe.

days.guide: Teach basics: two teams; bowler delivers to batter defending the wicket; runs scored by running between wickets; out if bowled, caught, run out. Practice straight-arm bowling.

questions.q: Name two ways a cricket batter gets out.
questions.a: Bowled (ball hits wicket), caught (fielder catches before bounce), run out, LBW (leg before wicket), stumped.

days.guide: Defensive and drive strokes.

questions.q: When would a batter play a defensive stroke?
questions.a: When the ball is aimed at the wicket and hard to hit safely — block it to protect the wicket.

days.guide: Fielding positions and backing up.

questions.q: What is backing up?
questions.a: A fielder positions behind a teammate receiving a throw to stop the ball if it's missed.

days.guide: Play a modified game, rotating batting order.

questions.q: How is a run scored in cricket?
questions.a: Both batters cross and reach the opposite crease safely (4 runs if the ball reaches the boundary on the ground, 6 if over it in the air).

days.guide: Compare striking/fielding strategy.

questions.q: One strategy shared by cricket, softball and kickball?
questions.a: Hit to open space where fielders aren't; fielders position to cover likely hits and back up throws.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison chart: 4 = compares cricket, softball and kickball on scoring, outs, field positions and strategy (placing hits, base running/running between wickets, fielding positioning) with accurate details; 3 = minor errors; 2 = partial; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Any available equipment; game-design template (name, objective, players, equipment, area diagram, rules, scoring, safety, modifications).
misconceptions: Too many rules. Correct: start simple; add rules only if play-testing shows a need.
Forgetting safety. Correct: include boundaries, equipment checks and contact rules.

days.guide: Combine two categories; write rules and scoring.

questions.q: What game categories exist?
questions.a: Invasion, net/wall, striking/fielding, target.

days.guide: Add safety rules; draw the area.

questions.q: Give two safety rules for a game you design.
questions.a: No contact above the waist; boundaries 3 m from walls; soft balls only.

days.guide: Play-test and note problems.

questions.q: Why play-test?
questions.a: To find unclear rules, unfair scoring or unsafe parts before finalizing.

days.guide: Revise rules; add modification.

questions.q: Give an example modification for younger players.
questions.a: Larger target, closer distances, softer ball, more players per side.

days.guide: Teach and play the final version; submit rules.

questions.q: What makes a game fun and fair?
questions.a: Everyone is active, rules are clear, scoring is balanced and teams are even.

weeks.assessment_key: Game rules and teaching rubric: 4 = clear objective, rules, scoring, diagram, safety rules, modification, evidence of revision after play-test, taught clearly with demo; 3 = one element weak; 2 = missing safety or unclear rules; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Music player; free square-dance music with calls (search 'beginner square dance calls'). Clear space for a square of 4 couples (or 2). Instructions for the Virginia reel or zapateado basic.
misconceptions: Rushing ahead of the music. Correct: move on the beat; listen for calls.
Ignoring partner etiquette. Correct: bow/curtsy, offer hands gently, thank partners.

days.guide: Teach honor your partner, do-si-do (pass right shoulders, back-to-back, return), swing, promenade (counterclockwise).

questions.q: Describe a do-si-do.
questions.a: Partners face, walk forward passing right shoulders, step side to side back-to-back, and walk backward to place passing left shoulders.

days.guide: Dance a simple square.

questions.q: In which direction do couples promenade?
questions.a: Counterclockwise around the square.

days.guide: Take a turn as caller on the beat.

questions.q: Why must calls come before the beat?
questions.a: So dancers have time to hear and start the move on the beat.

days.guide: Learn zapateado basic or Virginia reel.

questions.q: What is zapateado?
questions.a: A Mexican folk dance footwork style with rhythmic heel and toe stamping.

days.guide: Perform; self-assess timing and etiquette.

questions.q: Is square dancing MVPA?
questions.a: Yes — continuous moving dances can raise heart rate into the moderate range.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance and self-assessment: 4 = executes all calls on the beat, correct formations, consistent etiquette, can call one sequence; 3 = minor timing errors; 2 = frequent errors; 1 = unable to complete.

weeks.prep: Music in 4/4 (swing and salsa songs), heart-rate monitor or watch.
misconceptions: Not counting the beat. Correct: listen for the downbeat and count 1–8.
Leading by pushing/pulling. Correct: clear, gentle connection through the frame.

days.guide: Count beats and clap tempo; march 8-counts.

questions.q: How many beats are in an 8-count phrase?
questions.a: Eight beats (two measures of 4/4).

days.guide: East Coast swing basic (triple step, triple step, rock step) and underarm turn.

questions.q: What are the counts of the East Coast swing basic?
questions.a: 1&2, 3&4, 5-6 (triple, triple, rock step) — or the single-time version: step, step, rock step.

days.guide: Salsa basic (forward on 1-2-3, pause 4, back on 5-6-7, pause 8) and cross-body lead.

questions.q: On which counts does salsa pause?
questions.a: On 4 and 8.

days.guide: Dance 15 minutes; check HR against moderate zone (about 64–76% of max; max ≈ 220 − age).

questions.q: For a 14-year-old, what HR range is moderate intensity?

days.guide: Perform a 1-minute partner routine.

questions.q: What makes a partner routine look smooth?
questions.a: Staying on the beat, clear leads and follows, connected transitions.

weeks.assessment_key: Partner routine: 4 = at least 3 steps/turns combined, on the beat throughout, smooth transitions, respectful partnering, ~1 minute; 3 = minor timing errors; 2 = 1–2 steps only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Upbeat song (~120–130 bpm), clear space, optional video device and heart-rate monitor.
misconceptions: Choosing moves too hard for everyone. Correct: offer low-impact options (step-touch instead of jumping jack).
Losing count. Correct: map choreography on paper in 8-counts.

days.guide: Map four 8-count sections with fitness moves.

questions.q: How long is 4 × 8 counts at 120 bpm?
questions.a: 32 beats ÷ 120 beats/min = 16 seconds.

days.guide: Create transitions and formations.

questions.q: Give two formation ideas.
questions.a: Lines, V-shape, circle, staggered rows, canon (moves start one after another).

days.guide: Rehearse and add low/high options.

questions.q: Give a low-impact option for jumping squats.
questions.a: Regular squats or squat-and-reach without jumping.

days.guide: Lead family/friends through the routine.

questions.q: How do you cue a group?
questions.a: Call the move 4 counts before it starts and demonstrate facing the group (mirror image).

days.guide: Reflect; record HR.

questions.q: How does dance build community?
questions.a: Moving together in rhythm creates shared fun, cooperation and connection.

weeks.assessment_key: Routine performance: 4 = 32+ counts with varied fitness moves, transitions and formations, low-impact options, clear cueing, HR in MVPA range; 3 = minor issues; 2 = short or uncued; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Yoga mat or towel, strap or towel, sit-and-reach box. Find a beginner sun salutation video.
misconceptions: Forcing stretches. Correct: stretch to mild tension, never pain; breathe steadily.
Holding breath in balance poses. Correct: slow, steady breathing improves balance.

days.guide: Teach sun salutation A (mountain, upward salute, forward fold, half lift, plank/low push-up, upward dog/cobra, downward dog, forward fold, mountain); repeat 5 times.

questions.q: Name four poses in a sun salutation.
questions.a: Mountain, forward fold, plank, cobra/upward dog, downward dog.

days.guide: Tree, warrior III, chair; 30 seconds each.

questions.q: Give one cue for tree pose.
questions.a: Press foot into inner thigh or calf (not the knee), fix eyes on a point, hips level.

days.guide: PNF contract-relax: stretch hamstring with strap ~10 s, contract against the strap 5–6 s, relax and stretch deeper ~10–30 s; measure before and after.

questions.q: Why does PNF increase range of motion?
questions.a: Contracting then relaxing the muscle reduces its reflex resistance, allowing a deeper stretch.

days.guide: Create a 10-pose, 15-minute flow.

questions.q: Why sequence poses carefully?
questions.a: Warm up first, balance forward and backward bends, end with calming poses.

days.guide: Lead the flow; record flexibility.

questions.q: How often should you stretch to improve flexibility?
questions.a: At least 2–3 days a week, holding static stretches 10–30 seconds.

weeks.assessment_key: Yoga flow sequence: 4 = 10 poses in logical order, breath cues, safety modifications, led smoothly; flexibility measurements before/after PNF recorded. 3 = minor gaps; 2 = fewer poses or no measurements; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Journal, timer, a beginner tai chi video (e.g., '10-minute tai chi for beginners'), safe walking route.
misconceptions: Thinking exercise only helps the body. Correct: it improves mood, sleep and stress by releasing endorphins and lowering stress hormones over time.
Breathing from the chest. Correct: diaphragmatic breathing expands the belly and calms the nervous system.

days.guide: Rate mood 1–10 before and after a 20-minute run.

questions.q: Why might mood improve after exercise?
questions.a: Endorphins and other brain chemicals (e.g., dopamine, serotonin) rise, and regular exercise lowers cortisol over time.

days.guide: Box breathing and diaphragmatic breathing, then a 10-minute walk.

questions.q: How do you know you're breathing diaphragmatically?
questions.a: The hand on your belly rises more than the hand on your chest.

days.guide: Tai chi 15 minutes.

questions.q: What are benefits of tai chi?
questions.a: Balance, flexibility, relaxation and reduced stress through slow, controlled movement and breathing.

days.guide: 30-minute mindful walk; note five things seen, heard, felt.

questions.q: What is mindfulness?
questions.a: Paying attention to the present moment without judgment.

days.guide: Write a stress-relief plan with three activities.

questions.q: Name three physical activities that relieve stress.
questions.a: Running, yoga, walking in nature, dancing, swimming, tai chi.

weeks.assessment_key: Stress-relief plan: 4 = three activities with when/how often, why each works (physiological explanation), mood data from the week; 3 = activities and timing; 2 = list only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Baton or paper towel tube; pool-noodle hurdles on cones (low!); an exchange zone marked (30 m under current World Athletics rules; many school meets use 20 m); stopwatch; phone for video.
misconceptions: Incoming runner slowing down at the handoff. Correct: incoming runner sprints through; outgoing runner starts early from a go-mark.
Jumping over hurdles. Correct: run over them with a lead leg extended and trail leg pulled to the side.

days.guide: Practice upsweep and downsweep handoffs jogging, then at speed.

questions.q: In the downsweep, how does the receiver hold the hand?
questions.a: Arm extended back, palm up, thumb in, fingers together; the passer presses the baton down into the palm.

days.guide: Run a 4×100 (or shuttle) relay staying inside the marked exchange zone.

questions.q: What happens if the baton is passed outside the zone?
questions.a: The team is disqualified.

days.guide: Lead- and trail-leg drills walking beside hurdles.

questions.q: What does the trail leg do?
questions.a: It folds to the side with the knee high and toe up, then pulls through to the front.

days.guide: 3-step rhythm over three low hurdles; time it.

questions.q: Why use a consistent step pattern between hurdles?
questions.a: It allows the same lead leg each time and maintains speed.

days.guide: Video a clearance; identify a fix.

questions.q: Name one common hurdle fault.
questions.a: Jumping too high, leaning back, trail leg dragging low, or stuttering steps.

weeks.assessment_key: Hurdle technique analysis: proficient identifies one fault on video (e.g., floating too high, trail knee low), explains its effect (loses time, hits hurdle) and gives a correcting cue/drill (e.g., attack the hurdle, lean forward; trail-leg wall drill).

weeks.prep: Sand area or soft grass, tape measure, softball or 4-lb medicine ball, protractor (optional) for angle testing.
misconceptions: Hop and step on the wrong feet. Correct: hop takes off and lands on the same foot, step lands on the other, jump lands on both.
Throwing the shot like a baseball. Correct: the put is a push from the neck with the elbow high.

days.guide: Hop (same foot), step (opposite foot), jump (both feet landing) standing, then with a short approach.

questions.q: If you hop off your right foot, which foot do you land the hop on?
questions.a: The right foot; then step onto the left; then jump and land on both feet.

days.guide: Three measured jumps; record best.

questions.q: Where is the triple jump measured from?
questions.a: From the takeoff board/line to the nearest mark in the landing area.

days.guide: Standing put: ball at neck under jaw, elbow high, push up and out from the legs through the hips.

questions.q: Why push instead of throw?
questions.a: Rules require it, and pushing with the whole body prevents elbow and shoulder injury.

days.guide: Test release angles ~30°, 40°, 50°.

questions.q: Which angle gave the longest distance and why isn't it exactly 45°?
questions.a: Usually around 35–42°: the ball is released above the ground and people can push faster at lower angles, so the optimal angle is below 45°.

days.guide: Explain momentum transfer in the triple jump.

questions.q: How is momentum transferred?
questions.a: Horizontal speed from the approach is carried through each phase; each takeoff must keep speed while redirecting some upward, with arms and free leg driving forward.

weeks.assessment_key: Distance log and explanation: all trials recorded with best marks; explanation proficient if it covers hop-step-jump order with correct feet, the role of approach speed, minimizing braking at each contact, and the push technique and release angle for the put.

weeks.prep: Stopwatch, cones, measuring wheel or a local track, event cards, grade 7 marks.
misconceptions: Starting the 800 m too fast. Correct: run even splits (roughly equal 200 m times).
Not warming up before sprints. Correct: dynamic warm-up and strides prevent hamstring pulls.

days.guide: Run 4×200 at goal 800 pace with rest, checking splits.

questions.q: If your 800 m goal is 3:20, what is the target 200 m split?
questions.a: 3:20 = 200 s ÷ 4 = 50 seconds per 200 m.

days.guide: Choose three events and set goals.

questions.q: Why set goals based on past marks?
questions.a: They are realistic and measurable.

days.guide: Sprints and relay.

questions.q: What starting position is used in sprints?
questions.a: Crouch/block start or standing start with weight forward; drive out low.

days.guide: 800 m, triple jump, put; record.

questions.q: Why run even pace in the 800 m?
questions.a: It avoids early fatigue from lactate buildup and usually produces the fastest time.

days.guide: Reflect vs. goals and grade 7.

questions.q: What is a personal record (PR)?
questions.a: Your best-ever performance in an event.

weeks.assessment_key: Track meet results and reflection: 4 = all results recorded with units, compared to goals and grade 7, explains reasons (pacing, technique, training) and sets next goal; 3 = comparison without much reasoning; 2 = results only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Bicycle and helmet; daypack with water, snacks, first aid; map app; local parks/recreation guide; pool access if available.
misconceptions: Helmet worn tilted back. Correct: level, two fingers above eyebrows, side straps form a V under ears, one finger under chin strap.
Riding against traffic. Correct: ride with traffic on the right.

days.guide: Helmet fit; ABC check (Air, Brakes, Chain); hand signals (left arm straight = left; left arm bent up or right arm straight = right; arm down = stop).

questions.q: What does the ABC bike check stand for?
questions.a: Air (tires), Brakes, Chain (and cranks).

days.guide: Ride a planned 30–60 minute route with a parent.

questions.q: Which side of the road do cyclists ride on?
questions.a: The right side, with traffic.

days.guide: Water safety rules; swim 10 minutes if possible.

questions.q: Name two water safety rules.
questions.a: Swim with a buddy and near a lifeguard, enter feet first in unknown water, wear a life jacket in boats, reach or throw — don't go.

days.guide: Plan a hike with map, water, Leave No Trace.

questions.q: Name two Leave No Trace principles.
questions.a: Plan ahead, stay on trails, pack out trash, leave what you find, respect wildlife, minimize campfire impact, be considerate of others.

days.guide: List five community recreation programs.

questions.q: Why do community programs matter for lifetime fitness?
questions.a: They provide low-cost, social, ongoing opportunities to stay active after school sports.

weeks.assessment_key: Outing plan: 4 = route/map, time, gear list (water, helmet, first aid), safety rules, emergency contact and Leave No Trace; community list: 5 programs with cost and location. 3 = minor gaps; 2 = partial; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: PACER audio, stopwatch, mat, tape measure, ruler, cones for agility. Week 1 and week 19 scores.
misconceptions: Testing without warming up. Correct: warm up to get valid scores and prevent injury.
Comparing only to others. Correct: compare to your own previous scores and the Healthy Fitness Zone.

days.guide: PACER or mile; record.

questions.q: Why might PACER laps increase over a year?
questions.a: Improved cardiorespiratory endurance from training, plus growth and maturation.

days.guide: Curl-ups and push-ups to cadence.

questions.q: What is cadence and why use it?
questions.a: A set pace (one rep per 3 seconds) so tests are consistent and form is controlled.

days.guide: Sit-and-reach and trunk lift.

questions.q: Why is trunk-lift capped at 12 inches?
questions.a: Lifting higher can hyperextend and strain the lower back.

days.guide: Retest agility, power, reaction time.

questions.q: Which test measures power?
questions.a: Standing long jump or vertical jump.

days.guide: Graph week 1, mid-year, final; write summary.

questions.q: What does a line graph show best here?
questions.a: Change over time across the three test dates.

weeks.assessment_key: Progress graph and summary: 4 = all items graphed at three time points with labels/units, identifies greatest improvement and any decline with explanations, connects to SMART goals and training, sets a summer goal; 3 = complete graph with general summary; 2 = partial; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Planning template (14 days × FITT), fitness journal.
misconceptions: Training the same way every day. Correct: alternate cardio, strength, flexibility and rest to allow recovery.
No backup plan. Correct: write alternatives for bad weather and busy days.

days.guide: Outline 14 days with FITT.

questions.q: Write FITT for a cardio day.
questions.a: Example: Frequency 3×/week; Intensity moderate–vigorous (HR 140–170 or talk test); Time 30 min; Type jogging/biking.

days.guide: Choose enjoyable activities and justify.

questions.q: Why choose enjoyable activities?
questions.a: People stick with activities they enjoy, which makes lifelong fitness more likely.

days.guide: Add backup plans.

questions.q: Give a no-equipment backup workout.
questions.a: Body-weight circuit: squats, push-ups, lunges, planks, jumping jacks, 3 rounds.

days.guide: Start day 1 and log.

questions.q: What should a log entry include?
questions.a: Date, activity, time, intensity (HR/RPE), and notes on how it felt.

days.guide: Parent reviews for safety and balance; revise.

questions.q: How many rest/recovery days are appropriate in 14 days?
questions.a: About 2–4 rest or active-recovery days.

weeks.assessment_key: Two-week plan: 4 = 14 days with FITT for each session, balanced cardio/strength/flexibility, 2–4 rest days, warm-ups/cool-downs, backup plans, justified choices; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = unbalanced or missing FITT; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Fitness journal, watch or heart-rate monitor.
misconceptions: Skipping logging. Correct: log immediately after each session.
Pushing through pain. Correct: distinguish muscle effort from sharp joint pain; stop and rest for pain.

days.guide: Complete and log workout with HR and RPE.

questions.q: What RPE fits a moderate workout?
questions.a: About 5–6 out of 10.

days.guide: Strength and flexibility workout.

questions.q: Why stretch after strength training?
questions.a: Muscles are warm, so static stretching can maintain flexibility and aid relaxation.

days.guide: Cardio workout; record time and intensity.

questions.q: How can you check intensity without a monitor?
questions.a: Talk test or RPE.

days.guide: Activity or active rest day.

questions.q: What is active rest?
questions.a: Light activity (walking, easy stretching) that promotes recovery.

days.guide: Calculate adherence and adjust.

questions.q: You completed 6 of 7 planned sessions. What's your adherence?

weeks.assessment_key: Activity log week 1: proficient = 5+ entries with date, activity, duration, HR/RPE and notes; adherence calculated correctly; one adjustment written.

weeks.prep: Fitness journal; search your local high school's PE requirements (California requires 2 years of high school PE; students may be exempted after passing FitnessGram in grade 10 per district policy). Plan field day stations.
misconceptions: Thinking PE ends after school requirements. Correct: lifelong activity is the goal.
Evaluating a plan only by results. Correct: also evaluate adherence and enjoyment.

days.guide: Complete and log the workout.

questions.q: Why log even routine workouts?
questions.a: Logs show patterns and progress.

days.guide: Final scheduled workout.

questions.q: How did the final workout compare to day 1?
questions.a: Answers vary; compare HR, RPE or reps.

days.guide: Write evaluation: adherence, enjoyment, results, one change.

questions.q: What makes a fitness plan successful?
questions.a: It's followed consistently, is enjoyable, safe and leads toward goals.

days.guide: Research high school PE and write two goals.

questions.q: How many years of PE does California require for high school graduation?
questions.a: Two years (20 credits), with possible exemption options set by state law and district policy.

days.guide: Organize and lead a field day.

questions.q: What makes a good field day station?
questions.a: Clear instructions, safe setup, everyone active, a fun challenge from a unit this year.

weeks.assessment_key: Plan evaluation: 4 = adherence %, enjoyment, results with data, one specific change; field day leadership: 4 = 4+ stations planned, clear instructions, safety, everyone included; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = disorganized; 1 = incomplete.

SCI.overview: Science 8 follows California's integrated model: forces and energy, gravity and space, waves, Earth's history, heredity and natural selection, finishing with an engineering capstone. Each week has a hands-on investigation with household materials; have the child predict first, record data with units in a science notebook, and explain results in claim-evidence-reasoning form. Preview PhET simulations before using them and supervise any drops, launches or kitchen chemistry.

weeks.prep: Toy car, masking tape, meter stick, stopwatch/phone timer, graph paper; a composition notebook for the science notebook. Clear a 3-meter smooth floor path. Bookmark PhET 'Forces and Motion: Basics' (phet.colorado.edu).
misconceptions: Thinking speed and velocity are the same. Velocity includes direction: 2 m/s east and 2 m/s west are the same speed but different velocities.
Reading a distance-time graph as a picture of a hill. Steepness is speed; a flat segment means stopped.

days.guide: Help the child set up a notebook (table of contents, dated entries). Roll the car past while one person stands still and another walks alongside it; each describes the motion. Explain that motion is always described relative to a reference frame.

questions.q: To you walking beside the car at the same speed, how does the car appear to move?
questions.a: It appears not to move (stationary) relative to you, though it is moving relative to the floor.

days.guide: Mark 0.5-m intervals over 3 m. The child releases or pushes the car, you time it, and the child calculates average speed = distance ÷ time for 3 trials.

questions.q: The car covers 3 m in 2.4 s. What is its average speed?
Why do 3 trials?
questions.a: To reduce the effect of random errors like reaction time; average the results.

days.guide: The child graphs distance (y) vs time (x) for the car and for a walk that includes a stop. Ask what the steepness and flat parts mean.

questions.q: What does a flat (horizontal) section mean on a distance-time graph?
questions.a: The object is stopped — time passes but distance doesn't change.

questions.q: Which is faster: a steep line or a shallow line?
questions.a: The steep line.

days.guide: Open the PhET motion screen; the child changes push direction and records speed vs velocity observations. To check, ask: "A car moves 5 m/s north, then 5 m/s south. Same speed? Same velocity?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: A car moves 5 m/s north, then 5 m/s south. Same speed? Same velocity?
questions.a: Same speed (5 m/s), different velocity because direction changed.

days.guide: Give the quiz (key) and have the child write the lab summary paragraph. Finish by asking: "At 4 m/s, how far does an object go in 6 s?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: At 4 m/s, how far does an object go in 6 s?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) A car travels 3 m in 1.5 s → 2 m/s. 2) A walker goes 100 m in 80 s → 1.25 m/s. 3) At 4 m/s, how far in 6 s? 24 m. 4) Graphs: steeper line = faster; flat line = stopped; straight line = constant speed; curve getting steeper = speeding up. Lab data/graph: table with distance, time for 3 trials, average speed (distance ÷ time) with units; labeled axes (time on x, distance on y); accurate plotting. Summary paragraph names question, method, result with a number, and one source of error (reaction time).

weeks.prep: Rubber bands (or a small spring scale), a shoe, string, a ruler, three floor surfaces (carpet, tile, wood). Bookmark the PhET tug-of-war screen.
misconceptions: Thinking an object needs a net force to keep moving. Net force changes motion; with zero net force a moving object keeps moving at constant velocity.
Adding forces in opposite directions instead of subtracting. Opposite forces subtract; the net force points toward the larger one.

days.guide: Draw arrows from the center of an object; arrow length shows strength. The child draws force diagrams for 6 situations, labeling each force.

questions.q: Draw the forces on a book resting on a table.
questions.a: Gravity (weight) pointing down and the normal force from the table pointing up, equal in size, so net force is zero.

days.guide: In PhET tug-of-war, the child predicts motion before pressing Go for 8 combinations and calculates net force each time. Check understanding with: "100 N pulls left and 150 N pulls right. Net force and motion?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: 100 N pulls left and 150 N pulls right. Net force and motion?
questions.a: 50 N to the right; the cart accelerates right.

questions.q: If the net force is zero, can the cart be moving?
questions.a: Yes — it keeps moving at constant velocity (or stays at rest).

days.guide: Tie the shoe to a rubber band; pull it slowly at steady speed across each surface and measure stretch. Keep the same shoe, same pull speed and same rubber band (controlled variables).

questions.q: Why use the same shoe on all surfaces?
questions.a: To control variables so only the surface changes.

days.guide: The child graphs stretch for each surface (bar graph), lists controlled variables, and writes a CER paragraph. Finish by asking: "Why a bar graph instead of a line graph?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why a bar graph instead of a line graph?
questions.a: Surface type is categorical, not continuous.

days.guide: Give the force-diagram quiz and collect the CER. Before moving on, ask: "What force always opposes sliding motion?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What force always opposes sliding motion?
questions.a: Friction.

weeks.assessment_key: Force-diagram quiz: 1) Book on a table: gravity down, table's normal force up, equal → net 0. 2) 30 N right and 20 N left → 10 N right. 3) 50 N and 50 N opposite → 0 N, balanced. 4) Two people pull right with 40 N and 25 N, one pulls left with 60 N → 5 N right. CER rubric (4 levels): 4 = claim answers the question; evidence cites specific measured data (numbers with units) from the lab; reasoning links evidence to the science idea; 3 = all parts, reasoning thin; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only. Sample claim: 'Carpet produces the most friction because the rubber band stretched the most (e.g., 6 cm vs 3 cm on tile).'

weeks.prep: Index card, coin, cup; toy car, washers or coins, tape, a board-and-books ramp, meter stick, stopwatch.
misconceptions: Expecting heavier cars to roll down a ramp much faster. Gravity pulls harder on more mass, but more mass is harder to accelerate, so (ignoring friction) acceleration is about the same.
Thinking inertia is a force. Inertia is an object's resistance to changes in motion, which depends on mass.

days.guide: Place the card on a cup with a coin on top; flick the card out. The child explains why the coin drops into the cup (inertia) and writes Newton's first law.

questions.q: Why does the coin fall into the cup instead of flying off with the card?
questions.a: The coin's inertia keeps it at rest; the quick flick applies little friction force to it, so it stays put and gravity pulls it into the cup.

days.guide: Model a good plan: question, hypothesis, independent/dependent/controlled variables, numbered procedure, blank data table. The child writes the plan.

questions.q: Name the independent, dependent and two controlled variables.
questions.a: Independent: number of washers; dependent: time (and speed) down the ramp; controlled: ramp height, release point, distance, the car.

days.guide: Run 3 trials each for 0, 2, 4 and 6 washers; the child records times and calculates average speeds. Finish by asking: "If the 6-washer car's time is nearly the same as the empty car's, what does that suggest?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: If the 6-washer car's time is nearly the same as the empty car's, what does that suggest?
questions.a: Added mass doesn't much change speed down a ramp — gravity's pull increases with mass, but so does inertia.

days.guide: The child graphs average speed vs washers, then solves 8 F = ma problems. Connect: on a ramp both force and mass increase together.

questions.q: A 2-kg cart is pushed with 10 N. Acceleration?
questions.a: a = F/m = 5 m/s².

questions.q: Same 10 N on a 4-kg cart?
questions.a: 2.5 m/s² — double the mass, half the acceleration.

days.guide: The child writes the conclusion; give the quiz (key). Check understanding with: "What force gives a 5-kg object an acceleration of 3 m/s²?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What force gives a 5-kg object an acceleration of 3 m/s²?

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric (4 levels): question, hypothesis, variables (independent = washers, dependent = time/speed, controlled = ramp height, release point, distance), data table with 3 trials and averages, graph, conclusion that matches data (expected: little change in speed with added mass; small differences due to friction and timing error), sources of error. Quiz: 1) Newton's first law: an object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity unless acted on by an unbalanced force. 2) F = ma: 10 N on 2 kg → 5 m/s². 3) 3 kg accelerating at 4 m/s² → 12 N. 4) 20 N gives 4 m/s² → 5 kg. 5) Same force on double mass → half the acceleration.

weeks.prep: Balloons (3), string (5 m), straw, tape, marbles of two sizes, a ruler with a groove. Find a slow-motion crash test video (IIHS or NHTSA on YouTube).
misconceptions: Thinking action and reaction forces cancel. They act on different objects, so they don't cancel each other.
Thinking the bigger object exerts a bigger force in a collision. The forces are equal and opposite; the effects differ because masses differ.

days.guide: Thread the string through the straw, tape a balloon to it, release and measure distance for 3 inflation sizes. Identify the force pair.

questions.q: What is the force pair in the balloon rocket?
questions.a: The balloon pushes air out the back; the air pushes the balloon forward.

questions.q: Why does a bigger inflation go farther?
questions.a: More air pushed out for longer gives a larger/longer forward push.

days.guide: The child labels action-reaction pairs in 8 scenarios and explains why they don't cancel. Finish by asking: "Why don't action-reaction forces cancel?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why don't action-reaction forces cancel?
questions.a: They act on different objects; forces cancel only when they act on the same object.

days.guide: Roll marbles into each other along the groove; record same-size and different-size collisions. Before moving on, ask: "A moving marble hits an identical still marble head-on. What happens?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: A moving marble hits an identical still marble head-on. What happens?
questions.a: The moving one nearly stops and the other rolls away at about the same speed.

days.guide: Watch the crash-test video in slow motion. Discuss how seatbelts and airbags increase the time over which the dummy stops, reducing force.

questions.q: How does an airbag reduce injury?
questions.a: It increases the stopping time and spreads the force over a larger area, so the force on the person is smaller.

days.guide: Give the quiz and the two force-pair diagrams. To check, ask: "A truck hits a bug. Which feels the larger force?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: A truck hits a bug. Which feels the larger force?
questions.a: Neither — the forces are equal; the bug has far less mass, so it undergoes a huge acceleration.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) State Newton's third law: for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. 2) Swimmer: pushes water back; water pushes swimmer forward. 3) Rocket: pushes gas down/back; gas pushes rocket up/forward. 4) Hammer hits nail: hammer pushes nail in; nail pushes back on hammer. 5) Truck hits bug: forces equal; bug's tiny mass gets huge acceleration. Force-pair diagrams: arrows equal length, opposite direction, on different objects. Collision notes: equal marbles — the moving marble stops and the other moves on; big hits small — both move forward, small faster; small hits big — small bounces back, big moves slowly.

weeks.prep: Raw eggs (or water balloons), straws, tape, cardboard, cotton balls, rubber bands, plastic bags. Choose a 2-m drop site with easy cleanup. Prepare the Unit 1 test.
misconceptions: Thinking the goal is a stronger (harder) shell. Softer, crushable designs work better because they increase stopping time.
Changing many things at once when iterating. Change one main feature so you know what helped.

days.guide: Define criteria (must survive a 2-m drop; mass under 100 g) and constraints (only listed materials, 30 minutes to build). The child writes both lists.

questions.q: Criteria vs constraints?
questions.a: Criteria are what a successful design must do; constraints are limits (materials, time, cost, size).

days.guide: The child sketches 3 designs and scores them in a decision matrix (cost, mass, expected protection). Before moving on, ask: "Why use a decision matrix?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why use a decision matrix?
questions.a: It compares designs fairly against the criteria instead of choosing by gut feeling.

days.guide: Build and drop. Observe and record whether the egg survived and how the device changed during impact.

questions.q: Why does padding protect the egg?
questions.a: It increases the time it takes the egg to stop, so the force on it is smaller.

days.guide: Redesign one feature based on data, retest, and compare with another family member's design. To check, ask: "Your egg cracked on the side that hit first. What one change makes sense?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Your egg cracked on the side that hit first. What one change makes sense?
questions.a: Add more crushable padding on that side (or a parachute to reduce speed).

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test and collect the notebook pages. Finish by asking: "A 4-kg object accelerates at 2 m/s². Net force?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: A 4-kg object accelerates at 2 m/s². Net force?

weeks.assessment_key: Engineering notebook rubric (4 levels): criteria and constraints listed; 3 labeled sketches; decision matrix with scores; test data; redesign explained using evidence; reflection connects to force and collision time. Unit 1 test sample answers: speed = d/t (6 m in 3 s → 2 m/s); net force of 25 N right and 10 N left → 15 N right; F = ma (4 kg × 2 m/s² = 8 N); Newton's first law (inertia); third law pairs on different objects; crumple zones increase collision time to reduce force.

weeks.prep: A ramp (board + books), balls of different mass but similar size (golf ball, ping-pong ball, rubber ball), a paper cup with a 'door' cut in the rim, a ruler, masking tape.
misconceptions: Thinking kinetic energy doubles when speed doubles. KE depends on v², so doubling speed quadruples KE.
Thinking heavier objects always have more KE. A fast light object can have more KE than a slow heavy one.

days.guide: Brainstorm moving objects (a jogger, a bullet, a truck) and rank by kinetic energy. Introduce KE = ½mv² and units (joules).

questions.q: Rank: a slow-rolling bowling ball or a fast-thrown baseball?
questions.a: It depends on actual values; a fast baseball can have more KE because speed is squared.

days.guide: Roll balls of different mass from the same height into the cup; measure how far the cup slides. Check understanding with: "Why use the same ramp height for each ball?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Why use the same ramp height for each ball?
questions.a: So the speed at the bottom is about the same; only mass changes.

days.guide: Roll one ball from increasing heights; measure cup distance. To check, ask: "What happens to the cup distance as height increases?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What happens to the cup distance as height increases?
questions.a: It increases — more speed means more kinetic energy.

days.guide: The child graphs both data sets and calculates KE to explain why doubling speed matters more. Finish by asking: "A 2-kg ball goes 3 m/s, then 6 m/s. Compare KE." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: A 2-kg ball goes 3 m/s, then 6 m/s. Compare KE.
questions.a: 9 J vs 36 J — four times as much.

days.guide: Give the quiz (key). Before moving on, ask: "1000-kg car at 10 m/s: KE?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: 1000-kg car at 10 m/s: KE?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) KE = ½mv². 2) 2-kg ball at 3 m/s → 9 J. 3) 1000-kg car at 10 m/s → 50,000 J. 4) Same car at 20 m/s → 200,000 J (4 times). 5) 4-kg ball at 2 m/s → 8 J. Graph interpretation: mass vs KE is a straight line (proportional); speed vs KE curves upward (nonlinear). Graphs: labeled axes, two data sets, best-fit line or curve.

weeks.prep: Rubber bands, a ruler, a tray of flour or sand, a ball, magnets, paper clips, books.
misconceptions: Thinking potential energy only means height. Energy can be stored by stretching (elastic), position in a magnetic or electric field, or chemical bonds.
Forgetting that PE depends on the system (e.g., ball and Earth together).

days.guide: Drop a ball from 3 heights into flour; measure crater diameter. Check understanding with: "What does a bigger crater show?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What does a bigger crater show?
questions.a: More energy at impact — from more gravitational PE stored at greater height.

days.guide: Launch rubber bands stretched 5, 10 and 15 cm (point away from people); measure distance. To check, ask: "Why does a 15-cm stretch fly farther?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Why does a 15-cm stretch fly farther?
questions.a: More stretch stores more elastic PE, which becomes more KE.

days.guide: Bring a paper clip slowly toward a magnet and measure the jump distance; draw how arrangement changes stored energy. Finish by asking: "When is magnetic PE greatest between a magnet and paper clip?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: When is magnetic PE greatest between a magnet and paper clip?
questions.a: When they are held apart (separated), since the attraction can do work as they come together.

days.guide: The child draws before/after energy models for a roller coaster, a bow and arrow, and two magnets. Before moving on, ask: "Describe energy in a bow and arrow." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Describe energy in a bow and arrow.
questions.a: Elastic PE in the drawn bow becomes KE of the arrow.

days.guide: Give the quiz (key). Check understanding with: "Calculate GPE of a 2-kg book on a 1.5-m shelf." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Calculate GPE of a 2-kg book on a 1.5-m shelf.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) GPE = mgh; 2-kg book on a 1.5-m shelf → 2 × 9.8 × 1.5 = 29.4 J. 2) More stretch = more elastic PE. 3) Pulling two attracting magnets apart increases PE; letting them snap together converts it to KE. 4) Roller coaster: most GPE at the top, most KE at the bottom. Model diagrams rubric: before/after pictures with energy bars or labels for each energy type and a statement that total energy is conserved (some becomes thermal).

weeks.prep: Foam pipe insulation cut lengthwise (or paper track), marbles, tape, string, washers. Bookmark PhET 'Energy Skate Park.'
misconceptions: Thinking energy is 'used up' or lost when things slow down. Energy is conserved; it transforms into thermal energy and sound.
Thinking a ball can rise higher than its starting point without extra energy. Without added energy, it can't exceed its starting height.
