days.guide: Run Energy Skate Park with bar graphs on. The child records 3 patterns (KE high at bottom, PE high at top, total constant without friction).

questions.q: What happens to the total energy bar when friction is off?
questions.a: It stays constant; KE and PE trade off.

days.guide: Build a washer pendulum; observe swings and why it stops. Finish by asking: "Why does a pendulum eventually stop?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why does a pendulum eventually stop?
questions.a: Air resistance and friction at the pivot transform its mechanical energy into thermal energy (and a little sound).

days.guide: Build a foam coaster with a loop; find the minimum start height. Before moving on, ask: "Why must the marble start higher than the top of the loop?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why must the marble start higher than the top of the loop?
questions.a: It needs extra energy as KE at the top to stay on the track, plus energy lost to friction.

days.guide: The child writes a CER on where the marble's energy went. Check understanding with: "Where does energy go as a marble slows on a flat track?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Where does energy go as a marble slows on a flat track?
questions.a: Into thermal energy (heating the track and air) and sound through friction.

days.guide: Review the CER with the rubric; give a short energy transfer quiz. To check, ask: "Name the energy transformation in a falling ball." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Name the energy transformation in a falling ball.
questions.a: Gravitational PE to KE.

weeks.assessment_key: Coaster design: marble completes the loop; minimum start height recorded (theory for a frictionless slider is 2.5 times the loop radius above the bottom; real coasters need more because of friction and rolling). CER rubric (4 levels): 4 = claim answers the question; evidence cites specific measured data (numbers with units) from the lab; reasoning links evidence to the science idea; 3 = all parts, reasoning thin; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only. Proficient claim: 'The marble's energy wasn't destroyed; it was transformed into thermal energy and sound by friction, so the total stayed the same.'

weeks.prep: Tennis, rubber (bouncy) and clay (or play-dough) balls; meter stick; phone with slow-motion video. Prepare the Unit 2 test.
misconceptions: Thinking a rebound shows energy was 'lost.' It was transformed into heat, sound and deformation.
Confusing elastic and inelastic collisions. Elastic: little energy transformed (objects bounce); inelastic: much transformed (objects deform or stick).

days.guide: Drop each ball from 1 m; measure rebound height; calculate percent energy retained = rebound ÷ drop × 100. Finish by asking: "A tennis ball rebounds to 55 cm from 100 cm. Percent energy retained?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: A tennis ball rebounds to 55 cm from 100 cm. Percent energy retained?
questions.a: About 55% (GPE is proportional to height).

questions.q: Where did the other 45% go?
questions.a: Thermal energy, sound and deformation of the ball and floor.

days.guide: Film collisions in slow motion; identify where energy goes. Before moving on, ask: "What does the clay ball's flattening show?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What does the clay ball's flattening show?
questions.a: Energy went into permanent deformation — an inelastic collision.

days.guide: The child creates a concept map connecting force, motion, KE, PE and energy transfer. Check understanding with: "How are force and energy connected?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: How are force and energy connected?
questions.a: A force acting over a distance transfers energy (work).

days.guide: Practice with 3 KE graph questions. To check, ask: "A KE vs speed graph curves upward. Why?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: A KE vs speed graph curves upward. Why?
questions.a: KE depends on speed squared.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test. Finish by asking: "Calculate GPE of a 5-kg object 2 m high." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Calculate GPE of a 5-kg object 2 m high.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test sample answers: KE = ½mv² (3-kg at 4 m/s → 24 J); doubling speed quadruples KE; GPE = mgh (5-kg at 2 m → 98 J); energy is conserved, transforming to thermal energy; elastic vs inelastic; data question: steeper KE vs speed curve explained by v².

weeks.prep: Bathroom scale, NASA planet fact sheet, a few balls, a stretchy sheet or fabric, marbles. Bookmark PhET 'Gravity Force Lab.'
misconceptions: Thinking heavier objects fall faster. Without air resistance all objects fall with the same acceleration.
Confusing mass and weight. Mass (kg) is amount of matter and doesn't change; weight (N) is the gravitational force and depends on location.

days.guide: Drop two objects of different mass (e.g., a book and a closed water bottle) together; they land at the same time. Discuss mass vs weight.

questions.q: Why does a feather fall slower than a hammer on Earth but not on the Moon?
questions.a: Air resistance slows the feather on Earth; the Moon has no air, so both fall together (shown by Apollo 15).

days.guide: Stretch a sheet; place a heavy ball in the middle and roll marbles. Discuss what the model shows and its limits.

questions.q: Limit of the sheet model?
questions.a: It relies on Earth's gravity pulling down on the sheet and shows 2-D only; it is just an analogy.

days.guide: Use NASA data to calculate weight on each planet; graph mass vs surface gravity. To check, ask: "If you weigh 100 lb on Earth, about how much on Mars?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: If you weigh 100 lb on Earth, about how much on Mars?
questions.a: About 38 lb (Mars gravity ≈ 0.38 × Earth's).

days.guide: Use PhET Gravity Force Lab to change masses and distance; write an argument with evidence. Finish by asking: "What happens to gravitational force if one mass doubles?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What happens to gravitational force if one mass doubles?
questions.a: The force doubles.

days.guide: Give the quiz (key). Before moving on, ask: "Does your mass change on the Moon?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Does your mass change on the Moon?
questions.a: No — only your weight changes.

weeks.assessment_key: Argument rubric: claim that gravitational force depends on the masses (and distance); evidence from planet data (more massive planets generally have stronger surface gravity, e.g., Jupiter 24.8 m/s² vs Earth 9.8 vs Mars 3.7) and the PhET sim (doubling a mass doubles the force); reasoning. Quiz: mass stays the same on the Moon; 100 lb on Earth ≈ 38 lb on Mars and ≈ 17 lb on the Moon; gravity is always attractive; force decreases with distance.

weeks.prep: A lamp without a shade, a foam ball on a pencil, a dark room, a moon observation chart. Check tonight's moon phase (e.g., timeanddate.com).
misconceptions: Thinking Earth's shadow causes moon phases. Phases come from how much of the sunlit half we see; Earth's shadow only matters in lunar eclipses.
Thinking eclipses should happen every month. The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5°, so the Sun, Earth and Moon line up only at certain times.

days.guide: Start the 14-day moon log tonight; research tonight's phase. Check understanding with: "Where should you record each observation?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Where should you record each observation?
questions.a: Date, time, shape sketch, and position in the sky.

days.guide: In a dark room, hold the ball at arm's length and turn in a circle around the lamp; sketch the lit part at 8 positions. To check, ask: "When the ball is between you and the lamp, what phase do you see?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: When the ball is between you and the lamp, what phase do you see?
questions.a: New moon — the lit side faces away.

days.guide: Order phase photos; explain why we always see the same side. Finish by asking: "Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
questions.a: It rotates once for each orbit (about 27 days), so the same face points toward Earth.

days.guide: Use the lamp model to show solar and lunar eclipses. Before moving on, ask: "Why don't eclipses happen every month?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why don't eclipses happen every month?
questions.a: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to Earth's orbit, so it usually passes above or below the Sun-Earth line.

days.guide: Give the quiz; update the moon log. Check understanding with: "During which phase can a solar eclipse occur?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: During which phase can a solar eclipse occur?
questions.a: New moon.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: phases in order: new, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full, waning gibbous, third (last) quarter, waning crescent; cycle ≈ 29.5 days; solar eclipse: Moon between Sun and Earth at new moon; lunar eclipse: Earth between Sun and Moon at full moon; umbra = darkest part of a shadow. Sketch rubric: 8 phases correctly shaded and labeled.

weeks.prep: Flashlight, graph paper, a globe or ball with an axis, a lamp, sunrise/sunset data for your city and a Southern Hemisphere city (timeanddate.com).
misconceptions: Thinking seasons are caused by Earth's distance from the Sun. Earth is closest in early January — during Northern Hemisphere winter.
Thinking the tilt changes direction. The axis stays pointed toward the North Star as Earth orbits.

days.guide: The child writes what causes seasons, then examines Earth-Sun distance data. To check, ask: "When is Earth closest to the Sun?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: When is Earth closest to the Sun?
questions.a: Early January (about 147 million km).

days.guide: Shine the flashlight straight down and at an angle onto graph paper; count lit squares. Finish by asking: "Why is angled light weaker?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why is angled light weaker?
questions.a: The same energy spreads over a larger area.

days.guide: Graph day length for both cities. Before moving on, ask: "How do the graphs compare?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: How do the graphs compare?
questions.a: They are opposites: when one has long days, the other has short.

days.guide: Walk the tilted globe around the lamp. Check understanding with: "At the June solstice, which hemisphere tilts toward the Sun?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: At the June solstice, which hemisphere tilts toward the Sun?
questions.a: Northern.

days.guide: Write the seasons explanation; give the quiz. To check, ask: "What causes seasons?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What causes seasons?
questions.a: Earth's tilted axis.

weeks.assessment_key: Seasons explanation rubric: Earth's 23.5° tilt means each hemisphere receives more direct sunlight and longer days in its summer and less direct sunlight and shorter days in winter; references flashlight lab (same light spread over more area at an angle) and day-length data; addresses the distance misconception. Quiz: solstices ~June 21 and ~December 21; equinoxes ~March 20 and ~September 22 (about 12 hours of day everywhere); Southern Hemisphere has opposite seasons.

weeks.prep: String, a soft ball or eraser, open outdoor space; PhET 'Gravity and Orbits'; NASA galaxy images (nasa.gov / hubblesite.org).
misconceptions: Thinking there's no gravity in space. Astronauts in orbit are in free fall; gravity there is still about 90% of surface gravity.
Thinking orbiting objects need a push to keep moving. Inertia keeps them moving; gravity curves the path.

days.guide: Swing the ball on a string in a circle and release it (outdoors, safely). Note it flies off in a straight line.

questions.q: What does the string represent?
questions.a: Gravity — the inward pull that keeps the object curving.

days.guide: In the sim, turn gravity off and change masses; record effects. Before moving on, ask: "What happens when gravity is turned off?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What happens when gravity is turned off?
questions.a: The planet moves off in a straight line.

days.guide: Read about the solar nebula; draw a 4-panel model. Check understanding with: "How did the Sun form?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: How did the Sun form?
questions.a: Gravity pulled the center of a spinning gas cloud together until it was hot enough for fusion.

days.guide: Explore galaxy images; explain gravity's role. To check, ask: "About how many stars are in the Milky Way?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: About how many stars are in the Milky Way?
questions.a: Roughly 100–400 billion.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Finish by asking: "Why doesn't the Moon fly away?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why doesn't the Moon fly away?
questions.a: Earth's gravity pulls it inward.

weeks.assessment_key: Formation model rubric: 4 panels — a rotating cloud of gas and dust (solar nebula); gravity pulls it inward and it spins faster and flattens into a disk; the Sun forms in the hot center; planets form by accretion of particles. Quiz: an orbit results from inertia (forward motion) plus gravity (pull toward center); without gravity an orbiting object moves off in a straight line; the Milky Way is a spiral galaxy with hundreds of billions of stars held by gravity.

weeks.prep: Toilet paper roll, marker, calculator, NASA planet fact sheet, hallway or outdoor space. Prepare the Unit 3 test.
misconceptions: Thinking textbook diagrams show true scale. Planets are tiny and far apart; diagrams compress distances.
Thinking a light-year is time. It's a distance (about 9.5 trillion km).

days.guide: Compare diameters: Earth 12,756 km, Jupiter 142,984 km, Sun ~1,392,700 km. Before moving on, ask: "How many Earths fit across Jupiter? Across the Sun?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: How many Earths fit across Jupiter? Across the Sun?
questions.a: About 11 across Jupiter and about 109 across the Sun.

days.guide: Unroll the toilet paper; mark planets at their squares. Check understanding with: "Where is Earth?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Where is Earth?
questions.a: About 15 squares from the Sun.

days.guide: Explain why one model can't show both size and distance. To check, ask: "If Earth is a 2-mm peppercorn, how far from the Sun?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: If Earth is a 2-mm peppercorn, how far from the Sun?
questions.a: About 23.5 m, with a Sun about 22 cm wide.

days.guide: Review with a study guide. Finish by asking: "What is an AU?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What is an AU?
questions.a: Earth-Sun average distance, about 150 million km.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test. Before moving on, ask: "What is a light-year?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What is a light-year?
questions.a: The distance light travels in a year, about 9.5 trillion km.

weeks.assessment_key: Scale model rubric: planets placed at correct squares (1 square ≈ 10 million km): Mercury ~6, Venus ~11, Earth ~15, Mars ~23, Jupiter ~78, Saturn ~143, Uranus ~287, Neptune ~450 squares. Unit 3 test sample answers: gravity depends on mass and distance; phases from viewing angle of the sunlit half; solar eclipse at new moon, lunar at full; seasons from tilt; orbits from inertia + gravity; 1 AU ≈ 150 million km.

weeks.prep: A Slinky or long rope, a ruler, a pan of water, pebbles. Bookmark PhET 'Wave on a String.'
misconceptions: Thinking the material travels with the wave. Waves carry energy; the medium only vibrates in place.
Thinking higher frequency means faster waves. In the same medium speed is constant; higher frequency means shorter wavelength.

days.guide: Make transverse and longitudinal waves with the Slinky; sketch and label. Check understanding with: "Which kind of wave is sound?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Which kind of wave is sound?
questions.a: Longitudinal.

days.guide: In PhET, change amplitude and frequency; measure wavelength. To check, ask: "What happens to wavelength as frequency increases?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What happens to wavelength as frequency increases?
questions.a: It decreases.

days.guide: Drop a pebble from different heights; observe wave height. Finish by asking: "What does greater amplitude mean?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What does greater amplitude mean?
questions.a: More energy.

days.guide: Teach v = fλ; the child solves 8 problems. Before moving on, ask: "v = 340 m/s, f = 170 Hz. Wavelength?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: v = 340 m/s, f = 170 Hz. Wavelength?

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check understanding with: "Define wavelength." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Define wavelength.
questions.a: Distance from one crest to the next.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: label crest, trough, wavelength (crest to crest), amplitude (rest to crest). v = fλ: 1) f = 5 Hz, λ = 2 m → 10 m/s. 2) v = 340 m/s, f = 170 Hz → λ = 2 m. 3) v = 12 m/s, λ = 3 m → f = 4 Hz. 4) Transverse = vibrations perpendicular to wave direction (rope); longitudinal = parallel (sound, Slinky push).

weeks.prep: Paper cups, string, rubber bands, a tissue box, 4–5 identical glasses, water, a spoon, towels, foam, cardboard; install a free decibel-meter app.
misconceptions: Thinking sound travels best through air. Sound travels faster and often more clearly through solids and liquids, and not at all through a vacuum.
Confusing pitch with loudness. Pitch depends on frequency; loudness on amplitude.

days.guide: Pluck rubber bands over a tissue box; change tension and length and record pitch. To check, ask: "How does tightening a rubber band change pitch?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: How does tightening a rubber band change pitch?
questions.a: Higher pitch — it vibrates at a higher frequency.

days.guide: Make a cup-and-string telephone; compare transmission through string, air and a table. Finish by asking: "Why does the string phone work only when the string is tight?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why does the string phone work only when the string is tight?
questions.a: The vibrations travel through the taut string; a slack string doesn't transmit them well.

days.guide: Tap glasses filled to different levels; explain pitch differences. Before moving on, ask: "Which glass makes the lowest pitch when tapped?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Which glass makes the lowest pitch when tapped?
questions.a: The fullest — more water makes the glass vibrate more slowly (lower frequency).

days.guide: Play the same sound through each material and measure decibels with the app. Check understanding with: "Why keep phone volume and distance the same?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Why keep phone volume and distance the same?
questions.a: To control variables so only the material changes.

days.guide: Give the quiz and collect the absorption write-up. To check, ask: "Can sound travel through space?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Can sound travel through space?
questions.a: No — there's no medium.

weeks.assessment_key: Investigation report rubric (4 levels): question; hypothesis; controlled variables (same phone, volume, distance, sound); data table of decibel readings for each material with 3 trials; graph; conclusion (soft, porous materials like towels and foam usually absorb the most sound); sources of error. Quiz: pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude; sound needs a medium; tighter or shorter band → higher pitch.

weeks.prep: Flashlight, mirror, protractor, glass of water, pencil, coin, opaque cup, wax paper, aluminum foil, clear plastic, cardboard. Bookmark PhET 'Bending Light.'
misconceptions: Measuring reflection angles from the mirror's surface. Angles are measured from the normal (a line perpendicular to the surface).
Thinking refraction happens because light 'bends inside' water. It changes direction at the boundary because its speed changes.

days.guide: Shine the flashlight through each material; classify. Finish by asking: "Wax paper lets some light through but blurs it. Category?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Wax paper lets some light through but blurs it. Category?
questions.a: Translucent.

days.guide: Test the law of reflection with mirror, flashlight and protractor. Before moving on, ask: "Light hits a mirror at 40° from the normal. Reflection angle?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Light hits a mirror at 40° from the normal. Reflection angle?

days.guide: Observe a pencil in water and the 'appearing coin' trick; draw ray diagrams. Check understanding with: "Why does the coin appear when water is added?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Why does the coin appear when water is added?
questions.a: Light from the coin refracts at the water's surface and bends toward your eye.

days.guide: Use Bending Light to change materials and record ray paths. To check, ask: "When light enters a slower material at an angle, which way does it bend?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: When light enters a slower material at an angle, which way does it bend?
questions.a: Toward the normal.

days.guide: Give the ray-diagram quiz. Finish by asking: "State the law of reflection." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: State the law of reflection.
questions.a: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.

weeks.assessment_key: Ray diagram quiz: 1) Reflection: draw incident ray, normal, reflected ray; angle of incidence = angle of reflection (e.g., 30° in → 30° out). 2) Refraction from air into water: ray bends toward the normal. 3) From water into air: bends away from the normal. 4) Classify: clear plastic transparent, wax paper translucent, foil and cardboard opaque.

weeks.prep: A prism or glass of water, sunny window, white paper, red and blue cellophane, flashlight, colored objects. Prepare the semester exam (Units 1–4).
misconceptions: Thinking objects 'have' color. An object reflects certain wavelengths and absorbs the rest; color depends on the light.
Mixing up light and paint (pigment) color rules.

days.guide: Make a spectrum with a prism or water glass in sunlight. Before moving on, ask: "Why does white light separate?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why does white light separate?
questions.a: Different wavelengths refract by different amounts; violet bends most, red least.

days.guide: View colored objects through red and blue cellophane. Check understanding with: "A blue object through red cellophane looks how?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: A blue object through red cellophane looks how?
questions.a: Dark/black — the red filter blocks the blue light it reflects.

days.guide: Review forces and energy with a practice test. To check, ask: "Net force: 15 N right, 5 N left?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Net force: 15 N right, 5 N left?
questions.a: 10 N right.

days.guide: Review space and waves with a concept map. Finish by asking: "What causes a lunar eclipse?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What causes a lunar eclipse?
questions.a: Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon.

days.guide: Give the semester exam. Before moving on, ask: "What is the order of colors in the spectrum?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What is the order of colors in the spectrum?
questions.a: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

weeks.assessment_key: Semester exam sample answers: speed = d/t; net force; F = ma; Newton's three laws; KE = ½mv²; GPE = mgh; energy conservation; gravity and mass; phases, eclipses, seasons; wave parts and v = fλ; reflection and refraction; red object under blue light looks dark. Score by percent; 80% proficient.

weeks.prep: Flashlight, paper, pencil, phone. Prepare the Unit 4 test.
misconceptions: Thinking digital is always higher quality. Digital is more reliable to copy and transmit, but quality depends on sampling rate and compression.
Thinking Wi-Fi and cell signals are sound waves. They are electromagnetic (radio) waves.

days.guide: Agree on a binary code (e.g., short blink = 0, long blink = 1); send a 3-letter message with a flashlight. Check understanding with: "What number is 101 in binary?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What number is 101 in binary?
What caused errors?
questions.a: Noise — mistiming, missed blinks.

days.guide: Read about records, cassettes and digital audio; make a T-chart. To check, ask: "Advantage of digital?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Advantage of digital?
questions.a: Copies without degradation; easy to store, compress, transmit.

days.guide: Play telephone with a spoken message vs a numeric code. Finish by asking: "Why did the code survive better?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why did the code survive better?
questions.a: Discrete digits are easier to transmit accurately than continuous speech.

days.guide: Read about cell phones and Wi-Fi; summarize. Before moving on, ask: "What carries cell phone signals?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What carries cell phone signals?
questions.a: Radio waves (electromagnetic).

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test. Check understanding with: "Analog vs digital?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Analog vs digital?
questions.a: Analog is continuous; digital uses discrete values.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test sample answers: label wave parts; v = fλ; sound needs a medium; light reflection/refraction; transparent/translucent/opaque; analog = continuous signal, digital = discrete values (often 0s and 1s); digital signals resist noise because receivers only need to tell 0 from 1; binary 101 = 5; cell phones use radio waves to carry digitized data.

weeks.prep: Clear jar with lid, sand, soil, gravel, water; colored play-dough; small objects as 'fossils'; clear straws.
misconceptions: Thinking the top layer is oldest. By superposition, in undisturbed layers the bottom is oldest.
Thinking a fault or intrusion is older than the layers it cuts. Whatever cuts across layers is younger.

days.guide: Pour sand, soil and gravel into water in stages; let settle. To check, ask: "Which settles first?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Which settles first?
questions.a: Gravel (largest, heaviest particles).

days.guide: Build play-dough layers with fossils and a fault; core-sample with a straw. Finish by asking: "Which layer is oldest?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Which layer is oldest?
questions.a: The bottom one (if undisturbed).

days.guide: Order events in 4 diagrams with intrusions and faults. Before moving on, ask: "An igneous intrusion cuts through layers A–C. Older or younger?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: An igneous intrusion cuts through layers A–C. Older or younger?
questions.a: Younger than A–C.

days.guide: Correlate layers from three sites using index fossils. Check understanding with: "What makes a good index fossil?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What makes a good index fossil?
questions.a: Widespread, easily recognized, and lived for a short time.

days.guide: Give the sequencing quiz. To check, ask: "State the law of superposition." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: State the law of superposition.
questions.a: In undisturbed layers, the oldest is at the bottom.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: sequence two cross sections (accept sequences matching your diagrams); rules applied: superposition (oldest at bottom), cross-cutting relationships (intrusions/faults are younger than layers they cut), index fossils correlate layers of the same age.

weeks.prep: 5 m of adding-machine tape or toilet paper, meter stick, markers; 100 coins or M&Ms and a container.
misconceptions: Thinking humans and dinosaurs lived together. Non-avian dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago; humans appeared about 300,000 years ago.
Thinking half-life means half the time remains. It's the time for half the atoms to decay.

days.guide: Make the 4.6-m timeline; mark events. Finish by asking: "Where is the dinosaur extinction on a 4.6-m timeline?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Where is the dinosaur extinction on a 4.6-m timeline?
questions.a: 6.6 cm from the present end.

days.guide: Research the 5 mass extinctions and add them. Before moving on, ask: "Which was largest?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Which was largest?
questions.a: End-Permian, about 252 million years ago.

days.guide: Shake coins; remove 'decayed' ones; repeat and graph. Check understanding with: "After 3 half-lives, what fraction remains?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: After 3 half-lives, what fraction remains?

days.guide: Write a scientific explanation of how strata build the time scale. To check, ask: "Relative vs absolute dating?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Relative vs absolute dating?
questions.a: Relative orders events; absolute gives an age in years (radiometric).

days.guide: Give the quiz. Finish by asking: "How old is Earth?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: How old is Earth?
questions.a: About 4.6 billion years.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline: 4.6 m at 1 mm = 1 million years; first life ~3.5–3.8 billion years ago (3.5–3.8 m from present end); Cambrian explosion ~541 mya (54 cm); dinosaurs appear ~230 mya (23 cm); non-avian dinosaurs extinct ~66 mya (6.6 cm); Homo sapiens ~0.3 mya (0.3 mm). Five mass extinctions: end-Ordovician (~445 mya), Late Devonian (~372), end-Permian (~252, largest), end-Triassic (~201), end-Cretaceous (~66). Explanation rubric: rock strata order + index fossils give relative ages; radiometric dating gives absolute ages; major changes in fossils mark boundaries between eras and periods.

weeks.prep: Clay, a shell, plaster or glue; graph paper; marine family diversity data; whale fossil images (Pakicetus, Ambulocetus, Rodhocetus).
misconceptions: Thinking every organism becomes a fossil. Fossilization is rare; it requires rapid burial and usually hard parts.
Thinking 'transitional fossil' means a direct ancestor. It shows a mix of traits linking groups.

days.guide: Make a shell impression in clay and a cast. Before moving on, ask: "What conditions help fossilization?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What conditions help fossilization?
questions.a: Rapid burial in sediment, hard parts, low oxygen.

days.guide: Graph marine families over time. Check understanding with: "What does a sharp drop indicate?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What does a sharp drop indicate?
questions.a: A mass extinction.

days.guide: Analyze the three whale ancestors in order. To check, ask: "Describe the change from Pakicetus to Rodhocetus." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Describe the change from Pakicetus to Rodhocetus.
questions.a: From a four-legged land animal to an amphibious one with shorter limbs, more adapted to water.

days.guide: Explore a museum virtual collection; record 5 fossils. Finish by asking: "What is the fossil record?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What is the fossil record?
questions.a: All known fossils and their positions in rock layers.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Before moving on, ask: "Why are soft-bodied fossils rare?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why are soft-bodied fossils rare?
questions.a: Soft tissue decays quickly.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: interpret a fossil data table — e.g., sharp drops in marine families mark mass extinctions; diversity recovers and generally increases afterward; whale sequence shows hind limbs shrinking and adaptation to water over about 50–40 million years ago.

weeks.prep: Forelimb diagrams (human, cat, whale, bat), colored pencils, a cooked chicken wing (optional), paper towels.
misconceptions: Confusing homologous and analogous structures. Homologous share ancestry (same bones, different functions); analogous share function but not ancestry (bird wing vs insect wing).
Thinking vestigial structures have no function. They are reduced compared with ancestors; some still have minor functions.

days.guide: Color-code bones in four forelimbs. Check understanding with: "What do the four forelimbs share?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What do the four forelimbs share?
questions.a: The same bone pattern: one upper bone, two lower bones, wrist and finger bones.

days.guide: Examine the chicken wing (wash hands after). To check, ask: "Which human bones match the wing?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Which human bones match the wing?
questions.a: Humerus, radius and ulna.

days.guide: Research 4 vestigial structures. Finish by asking: "What does a whale's pelvis suggest?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What does a whale's pelvis suggest?
questions.a: Whales descended from four-legged land ancestors.

days.guide: Build a cladogram from a shared-traits table. Before moving on, ask: "What does a branch point represent?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What does a branch point represent?
questions.a: A common ancestor with a new trait.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check understanding with: "Homologous or analogous: bat wing and bird wing?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Homologous or analogous: bat wing and bird wing?
questions.a: As wings, analogous; as forelimbs, homologous.

weeks.assessment_key: Cladogram rubric: shared traits placed at branch points; organisms with more shared derived traits branch closer together. Quiz: human arm, cat leg, whale flipper and bat wing are homologous; bird wing and butterfly wing are analogous; whale pelvis and human tailbone are vestigial.

weeks.prep: Print embryo image cards (fish, chicken, pig, human at early and late stages; reputable sources such as university or museum sites). Prepare the Unit 5 practice test and test.
misconceptions: Thinking human embryos 'become fish' first. Early vertebrate embryos share structures (pharyngeal arches, tails) from common ancestry; they develop differently, not through adult fish stages.
Treating one line of evidence as proof. Scientists combine fossils, anatomy, embryology and DNA.

days.guide: Compare early and late embryo images. To check, ask: "What do early vertebrate embryos share?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What do early vertebrate embryos share?
questions.a: Pharyngeal arches (pouches) and a tail.

days.guide: Write a paragraph on what the similarities suggest. Finish by asking: "What do embryo similarities suggest?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What do embryo similarities suggest?
questions.a: The organisms share a common ancestor.

days.guide: Make a graphic organizer of three lines of evidence. Before moving on, ask: "Name three lines of evidence for evolution." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Name three lines of evidence for evolution.
questions.a: Fossil record, anatomical similarities, embryological similarities (also DNA).

days.guide: Practice test with corrections. Check understanding with: "After 2 half-lives, what fraction remains?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: After 2 half-lives, what fraction remains?

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test. To check, ask: "What era did dinosaurs live in?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What era did dinosaurs live in?
questions.a: Mesozoic.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test sample answers: superposition and cross-cutting relationships; index fossils; geologic time scale with eras (Paleozoic, Mesozoic, Cenozoic); five mass extinctions; half-life (after 2 half-lives, 1/4 remains); whale transitional fossils; homologous vs analogous vs vestigial; embryos of vertebrates share pharyngeal arches and tails early, suggesting common ancestry.

weeks.prep: A potato with eyes or an onion, a pothos (or other houseplant) cutting, a glass of water, index cards for the trait model.
misconceptions: Thinking asexual offspring are always identical forever. They are clones of the parent except for rare mutations.
Thinking sexual reproduction is always 'better.' Each strategy has advantages depending on the environment.

days.guide: Start the pothos cutting and potato eye; predict traits of the offspring. Finish by asking: "Will the new pothos look like the parent?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Will the new pothos look like the parent?
questions.a: Yes — it is a clone (same genes).

days.guide: Venn diagram: budding, binary fission, fragmentation vs sexual reproduction. Before moving on, ask: "Example of binary fission?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Example of binary fission?
questions.a: Bacteria splitting in two.

days.guide: Model gametes by drawing one card per trait from each parent. Check understanding with: "Why are offspring different?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Why are offspring different?
questions.a: Each gets a random mix of genes from two parents.

days.guide: Write an argument on advantages of each in changing environments. To check, ask: "Advantage of sexual reproduction?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Advantage of sexual reproduction?
questions.a: Variation that can help some offspring survive change.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Finish by asking: "Define gamete." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Define gamete.
questions.a: A sex cell (egg or sperm) with half the chromosomes.

weeks.assessment_key: Variation model: offspring receive one card per trait from each parent at random; 5 offspring show different combinations. Quiz: asexual = one parent, offspring genetically identical (budding, binary fission, fragmentation, cuttings); sexual = two parents, gametes combine, offspring vary; variation helps a population survive environmental change; asexual is fast and needs no mate.

weeks.prep: Coins (2 per child), paper, colored pencils. A summary of Mendel's pea data (e.g., 705 purple : 224 white flowers in F2).
misconceptions: Thinking dominant means most common. Dominant means it shows when present; some dominant traits are rare.
Mixing up genotype and phenotype. Genotype = alleles (Bb); phenotype = observable trait (brown).

days.guide: Read about Mendel; analyze F1 and F2 data. Before moving on, ask: "Mendel crossed purple × white; F1 all purple; F2 705 purple : 224 white. Ratio?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Mendel crossed purple × white; F1 all purple; F2 705 purple : 224 white. Ratio?
questions.a: About 3:1.

days.guide: Flip two coins 50 times to model offspring. Check understanding with: "What fraction of flips should be two tails (recessive)?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What fraction of flips should be two tails (recessive)?
questions.a: About 1/4.

days.guide: Complete 10 Punnett squares. To check, ask: "Cross Bb × bb." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Cross Bb × bb.

days.guide: Survey family traits; discuss limits. Finish by asking: "Why might single-gene models not fit?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why might single-gene models not fit?
questions.a: Many traits involve several genes and environment.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Before moving on, ask: "Genotype vs phenotype?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Genotype vs phenotype?
questions.a: Genotype: alleles; phenotype: observable trait.

weeks.assessment_key: Punnett square quiz: 1) Bb × Bb → 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb; 3 dominant : 1 recessive phenotype. 2) BB × bb → all Bb; all dominant. 3) Bb × bb → 1 Bb : 1 bb; 1:1. 4) Define allele, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, heterozygous. 5) Probability of bb from Bb × Bb = 25%.

weeks.prep: Candy or beads (4 colors), toothpicks; strawberries, zip bag, dish soap, salt, cold rubbing alcohol, coffee filter, clear cup; codon chart.
misconceptions: Thinking genes are traits. Genes are DNA instructions for proteins; proteins produce traits.
Pairing A with C. Bases pair A–T and C–G.

days.guide: Build a DNA ladder with candy bases. Check understanding with: "Complementary strand of A-T-G-C-C-A?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Complementary strand of A-T-G-C-C-A?
questions.a: T-A-C-G-G-T.

days.guide: Extract strawberry DNA. To check, ask: "What does the soap do?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What does the soap do?
questions.a: Breaks down cell and nuclear membranes.

days.guide: Translate an mRNA sequence with a codon chart. Finish by asking: "Translate AUG-GCA-UUU-UAA." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Translate AUG-GCA-UUU-UAA.
questions.a: Methionine – Alanine – Phenylalanine – Stop.

days.guide: Read about proteins and traits; summarize. Before moving on, ask: "What does hemoglobin do?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What does hemoglobin do?
questions.a: Carries oxygen in red blood cells.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check understanding with: "Gene → ? → trait" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Gene → ? → trait
questions.a: Protein.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric: procedure, observations (white stringy DNA at the alcohol layer), explanation (soap breaks membranes, salt clumps DNA, DNA is not soluble in alcohol). Quiz: DNA is a double helix of nucleotides; A–T, C–G; complementary strand of ATGC is TACG; a gene codes for a protein; codon AUG = methionine (start); proteins such as melanin-producing enzymes and hemoglobin affect traits.

weeks.prep: Codon chart, paper strips.
misconceptions: Thinking all mutations are harmful. Many are neutral; some are helpful in certain environments.
Thinking a substitution always changes the protein. Some codons code the same amino acid.

days.guide: Change letters in 'THE CAT ATE THE RAT' to model mutations. To check, ask: "Delete the first 'E' and regroup in threes." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Delete the first 'E' and regroup in threes.
questions.a: THC ATA TET HER AT — a frameshift garbles every word after it.

days.guide: Apply mutations to a DNA sequence and translate. Finish by asking: "Which mutation type usually has the biggest effect?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Which mutation type usually has the biggest effect?
questions.a: Insertion or deletion (frameshift).

days.guide: Research sickle cell and lactase persistence. Before moving on, ask: "Why is the sickle cell allele common in malaria regions?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why is the sickle cell allele common in malaria regions?
questions.a: Carriers resist malaria.

days.guide: Draw a gene→protein→trait model. Check understanding with: "Sickle cell model?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Sickle cell model?
questions.a: Base substitution → altered hemoglobin → sickle-shaped cells.

days.guide: Give the quiz. To check, ask: "Can a mutation be neutral?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Can a mutation be neutral?
questions.a: Yes.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: substitution, insertion, deletion; insertions/deletions cause frameshifts; sickle cell from a single base substitution in the hemoglobin gene, carriers have some malaria resistance; lactase persistence lets adults digest milk. Model rubric: gene change → protein change → trait.

weeks.prep: Images of teosinte and modern corn, wolves and dog breeds; short readings on insulin-producing bacteria, Golden Rice and CRISPR. Prepare the Unit 6 test.
misconceptions: Confusing artificial selection with genetic engineering. Selective breeding chooses parents; genetic engineering directly changes DNA.
Thinking GMOs are all the same. Each modification must be evaluated.

days.guide: Compare teosinte to corn and wolves to dogs. Finish by asking: "Trait humans selected in corn?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Trait humans selected in corn?
questions.a: Larger ears with many soft kernels.

days.guide: Read about insulin and Golden Rice. Before moving on, ask: "How do bacteria make human insulin?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: How do bacteria make human insulin?
questions.a: The human insulin gene is inserted into bacterial DNA (a plasmid); bacteria then produce insulin.

days.guide: Read about CRISPR; pro/con chart. Check understanding with: "One pro and one con of editing human embryos?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: One pro and one con of editing human embryos?
questions.a: Pro: prevent genetic diseases; con: unknown effects passed to future generations, ethical concerns.

days.guide: Practice test. To check, ask: "BB × bb offspring?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: BB × bb offspring?
questions.a: All Bb.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test. Finish by asking: "What does Golden Rice produce?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What does Golden Rice produce?
questions.a: Beta-carotene (vitamin A precursor).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test sample answers: asexual vs sexual; Punnett squares; DNA bases; gene→protein→trait; mutation types; artificial selection; insulin gene inserted into bacteria; Golden Rice makes beta-carotene; CRISPR edits DNA at targeted sites.

weeks.prep: Tweezers, spoons, clothespins, beads/beans/paper dots of several colors, patterned fabric, timer, cups.
misconceptions: Thinking individuals evolve. Populations change over generations; individuals don't change their genes.
Thinking organisms 'try' to adapt. Variation exists first; the environment selects.

days.guide: Use tools as beaks to collect foods. Before moving on, ask: "Which beak works best for small seeds?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Which beak works best for small seeds?
questions.a: Tweezers.

days.guide: Scatter dots on fabric; hunt 30 s. Check understanding with: "Which colors survive?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Which colors survive?
questions.a: Those matching the background.

days.guide: Survivors reproduce; repeat 3 generations. To check, ask: "What happens to camouflaged colors?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What happens to camouflaged colors?
questions.a: They increase.

days.guide: Write a CER on population change. Finish by asking: "What is natural selection?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What is natural selection?
questions.a: Individuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Before moving on, ask: "Define adaptation." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Define adaptation.
questions.a: An inherited trait that improves survival and reproduction.

weeks.assessment_key: Simulation data: color frequencies tracked for 3 generations; colors matching the fabric increase. CER rubric (4 levels): 4 = claim answers the question; evidence cites specific measured data (numbers with units) from the lab; reasoning links evidence to the science idea; 3 = all parts, reasoning thin; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only. Claim example: 'The green dots increased from 25% to 60% because they were camouflaged and survived to reproduce.'

weeks.prep: PhET 'Natural Selection' sim, graph paper, calculator; HHMI BioInteractive film 'The Making of the Fittest: Natural Selection and Adaptation' (rock pocket mouse, free online).
misconceptions: Thinking a mutation appears because the environment needs it. Mutations are random; selection acts on them.
Graphing raw counts when populations change size. Use percentages.

days.guide: Run PhET with brown fur and wolves for 10 generations. Check understanding with: "In the equator environment with wolves, which fur increases?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: In the equator environment with wolves, which fur increases?
questions.a: Brown.

days.guide: Convert counts to percentages; graph. To check, ask: "12 brown of 40 total — percent?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: 12 brown of 40 total — percent?

days.guide: Watch the rock pocket mouse film. Finish by asking: "Why are dark mice common on lava?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why are dark mice common on lava?
questions.a: Camouflage from owls.

days.guide: Calculate a 10% survival advantage over 5 generations. Before moving on, ask: "Start 10%; trait carriers survive 1.1× as well. After 5 generations?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Start 10%; trait carriers survive 1.1× as well. After 5 generations?

days.guide: Give the graph quiz. Check understanding with: "What is selective pressure?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What is selective pressure?
questions.a: An environmental factor that affects survival.

weeks.assessment_key: Graph analysis quiz: read trait percentages; identify selective pressure; in PhET with wolves, brown fur increases in the brown (equator) environment and white fur in the arctic; rock pocket mice: dark mice increase on dark lava rock because owls see light mice; 10% advantage from 10% → about 15% after 5 generations.

weeks.prep: Grant finch beak-depth data (HHMI BioInteractive), peppered moth data, beans or candies.
misconceptions: Thinking antibiotics make bacteria resistant. Resistant bacteria already exist; antibiotics kill the others.
Thinking finch beaks grew during the drought. Birds with deeper beaks survived.

days.guide: Analyze finch data before/after 1977 drought. To check, ask: "What happened to average beak depth?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What happened to average beak depth?
questions.a: Increased — deeper beaks could crack hard seeds.

days.guide: Graph peppered moth frequencies. Finish by asking: "Why did dark moths increase?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why did dark moths increase?
questions.a: Soot darkened trees, so dark moths were camouflaged from birds.

days.guide: Model antibiotic resistance with beans. Before moving on, ask: "Why finish antibiotics?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why finish antibiotics?
questions.a: To kill remaining bacteria and avoid selecting for resistant ones.

days.guide: Write a 4-paragraph case study. Check understanding with: "Steps of natural selection?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Steps of natural selection?
questions.a: Variation, inheritance, selection, time.

days.guide: Review with rubric. To check, ask: "What happened to dark moths after clean air laws?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What happened to dark moths after clean air laws?
questions.a: They declined.

weeks.assessment_key: Case study rubric: describes variation, selective pressure, differential survival/reproduction, inheritance, change over generations, with data.

weeks.prep: Notebook; reading on a California species such as the island fox (Channel Islands National Park / NPS site). Prepare a data-based practice test and the Unit 7 test.
misconceptions: Confusing acclimation with adaptation. Acclimation is a change within one individual's lifetime (tanning, thicker blood cells at altitude); adaptations are inherited traits shaped over generations.
Saying organisms evolve 'because they need to.' Natural selection acts on variation already present.

days.guide: Explain the difference with two examples (a tan vs naturally dark skin in high-UV regions). The child sorts 10 examples and justifies each.

questions.q: Is a person's tan an adaptation?
questions.a: No — it's acclimation, a change within one lifetime that isn't inherited.

questions.q: Is a polar bear's thick white fur an adaptation?
questions.a: Yes — an inherited trait shaped by natural selection.

days.guide: The child researches a California species (e.g., the island fox, smaller than its mainland gray-fox ancestor) and makes an infographic of 3 adaptations with how each helps survival. Before moving on, ask: "Why might island foxes be small?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why might island foxes be small?
questions.a: Limited food on small islands favored smaller bodies that need less energy (island dwarfism).

days.guide: The child builds a concept map linking fossils, anatomy, embryos, genetics and natural selection, writing a linking phrase on every arrow. Check understanding with: "How are mutations and natural selection linked?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: How are mutations and natural selection linked?
questions.a: Mutations create new variation; natural selection determines which variations become more common.

days.guide: The child completes the practice test independently, then corrects with the key. To check, ask: "Define common descent." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Define common descent.
questions.a: The idea that different species share common ancestors.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test (key). Finish by asking: "Can an individual organism evolve?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Can an individual organism evolve?
questions.a: No — populations evolve over generations.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test sample answers: 1) Steps of natural selection: variation, inheritance, overproduction/competition, differential survival and reproduction, change in trait frequency over generations. 2) Graph: dark mice rise from 5% to 80% on lava → selection by owl predation. 3) Adaptation vs acclimation: polar bear fur = adaptation; a person's tan = acclimation. 4) Finches: deeper beaks after 1977 drought. 5) Antibiotic resistance: resistant bacteria survive and multiply. 6) Evidence for common descent: fossils, anatomy, embryos, DNA.

weeks.prep: Recyclables, tape, cardboard, rubber bands, a kitchen scale. Have the child choose a capstone challenge: helmet padding test, phone-drop protector, soundproof box, or solar oven.
misconceptions: Writing vague criteria ('it works well'). Criteria must be measurable (e.g., 'reduces sound by at least 20 dB').
Researching only products, not the science. Connect each design idea to forces, energy or waves.

days.guide: Talk through the four options; the child picks one and writes a design brief with the problem, user, criteria and constraints. Before moving on, ask: "Write a measurable criterion for a solar oven." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Write a measurable criterion for a solar oven.
questions.a: Example: 'Raise the inside temperature at least 20 °C above air temperature within 30 minutes.'

days.guide: The child researches existing solutions and the science behind them. Check understanding with: "What science explains a phone-drop protector?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What science explains a phone-drop protector?
questions.a: Increasing collision time reduces force (Newton's laws, impulse).

days.guide: The child sketches at least 3 labeled solutions. To check, ask: "Why sketch several ideas?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Why sketch several ideas?
questions.a: To compare options before committing materials.

days.guide: The child scores designs in a decision matrix and chooses one. Finish by asking: "How do weights help in a matrix?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: How do weights help in a matrix?
questions.a: They make the most important criteria count more.

days.guide: The child writes a materials list and a test plan with measurable outcomes and number of trials. Before moving on, ask: "How many trials per test?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: How many trials per test?
questions.a: At least 3, to average out errors.

weeks.assessment_key: Design brief rubric: problem statement, user, measurable criteria (2–4), constraints (materials, size, budget, time), science background. Decision matrix: 3+ designs scored on weighted criteria with totals; choice justified by scores.

weeks.prep: Project materials and measuring tools (thermometer, decibel app, scale, ruler).
misconceptions: Changing several variables between versions. Change one main feature so the test shows what caused improvement.
Deciding by feel instead of data.

days.guide: The child builds prototype version 1 following the plan, noting any changes made during building. Check understanding with: "Why document changes during the build?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Why document changes during the build?
questions.a: So results can be explained and the design reproduced.

days.guide: Run 3 tests; record data in a table with units. To check, ask: "Version 1 readings: 18, 22, 20 dB reduction. Average?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Version 1 readings: 18, 22, 20 dB reduction. Average?
questions.a: 20 dB.

days.guide: The child analyzes data, identifies the weakest part, and redesigns one feature. Finish by asking: "What's an example of using data to redesign?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What's an example of using data to redesign?
questions.a: If heat escapes through the lid, add insulation there.

days.guide: Build and test version 2; compare averages. Before moving on, ask: "V1 average 20 dB, V2 average 27 dB. Improvement?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: V1 average 20 dB, V2 average 27 dB. Improvement?
questions.a: 7 dB more reduction.

days.guide: Cumulative review with study guide. Check understanding with: "F = ma: 3 kg at 2 m/s²?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: F = ma: 3 kg at 2 m/s²?

weeks.assessment_key: Testing data and iteration log rubric: data tables for version 1 and version 2 (3 trials each, averages, units); weakest part identified with evidence; one targeted change; comparison of averages; conclusion about whether criteria were met.

weeks.prep: Poster board or slides. Prepare the final exam: part 1 physical and Earth science; part 2 life science.
misconceptions: Presenting only the final design. Show the process, data and iteration.

days.guide: The child creates slides or a poster showing problem, designs, data and the final solution. To check, ask: "What should a data slide include?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What should a data slide include?
questions.a: A labeled graph or table comparing versions.

days.guide: The child presents and answers questions. Finish by asking: "How do you answer a question about a failure?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: How do you answer a question about a failure?
questions.a: Explain what the data showed and what you'd change.

days.guide: Final exam part 1. Before moving on, ask: "v = fλ: f = 10 Hz, λ = 3 m?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: v = fλ: f = 10 Hz, λ = 3 m?

days.guide: Final exam part 2. Check understanding with: "Bb × Bb: chance of bb?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Bb × Bb: chance of bb?

days.guide: The child writes a reflection on growth and goals for high school Biology. To check, ask: "What should the reflection include?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What should the reflection include?
questions.a: Skills gained, favorite investigation, a goal.

weeks.assessment_key: Capstone presentation rubric (4 levels): problem and criteria; science explanation; data from both versions; iteration reasoning; delivery and Q&A. Final exam sample answers: speed, net force, F = ma, Newton's laws, KE/PE, energy conservation, gravity, phases, seasons, waves (v = fλ), light, analog/digital, superposition, geologic time, fossils, homologous structures, Punnett squares, DNA, mutations, natural selection.

VAPA.overview: VAPA 8 rotates through four arts: drawing and painting (weeks 1–9), music literacy, keyboard, American music history and composition (weeks 10–18), theatre and playwriting (weeks 19–27), photography and stop-motion animation (weeks 28–31), and dance (weeks 32–34), ending with a portfolio and showcase. Each day is a short look-model-make cycle: show an example or demonstrate, let the child practice, then talk about what they see using art vocabulary. Praise specific choices ('your darkest darks make the egg look round') rather than talent, and keep every drawing, recording and script for the year-end portfolio. No prior arts background is needed: the vocabulary answers below give you what to listen for.

weeks.prep: Sketchbook, HB/2B/4B pencils, kneaded or white eraser, a timer and household objects (shoe, banana, mug). A family member or pet to model for gestures.
misconceptions: Drawing what you think an object looks like (symbols) rather than what you see. Correct: look at the object far more than the paper.
Pressing hard with one pencil. Correct: use light HB lines to start and softer B pencils for dark accents.

days.guide: The child decorates the cover, then does five one-minute gesture drawings, capturing the whole pose with fast, loose lines.

questions.q: What is the purpose of gesture drawing?
questions.a: To quickly capture movement, pose and overall proportion rather than details.

days.guide: Three blind contour drawings of the hand — eyes on the hand only, pencil moving slowly as the eyes trace edges. Write observations.

questions.q: Why draw without looking at the paper?
questions.a: It trains the eye and hand to coordinate and forces careful observation of edges instead of drawing from memory.

days.guide: Modified contour of a shoe: look about 80% at the shoe, 20% at the paper; include inner contours (laces, seams).

questions.q: What is a contour line?
questions.a: A line that follows the edges (outer and inner) of a form.

days.guide: Draw a banana or mug, then add cross-contour lines wrapping around the form like bands.

questions.q: What do cross-contour lines show?
questions.a: The three-dimensional surface and curvature of a form, like lines of latitude on a globe.

days.guide: The child chooses the best drawing and writes a reflection on progress.

questions.q: Name two kinds of line drawing practiced this week.
questions.a: Any two: gesture, blind contour, modified contour, cross-contour.

weeks.assessment_key: Sketchbook check (8 drawings): 4 = all 8 complete (5 gestures, 3 blind contours, contour shoe, cross-contour object — at least 8 total), careful observation evident, reflection names a specific improvement and a technique; 3 = complete with brief reflection; 2 = missing 2–3 drawings; 1 = mostly incomplete.

weeks.prep: Pencils (HB–4B), blending stump or tissue, a desk lamp in a dark room, white egg or ball, mug and small box.
misconceptions: Outlining shapes in dark lines then filling in. Correct: form is shown by value changes, not outlines.
Using only middle grays. Correct: include white highlights and the darkest darks for full contrast.

days.guide: Make a 9-step value scale from white to darkest black and a smooth gradient bar.

questions.q: What is value?
questions.a: The lightness or darkness of a color or tone.

days.guide: Fill four squares with hatching, cross-hatching, stippling and blending.

questions.q: Which technique uses dots?
questions.a: Stippling.

days.guide: Shade a lamp-lit sphere showing highlight, light, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow.

questions.q: Where is the core shadow on a sphere?
questions.a: The darkest band on the form, just past where light stops hitting it, between the lit side and the reflected light.

days.guide: Draw the lit still life with a full value range.

questions.q: What makes a cast shadow look believable?
questions.a: It's darkest and sharpest near the object and lighter and softer farther away, and it falls opposite the light source.

days.guide: Self-critique with a checklist and darken the darkest areas.

questions.q: Why does increasing contrast make a drawing look more 3-D?
questions.a: Strong lights next to deep darks create the illusion of form and depth.

weeks.assessment_key: Value rubric (4 levels): Full value range (highlight to darkest dark); Form (core shadow, reflected light, cast shadow on each object); Technique (smooth, controlled shading); Observation (proportions and placement match the setup). Proficient = 3+ in each.

weeks.prep: Ruler, sharp pencils, drawing paper. Draw a sample: horizon line with one vanishing point.
misconceptions: Drawing receding lines in different directions. Correct: all receding (depth) lines go to the single vanishing point; verticals stay vertical and horizontals stay horizontal.
Forgetting the horizon line is eye level. Correct: boxes above it show their bottoms, below it their tops.

days.guide: Draw boxes above, on and below the horizon line.

questions.q: If a box is below the horizon line, which side can you see?
questions.a: The top.

days.guide: Draw block initials in one-point perspective.

questions.q: Which lines in block letters stay parallel to the page edges?
questions.a: The front face's horizontal and vertical lines; only depth lines go to the vanishing point.

days.guide: Draw a hallway, road or railroad track receding to the VP.

questions.q: Why do railroad tracks seem to meet?
questions.a: Parallel lines moving away from us appear to converge at a vanishing point on the horizon.

days.guide: Draw the bedroom interior with furniture.

questions.q: Where is the vanishing point in a room drawing?
questions.a: On the back wall at the viewer's eye level (horizon line).

days.guide: Add value; check lines with a ruler.

questions.q: What is the horizon line?
questions.a: A horizontal line representing the viewer's eye level.

weeks.assessment_key: One-point room drawing: 4 = accurate horizon line and single VP, all depth lines converge correctly, at least 4 furniture items in correct perspective, ruler-straight lines, value added; 3 = 1–2 minor errors; 2 = several lines miss the VP; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Ruler, pencils, fine-tip markers. Pull up Raphael's 'School of Athens' (1509–1511) and a modern cityscape on Google Arts & Culture.
misconceptions: Putting vanishing points too close together. Correct: place them far apart (near paper edges) to avoid distortion.
Tilting vertical lines. Correct: in two-point perspective, verticals stay vertical.

days.guide: Draw 6 boxes in two-point perspective above, at and below eye level.

questions.q: How many vanishing points in two-point perspective and where?
questions.a: Two, both on the horizon line, usually far apart.

days.guide: Draw a house with roof, doors, windows.

questions.q: How do you find the center of a wall to place a roof peak?
questions.a: Draw an X corner to corner on the wall; the crossing point is the perspective center.

days.guide: Analyze perspective in 'School of Athens.'

questions.q: Where is the vanishing point in 'School of Athens'?
questions.a: Near the center, between Plato and Aristotle, drawing the viewer's eye to them.

days.guide: Begin a cityscape with at least 5 buildings.

questions.q: How can you show some buildings are closer?
questions.a: Make them larger, lower on the page or overlapping others, with more detail.

days.guide: Ink and shade.

questions.q: Why use a consistent light source when shading?
questions.a: So all shadows fall the same way, making the scene believable.

weeks.assessment_key: Two-point cityscape: 4 = 5+ buildings converging correctly to two VPs, vertical lines vertical, overlap and detail create depth, clean inking, consistent shading; 3 = minor errors; 2 = frequent convergence errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Drawing materials; critique sheet (Describe, Analyze, Interpret, Evaluate — Feldman method).
misconceptions: Skipping thumbnails. Correct: small sketches let you test compositions quickly.
Evaluation without evidence. Correct: support judgments with specific details.

days.guide: Three thumbnails for 'A place that matters to me.'

questions.q: What is a thumbnail sketch?
questions.a: A small, quick sketch to plan composition.

days.guide: Lightly sketch the chosen composition.

questions.q: Why sketch lightly first?
questions.a: Light lines are easy to erase and adjust before committing.

days.guide: Add value and detail.

questions.q: Which technique from this unit could create depth?
questions.a: Perspective, overlapping, value contrast, size variation.

days.guide: Complete and sign.

questions.q: Where do artists usually sign?
questions.a: In a lower corner, small enough not to distract.

days.guide: Write a four-step critique.

questions.q: What happens in the 'Interpret' step?
questions.a: You explain the meaning, mood or message of the artwork based on evidence.

weeks.assessment_key: Final drawing rubric (4 levels): composition, value range, technique (perspective/contour/shading from the unit), craftsmanship, personal meaning. Critique: 4 = all four steps (describe what is seen, analyze elements and principles, interpret meaning, evaluate with reasons).

weeks.prep: Mirror, pencils, paper, ruler. Draw a sample proportion guide.
misconceptions: Placing eyes high on the head. Correct: eyes are about halfway between the top of the head and the chin.
Drawing eyes as almond outlines only. Correct: include the eyelid crease, iris partly covered by the upper lid, and shadows.

days.guide: Draw an oval head with a vertical center line; eye line halfway down; bottom of the nose about halfway between the eye line and the chin; mouth about one-third of the way from nose to chin. Label.

questions.q: Where are the eyes located on an adult head?
questions.a: About halfway between the top of the head and the chin.

questions.q: How far apart are the eyes?
questions.a: About one eye-width apart.

days.guide: Four eyes and four noses from the mirror, shading eyelids and nostrils.

questions.q: Why is the top of the iris often hidden?
questions.a: The upper eyelid covers part of it.

days.guide: Four mouths and two ears; note ear placement.

questions.q: Where do the ears line up?
questions.a: Roughly between the eyebrow/eye line and the bottom of the nose.

days.guide: Observe three family members and record differences.

questions.q: Why do real faces differ from the guideline?
questions.a: Proportions vary person to person; the guideline is an average starting point.

days.guide: Draw a self-portrait from a mirror; compare to a photo; note one correction.

questions.q: Where do the corners of the mouth usually line up?
questions.a: Roughly below the centers of the eyes (pupils).

weeks.assessment_key: Self-portrait proportion check: 4 = eyes at halfway line, one eye-width apart, nose and mouth placed by guidelines, ears aligned eye-to-nose, value shading, one correction noted; 3 = one placement error; 2 = several errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Acrylic or tempera in red, yellow, blue, white, black; brushes; palette; heavy paper; water cup. Write a 10-question color vocabulary quiz. Pull up 'The Old Guitarist' (1903–04) and 'The Dessert: Harmony in Red' (1908).
misconceptions: Thinking adding black makes a darker version of a color. Correct: it makes a shade but can muddy color; complements can also darken.
Confusing tints and tones. Correct: tint = + white; shade = + black; tone = + gray.

days.guide: Mix and paint a 12-part wheel.

questions.q: Name the secondary colors and how to mix them.
questions.a: Orange (red + yellow), green (yellow + blue), violet (blue + red).

days.guide: Paint a tint-to-shade strip and a tone strip.

questions.q: What is a tint?
questions.a: A color plus white.

days.guide: Paint four thumbnails in different schemes.

questions.q: What are complementary colors? Give a pair.
questions.a: Colors opposite each other on the wheel, e.g., blue and orange.

days.guide: Compare the two paintings and how color shapes mood.

questions.q: How does color affect mood in 'The Old Guitarist'?
questions.a: Dominant blues create a cold, sad, lonely mood matching the frail, poor man.

days.guide: Give the quiz; child writes which thumbnail best conveys a mood.

questions.q: What is an analogous scheme?
questions.a: Colors next to each other on the wheel, e.g., yellow, yellow-orange, orange.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) primary: red, yellow, blue 2) secondary: orange, green, violet 3) tertiary: primary + neighboring secondary (e.g., red-orange) 4) tint = + white 5) shade = + black 6) tone = + gray 7) complementary = opposites 8) analogous = neighbors 9) monochromatic = one hue with tints/shades 10) warm (red/orange/yellow) vs cool (blue/green/violet). Written choice: names scheme, mood and specific color evidence.

weeks.prep: Images via Smithsonian Learning Lab or Google Arts & Culture: Gilbert Stuart's 'Lansdowne' portrait of George Washington (1796) and Kehinde Wiley's portrait of Barack Obama (2018); Frida Kahlo's 'Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird' (1940).
misconceptions: Thinking a portrait must be realistic. Correct: portraits can use symbols, color and setting to convey identity.
Using random symbols. Correct: each symbol should have a reason connected to the subject.

days.guide: Compare pose and background in both portraits.

questions.q: How do the backgrounds differ?
questions.a: Stuart uses classical columns, drapery and a rainbow sky to show authority; Wiley seats Obama in a chair against green foliage with flowers symbolizing places in his life (chrysanthemums for Chicago, jasmine for Hawaii, African blue lilies for Kenya).

days.guide: Analyze three Kahlo symbols.

questions.q: What might the thorn necklace and dead hummingbird mean?
questions.a: Thorns suggest pain and suffering (like Christ's crown of thorns); the hummingbird, a Mexican folk charm for luck in love, is dead — often linked to her divorce from Diego Rivera. The black cat suggests bad luck/death; butterflies suggest rebirth.

days.guide: Examine portraits from a culture/community and write how art reinforces identity.

questions.q: How can portraits reinforce group identity?
questions.a: They show shared clothing, symbols, settings or values that a community recognizes and celebrates.

days.guide: List 5 symbols, colors and a setting; 3 thumbnails.

questions.q: Why choose a color scheme for your portrait?
questions.a: Color sets the mood and can carry meaning about personality.

days.guide: Get feedback; revise composition on final paper.

questions.q: What feedback question helps most?
questions.a: 'What do you think this portrait says about me?' — to see whether the symbols read clearly.

weeks.assessment_key: Identity portrait plan: 4 = 5 symbols with meanings in a key, chosen color scheme with reason, setting, three thumbnails and a revised final composition reflecting feedback; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = symbols without meanings; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Paints, canvas board or heavy paper, brushes (large flat, medium round, small detail), palette.
misconceptions: Painting details first. Correct: work from big shapes to small details, dark/thin layers first.
Using straight black for shadows on skin. Correct: mix shadows from complements or darker skin mixes.

days.guide: Transfer sketch; thin underpainting.

questions.q: What is an underpainting?
questions.a: A thin first layer blocking in big shapes and values to guide later layers.

days.guide: Add mid-tones and shadows; mix skin tones from primaries plus white.

questions.q: How do you mix a basic skin tone from primaries?
questions.a: Mix red, yellow and a little blue to make a brown, then adjust lightness with white and warmth with red/yellow.

days.guide: Paint symbols and details; highlights last.

questions.q: Why add highlights last?
questions.a: Light colors sit on top and stay clean; they'd be muddied by later layers.

days.guide: Refine edges, squint to check values, sign.

questions.q: Why squint at a painting?
questions.a: It blurs details so you can see value and big shapes clearly.

days.guide: Write a 150-word statement and self-evaluate.

questions.q: What belongs in an artist statement?
questions.a: What the work is, what the symbols and color choices mean, process, and what you want viewers to feel or understand.

weeks.assessment_key: Portrait rubric (4 criteria × 4 levels): Composition (planned symbols and setting), Color (intentional scheme, mixed tones), Technique (layering, edges, highlights), Meaning (symbols clearly convey identity). Artist statement: ~150 words explaining symbols and colors.

weeks.prep: musictheory.net lessons, metronome app, staff paper, pots or drum pad. Write a 4-measure dictation in 4/4 (e.g., quarter-quarter-half | eighths×4-half | dotted half-quarter | whole) and a sight-reading rhythm.
misconceptions: Counting a dotted half note as 2 beats. Correct: the dot adds half the note's value, so a dotted half = 3 beats in 4/4.
Thinking 6/8 has six beats felt evenly. Correct: 6/8 is usually felt in 2 big beats, each a dotted quarter.
