days.guide: Lessons on note durations; clap and count 8 patterns.

questions.q: In 4/4, how many beats do whole, half, quarter and eighth notes get?
questions.a: 4, 2, 1 and ½.

days.guide: Count and tap in 4/4, 3/4, 6/8 at 80 bpm.

questions.q: What does the top number of a time signature mean?
questions.a: Number of beats (or pulses) per measure; the bottom shows which note gets the beat.

days.guide: Clap syncopated patterns; find syncopation in 'The Entertainer.'

questions.q: What is syncopation?
questions.a: Accents on weak beats or off-beats, giving a 'pushed' feel.

days.guide: Compose and perform a 4-measure body-percussion rhythm.

questions.q: Does each 4/4 measure add up to 4 beats?
questions.a: Check every measure totals 4.

days.guide: Give the dictation and sight-reading.

questions.q: How many eighth notes fit in one measure of 4/4?
questions.a: Eight.

weeks.assessment_key: Rhythm dictation: 1 pt per correct measure (4) — compare to your written answer. Performance check: steady tempo at 80 bpm, correct durations, rests observed (3/3 proficient).

weeks.prep: musictheory.net note-identification exercise; keyboard app or piano. Write a quiz: 10 notes (5 treble, 5 bass) and 5 intervals.
misconceptions: Mixing up treble and bass clef names. Correct: treble lines E-G-B-D-F, spaces F-A-C-E; bass lines G-B-D-F-A, spaces A-C-E-G.
Counting intervals from 0. Correct: count the starting note as 1 (C to E = third).

days.guide: Learn treble names; 20 correct in a row.

questions.q: Name the treble clef lines and spaces.
questions.a: Lines E-G-B-D-F ('Every Good Boy Does Fine'); spaces F-A-C-E.

days.guide: Learn bass clef names.

questions.q: Name the bass clef lines and spaces.
questions.a: Lines G-B-D-F-A ('Good Boys Do Fine Always'); spaces A-C-E-G ('All Cows Eat Grass').

days.guide: Sharps, flats, naturals on a keyboard.

questions.q: What does a sharp do?
questions.a: Raises a note a half step (to the next key to the right).

days.guide: Identify intervals by sight and ear.

questions.q: What interval opens 'Twinkle, Twinkle' (first to third note)?
questions.a: A perfect fifth (C up to G).

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: C up to F is what interval?
questions.a: A fourth (C-D-E-F = 4).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: score against your chosen notes using EGBDF/FACE (treble) and GBDFA/ACEG (bass); interval items counted inclusively (e.g., C–E 3rd, C–G 5th, C–C octave, D–F 3rd, E–A 4th). 12/15 proficient.

weeks.prep: Keyboard or online keyboard app; metronome; sheet music for 'Ode to Joy' (right hand: E E F G G F E D C C D E E D D).
misconceptions: Running out of fingers in a scale. Correct: C major RH 1-2-3, thumb under, 1-2-3-4-5.
Forgetting the formula's half steps. Correct: half steps fall between notes 3–4 and 7–8.

days.guide: Locate all Cs (just left of the two-black-key groups); five-finger C-G each hand.

questions.q: How do you find C on a keyboard?
questions.a: It's the white key just left of each group of two black keys.

days.guide: C major scale hands separately with thumb-under at 60 bpm.

questions.q: What is the RH fingering for C major?
questions.a: 1-2-3-1-2-3-4-5 ascending (thumb under after E).

days.guide: Build G and F major with W-W-H-W-W-W-H.

questions.q: What sharp or flat is in G major? F major?
questions.a: G major has F♯; F major has B♭.

days.guide: Learn 'Ode to Joy' RH.

questions.q: Who composed 'Ode to Joy'?
questions.a: Ludwig van Beethoven (Symphony No. 9).

days.guide: Play scale and melody for family; self-evaluate.

questions.q: What does the checklist look for?
questions.a: Correct notes, correct fingering, steady beat, smooth tone.

weeks.assessment_key: Playing check: C major scale (correct notes, thumb-under fingering, steady 60 bpm) and 'Ode to Joy' (correct notes and rhythm, steady tempo). 4 = no errors, 3 = 1–2 errors, 2 = several errors/stops, 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Keyboard; Chrome Music Lab Chords. 12-bar blues chart in C: | C | C | C | C | F | F | C | C | G | F | C | C |.
misconceptions: Thinking minor means 'sad and wrong.' Correct: minor triads lower the third a half step; they have a darker color.
Losing the beat when changing chords. Correct: practice changes slowly with a metronome.

days.guide: Build C, F, G triads; compare major and minor.

questions.q: Spell C major and C minor triads.
questions.a: C major: C-E-G. C minor: C-E♭-G.

days.guide: Play I-IV-V-I in C with LH.

questions.q: What are I, IV and V in C major?
questions.a: C, F and G.

days.guide: Play the 12-bar blues in C.

questions.q: Write the 12-bar blues progression.
questions.a: I-I-I-I | IV-IV-I-I | V-IV-I-I (C C C C | F F C C | G F C C).

days.guide: Accompany 'Ode to Joy' with LH chords.

questions.q: Which chords fit most of 'Ode to Joy' in C?
questions.a: Mostly C (I) and G (V).

days.guide: Perform the 12-bar blues with a steady beat.

questions.q: How many bars are in one chorus of blues?
questions.a: Twelve.

weeks.assessment_key: Chord performance check: correct triads (C, F, G), correct 12-bar order, steady beat with no stopping at changes. 4 = all correct; 3 = one error; 2 = several errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Keyboard; recordings of Beethoven's 'Für Elise' and a verse-chorus pop song (preview lyrics). Form chart template.
misconceptions: Thinking every piece repeats the same way. Correct: identify sections by contrast and return.
Recording once and stopping. Correct: listen back critically and re-record.

days.guide: Diagram 'Für Elise' as rondo A-B-A-C-A.

questions.q: What is rondo form?
questions.a: A recurring main theme (A) alternating with contrasting sections: A-B-A-C-A.

days.guide: Compare verse-chorus form to 'Für Elise.'

questions.q: How does verse-chorus form work?
questions.a: Verses with changing lyrics alternate with a repeated chorus; often there's a bridge.

days.guide: Rehearse with dynamics and articulation; set criteria.

questions.q: What does 'p' and 'f' mean?
questions.a: Piano = soft; forte = loud.

days.guide: Record and listen back.

questions.q: What should you listen for?
questions.a: Correct notes and rhythm, steady tempo, dynamics, smooth phrasing.

days.guide: Perform; self-evaluate.

questions.q: What is articulation?
questions.a: How notes are played/connected, e.g., legato (smooth) or staccato (short).

weeks.assessment_key: Recorded performance: meets self-set criteria for accuracy, tempo and dynamics (4 levels). Listening comparison: 4 = correct form diagrams for both (rondo A-B-A-C-A; verse-chorus), compares dynamics and tempo with specific moments.

weeks.prep: Recordings via Library of Congress or Smithsonian Folkways: Fisk Jubilee Singers, field/work songs, Bessie Smith, B.B. King. Keyboard. Connects to the HSS unit on slavery.
misconceptions: Thinking spirituals were just religious songs. Correct: they expressed faith and hope and could carry coded messages about freedom.
Writing blues lyrics without AAB. Correct: line 1 is stated, repeated, then answered by a rhyming line 3.

days.guide: Listen to the Fisk Jubilee Singers; analyze 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot.'

questions.q: Who were the Fisk Jubilee Singers?
questions.a: A choir of Black students from Fisk University (Nashville) who began touring in 1871, bringing spirituals to worldwide audiences and raising money for the school.

days.guide: Listen to work songs; identify call-and-response.

questions.q: What is call-and-response?
questions.a: A leader sings a phrase and the group answers.

days.guide: Listen to Bessie Smith and B.B. King; identify 12-bar form and AAB lyrics.

questions.q: What does AAB lyric form mean?
questions.a: The first line is sung twice (A, A), then a third line (B) answers or resolves it.

days.guide: Write three verses in AAB form.

questions.q: Write a sample AAB blues verse.
questions.a: 'My phone just died right in the middle of my game, / My phone just died right in the middle of my game, / Now I'm sittin' here and nothing feels the same.'

days.guide: Perform the lyrics over the 12-bar progression.

questions.q: How does each AAB verse line up with the 12 bars?
questions.a: Each line takes 4 bars: A over bars 1–4 (I), A over 5–8 (IV-I), B over 9–12 (V-IV-I).

weeks.assessment_key: Blues lyric and performance: 4 = three AAB verses with rhyming B lines, personal topic, sung/spoken in time over correct 12-bar progression; 3 = minor timing issues; 2 = form errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Recordings: Scott Joplin 'Maple Leaf Rag' (1899), Louis Armstrong 'West End Blues' (1928), Duke Ellington 'Take the A Train' (composed by Billy Strayhorn), Ella Fitzgerald; PBS LearningMedia jazz videos; C blues backing track. Listening quiz of 6 clips.
misconceptions: Thinking jazz improvisation is random. Correct: it follows the chord progression, scales and style.
Confusing ragtime and jazz. Correct: ragtime is composed, written-out piano music; jazz adds improvisation and swing.

days.guide: Listen to 'Maple Leaf Rag'; identify syncopation.

questions.q: What instrument is ragtime usually played on?
questions.a: Piano.

days.guide: Analyze Armstrong's trumpet improvisation in 'West End Blues.'

questions.q: What is famous about the opening of 'West End Blues'?
questions.a: Armstrong's dazzling unaccompanied trumpet cadenza, a landmark of jazz improvisation.

days.guide: Compare Ellington's big band with a modern big band.

questions.q: What sections make up a big band?
questions.a: Saxophones, trumpets, trombones and a rhythm section (piano, bass, drums, guitar).

days.guide: Improvise on the C blues scale over a backing track.

questions.q: Spell the C blues scale.

days.guide: Give the listening quiz.

questions.q: What is scat singing, and who was famous for it?
questions.a: Improvised singing with nonsense syllables; Ella Fitzgerald (and Louis Armstrong).

weeks.assessment_key: Listening quiz key (match to your clips): ragtime — Joplin, piano, syncopated, composed; New Orleans/early jazz — Armstrong, trumpet improvisation; big band swing — Ellington, sax/brass sections; vocal jazz — Fitzgerald, scat; blues — 12-bar, AAB. 5/6 proficient.

weeks.prep: Chrome Music Lab Song Maker; staff paper.
misconceptions: Making phrases that wander. Correct: use a motif and repeat or vary it.
Ending on a random note. Correct: answer phrases usually end on the tonic (home note).

days.guide: Create 4 two-measure motifs; choose the strongest.

questions.q: What is a motif?
questions.a: A short musical idea that is repeated and developed.

days.guide: Develop into an 8-measure question-answer phrase.

questions.q: How does an 'answer' phrase sound different from a 'question' phrase?
questions.a: The question ends unresolved (often on a note other than the tonic); the answer ends on the tonic, sounding finished.

days.guide: Organize into ABA form.

questions.q: What is ABA form?
questions.a: Section A, a contrasting section B, then a return of A.

days.guide: Add chords.

questions.q: Which chord usually ends a piece in C major?
questions.a: C major (I).

days.guide: Share with family; record feedback.

questions.q: Why get feedback on a draft?
questions.a: Listeners notice what's memorable or confusing.

weeks.assessment_key: Composition draft: 4 = clear motif, 8-measure question-answer phrase ending on tonic, ABA form with contrasting B, chords that fit, feedback recorded; 3 = one element weak; 2 = no clear form; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Song Maker or MuseScore (free); rubric for composition and program notes.
misconceptions: Too much repetition or too much new material. Correct: balance unity (repetition) and variety (contrast).
Program notes that only describe notes. Correct: explain expressive intent — mood, story, choices.

days.guide: Revise for unity and variety.

questions.q: How can you add variety while keeping unity?
questions.a: Change rhythm, register, dynamics or harmony of the motif in the B section, then return to A.

days.guide: Notate the final version.

questions.q: What must notation include?
questions.a: Clef, time signature, key, correct note values per measure, title and composer.

days.guide: Write program notes on expressive intent.

questions.q: What goes in program notes?
questions.a: Title, inspiration, form, mood and how musical choices express it.

days.guide: Rehearse or finalize.

questions.q: How do you check your notation is correct?
questions.a: Play it back and compare to what you intended; check each measure's beats.

days.guide: Present composition and notes.

questions.q: What does 'expressive intent' mean?
questions.a: The feeling or idea the composer wants to communicate.

weeks.assessment_key: Composition and program notes rubric: Form (ABA, clear phrases), Melody/harmony (motif developed, fitting chords), Notation (accurate rhythm/time signature), Program notes (explains intent and choices), Presentation. 4 levels each; proficient = 3+.

weeks.prep: Open space, mirror, a phone for recording. Tongue-twister list: 'red leather, yellow leather,' 'unique New York,' 'toy boat,' 'she sells seashells,' 'Peter Piper.' One-sentence character descriptions on cards.
misconceptions: Speaking loudly by straining the throat. Correct: projection comes from breath support (diaphragm), not shouting.
Acting only with the face. Correct: the whole body, posture and walk communicate character.

days.guide: Breathing (inhale 4, exhale on 'sss' for 8+), projection to the far wall, five tongue twisters; record before and after.

questions.q: What supports vocal projection?
questions.a: Deep diaphragmatic breathing, open throat and good posture.

days.guide: Mirror exercise with a partner; character walks leading with head, chest or hips.

questions.q: What might leading with the chest suggest about a character?
questions.a: Confidence, pride or authority.

days.guide: Three fairy-tale tableaux; photograph.

questions.q: What is a tableau?
questions.a: A frozen stage picture showing a moment of a story through poses and levels.

days.guide: Develop a walk, posture and voice from one sentence.

questions.q: Name three tools of the actor's instrument.
questions.a: Voice, body, imagination (also face/expression and concentration).

days.guide: 30-second character introduction.

questions.q: How can you show age with the body?
questions.a: Posture, walking speed, gestures, voice pitch and energy.

weeks.assessment_key: Character introduction rubric: 4 = distinct voice (pitch, pace, volume), clear physicality and walk, stays in character for 30 seconds, projects clearly; 3 = mostly consistent; 2 = breaks character or unclear; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Scenario cards with two characters who want different things (e.g., teen wants to go to a party, parent wants homework done). A familiar film scene to analyze.
misconceptions: Playing emotions instead of objectives. Correct: actors play what the character wants (action verbs); emotion follows.
Using only one tactic. Correct: when a tactic fails, the character changes tactics (charm, plead, threaten).

days.guide: Teach objective (what the character wants), obstacle (what's in the way), tactic (how they try to get it); analyze a film scene.

questions.q: Define objective, obstacle and tactic.
questions.a: Objective: what the character wants. Obstacle: what blocks it. Tactic: the action used to try to get it (persuade, flatter, threaten).

days.guide: Improvise three scenes with conflicting objectives.

questions.q: What makes an improv scene work?
questions.a: Clear wants, listening, 'yes, and' acceptance, and real conflict.

days.guide: Say 'I'm fine' five ways with different subtext.

questions.q: What is subtext?
questions.a: The unspoken meaning or feeling beneath the words.

days.guide: Break a short scene into beats; mark objectives.

questions.q: What is a beat?
questions.a: A unit of a scene in which one objective or tactic is pursued; a new beat starts when it changes.

days.guide: Perform an improvised scene and identify tactics.

questions.q: Name three tactics as action verbs.
questions.a: Charm, beg, bribe, threaten, guilt, reason, tease.

weeks.assessment_key: Improv and beat analysis: 4 = clear objective pursued with at least two tactic shifts, responds to partner; beat analysis marks each beat with objective/tactic verbs; 3 = one tactic shift; 2 = unclear objective; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Four age-appropriate public-domain monologues (e.g., Puck's epilogue from 'A Midsummer Night's Dream,' Portia's 'quality of mercy' speech from 'The Merchant of Venice,' a speech from 'The Importance of Being Earnest'). Highlighters.
misconceptions: Memorizing the words without meaning. Correct: understand every line and paraphrase it first.
Rushing. Correct: use pauses and emphasis tied to the beats.

days.guide: Read four and choose one.

questions.q: What makes a monologue a good choice?
questions.a: Age-appropriate, understandable, has a clear objective and emotional journey, right length (about 1 minute).

days.guide: Research play, playwright, period.

questions.q: Who wrote 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' and when?
questions.a: William Shakespeare, around 1595–96.

days.guide: Mark objectives, beats, emphasis.

questions.q: Why mark operative words?
questions.a: They are the key words to stress so meaning is clear.

days.guide: Memorize line by line (add one line at a time, repeat from the start).

questions.q: Describe the line-by-line method.
questions.a: Learn line 1, then lines 1–2, then 1–3, always going back to the beginning.

days.guide: Perform off-book.

questions.q: What does 'off-book' mean?
questions.a: Performing from memory without the script.

weeks.assessment_key: Off-book check: 4 = fully memorized (no more than 1 prompt), clear objective, beats show in shifts of voice/body, good projection and diction; 3 = 2–3 prompts; 2 = many prompts; 1 = not memorized.

weeks.prep: A two-person scene script (public domain or written for the course); a family scene partner; simple props and costume pieces; recording device. Stage-direction diagram (upstage/downstage, stage left/right from the actor's view).
misconceptions: Confusing stage left/right. Correct: they are from the actor's perspective facing the audience.
Waiting for your line instead of listening. Correct: react truthfully to the partner.

days.guide: Read through; discuss characters.

questions.q: What questions should you ask about your character?
questions.a: Who am I? What do I want? What's in my way? What's my relationship to the other character?

days.guide: Block with stage directions.

questions.q: Where is downstage?
questions.a: Toward the audience.

days.guide: Rehearse listening and reacting.

questions.q: Why does listening matter in acting?
questions.a: Real reactions make the scene believable and keep it alive.

days.guide: Add props and costume pieces.

questions.q: Why rehearse with props early?
questions.a: So handling them becomes natural and doesn't interrupt the scene.

days.guide: Perform and record.

questions.q: What does 'cheat out' mean?
questions.a: Angle the body toward the audience so faces and voices can be seen and heard.

weeks.assessment_key: Scene video rubric: Memorization, Blocking (uses stage space, opens to audience), Listening/reacting, Voice (projection, diction), Character choices. 4 levels each; proficient = 3+.

weeks.prep: A recorded production (PBS Great Performances or a free filmed school production — preview for content). Note sheet: set, costume, lighting, sound, acting.
misconceptions: Reviews that only summarize the plot. Correct: evaluate choices with evidence.
Saying 'it was good/bad' without reasons. Correct: explain why with specific moments.

days.guide: Watch part 1; note design choices.

questions.q: What does the set tell the audience?
questions.a: Time, place, mood and sometimes character's status.

days.guide: Finish; note acting choices.

questions.q: Give an example of an acting choice to note.
questions.a: A change in voice, a pause, a gesture or movement that revealed character.

days.guide: Analyze how set, costume and lighting support the story.

questions.q: How can lighting change mood?
questions.a: Warm, bright light can feel happy; cool, dim or harsh light can feel tense or sad; spotlights focus attention.

days.guide: Write a 300-word review with evidence.

questions.q: What does a strong review include?
questions.a: Brief context, analysis of acting and design with specific examples, an overall evaluation with reasons.

days.guide: Share and discuss.

questions.q: How is a review different from a summary?
questions.a: A review evaluates and gives opinions supported by evidence; a summary retells events.

weeks.assessment_key: Theatre review: 4 = ~300 words, brief context, analyzes acting and at least two design elements with specific moments, clear supported evaluation, organized paragraphs; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = mostly summary; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Notebook, script-format template. Plot diagram (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution).
misconceptions: Too many characters or locations for a short play. Correct: 2–3 characters and one setting for 5–8 minutes.
No clear conflict. Correct: a character must want something and face an obstacle.

days.guide: Brainstorm 10 premises.

questions.q: What is a premise?
questions.a: A short statement of the play's basic situation: who, where and what conflict.

days.guide: Choose one; write a premise paragraph.

questions.q: What three elements must the premise include?
questions.a: Characters, setting and central conflict.

days.guide: Outline exposition, rising action, climax, resolution.

questions.q: What is the climax?
questions.a: The turning point of highest tension where the conflict comes to a head.

days.guide: Character sketches with objectives and obstacles.

questions.q: Why write character sketches?
questions.a: So each character has clear wants, traits and a distinct voice.

days.guide: Pitch the play; revise.

questions.q: What should a pitch include?
questions.a: Title, premise, main characters, conflict and why it's interesting, in under a minute.

weeks.assessment_key: Play outline and sketches: 4 = clear premise, complete plot structure with a strong climax, 2–3 character sketches each with objective, obstacle and traits, revised after pitch; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = weak conflict; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Script template and word processor. Example script page showing character names, dialogue and italic stage directions in parentheses.
misconceptions: Writing narration in stage directions. Correct: stage directions describe only what can be seen or heard.
Dialogue that states feelings directly. Correct: let subtext and action reveal feelings.

days.guide: Study script format; write page one.

questions.q: How are stage directions formatted?
questions.a: In italics and/or parentheses, in present tense, describing action, setting and sound.

days.guide: Draft the first half.

questions.q: How does dialogue reveal character?
questions.a: Word choice, rhythm, what characters avoid saying and how they respond show personality and relationships.

days.guide: Draft climax and resolution.

questions.q: Does your climax resolve the central conflict?
questions.a: It should show the conflict peaking and lead to a resolution.

days.guide: Solve two staging challenges in stage directions.

questions.q: How might you stage a storm simply?
questions.a: Sound effects, flickering lights, actors swaying, fabric waving.

days.guide: Finish draft; read aloud and mark unnatural lines.

questions.q: Why read your script aloud?
questions.a: To hear lines that sound stiff, too long or unnatural.

weeks.assessment_key: First draft: 4 = correct script format, 5–8 pages, complete arc (exposition to resolution), distinct character voices, creative staging solutions; 3 = minor format issues; 2 = incomplete arc; 1 = unfinished.

weeks.prep: Copies of the script; family readers; glow-and-grow feedback form.
misconceptions: Defending the script during feedback. Correct: listen, take notes, decide later.
Only fixing typos. Correct: revise dialogue and structure.

days.guide: Hold a table read.

questions.q: What is a table read?
questions.a: Actors read the script aloud around a table to hear it before staging.

days.guide: Collect glow-and-grow feedback.

questions.q: What is a 'grow' comment?
questions.a: A specific, kind suggestion for improvement.

days.guide: Revise dialogue for clarity and voice.

questions.q: How can you make two characters sound different?
questions.a: Vary vocabulary, sentence length, slang/formality and rhythm.

days.guide: Cut or add scenes for pacing.

questions.q: What is pacing?
questions.a: The speed at which the story moves.

days.guide: Finalize second draft.

questions.q: What is the purpose of revision notes?
questions.a: To record what was changed and why.

weeks.assessment_key: Second draft and revision notes: 4 = notes list at least 4 specific changes linked to feedback (dialogue, structure, pacing), second draft clearly improved; 3 = 2–3 changes; 2 = surface edits only; 1 = no revision.

weeks.prep: Scripts, simple props and costumes, sound effects (phone), an audience, recording device.
misconceptions: Staged readings without movement. Correct: simple blocking and eye contact bring a reading to life.
Skipping a full run-through. Correct: run the whole show at least once with props.

days.guide: Cast and plan props and set.

questions.q: What is a staged reading?
questions.a: A performance with scripts in hand, minimal set, props and blocking.

days.guide: Rehearse with blocking.

questions.q: Why give each actor clear blocking?
questions.a: So movement is purposeful and the audience can see everyone.

days.guide: Run-through with props and sound.

questions.q: What is a cue?
questions.a: A signal (line or action) for an actor, sound or light change.

days.guide: Perform and record.

questions.q: What should actors do if they make a mistake?
questions.a: Stay in character and keep going.

days.guide: Write a reflection.

questions.q: What should a reflection include?
questions.a: What worked, what didn't, audience response and what you'd change.

weeks.assessment_key: Staged reading and reflection: 4 = organized performance with blocking, props/sound, clear voices; reflection uses audience response and video to evaluate specific choices and changes; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = disorganized; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Phone or camera with grid lines turned on. Images: Dorothea Lange's 'Migrant Mother' (1936, Nipomo, California) and Ansel Adams's Yosemite photographs (e.g., 'Monolith, the Face of Half Dome,' 'Clearing Winter Storm').
misconceptions: Always centering the subject. Correct: placing it on rule-of-thirds lines often makes a stronger composition.
Shooting everything from eye level. Correct: change point of view for interest.

days.guide: Analyze 'Migrant Mother' and Adams's images.

questions.q: What was Lange's purpose in 'Migrant Mother'?
questions.a: To document the suffering of migrant farm workers during the Great Depression for the Farm Security Administration and build support for aid.

days.guide: Take 10 rule-of-thirds photos.

questions.q: What is the rule of thirds?
questions.a: Divide the frame into a 3×3 grid and place key subjects along the lines or at intersections.

days.guide: 10 photos with leading lines and natural frames.

questions.q: What are leading lines?
questions.a: Lines (roads, fences, rails) that guide the viewer's eye toward the subject.

days.guide: Photograph one object from 5 viewpoints.

questions.q: How does a worm's-eye view change a subject?
questions.a: Shooting from below makes the subject look larger, powerful or imposing.

days.guide: Select and caption 5 best photos.

questions.q: What is framing?
questions.a: Using elements like doorways or branches to surround and highlight the subject.

weeks.assessment_key: Photo portfolio: 4 = 5 strong photos each clearly demonstrating a named technique (rule of thirds, leading lines, framing, point of view), in focus, captions explain the technique and effect; 3 = 4 strong; 2 = techniques unclear; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Phone/camera, free photo editor (built-in Photos app, Snapseed). Examples of one event shown in news, ads and social media. Consent/permission form or verbal script.
misconceptions: Thinking photos are always objective. Correct: framing, cropping and editing shape the message.
Posting photos of people without permission. Correct: ask consent, especially for minors and private moments.

days.guide: Compare how one event is shown across media.

questions.q: How can cropping change a photo's message?
questions.a: It can remove context, changing what viewers believe happened.

days.guide: Plan a 10-photo essay on 'A day in my community.'

questions.q: What makes a photo essay a story?
questions.a: A sequence with a beginning, middle and end, variety of shots (wide, medium, close-up) and a theme.

days.guide: Shoot following the plan.

questions.q: Why vary wide, medium and close-up shots?
questions.a: Wide shots set the scene, medium show action, close-ups show detail and emotion.

days.guide: Edit (crop, exposure) and sequence.

questions.q: What does adjusting exposure do?
questions.a: Makes the image lighter or darker.

days.guide: Write captions, get consent, present.

questions.q: Why get consent before sharing someone's photo?
questions.a: It respects privacy and their right to control their image; some situations can harm the person if shared.

weeks.assessment_key: Photo essay: 4 = 10 photos in a logical sequence with variety of shots, thoughtful edits, informative captions, consent obtained, ethical choices explained; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = weak sequence or missing captions; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Phone with Stop Motion Studio (free), clay or LEGO figures, tripod or stack of books, steady lighting, a short stop-motion example (e.g., an Aardman clip).
misconceptions: Moving figures too far between frames. Correct: tiny moves create smooth motion.
Bumping the camera. Correct: fix the camera with a tripod or tape.

days.guide: Watch an example; calculate frames for 30 s at 12 fps.

questions.q: How many frames for 30 seconds at 12 frames per second?

days.guide: Make a 3-second bouncing-ball test.

questions.q: How many frames is 3 seconds at 12 fps?
questions.a: 36 frames.

questions.q: How can you show the ball speeding up as it falls?
questions.a: Space the ball's positions farther apart near the bottom (ease in/out) and squash it on impact.

days.guide: Write a 30-second story idea.

questions.q: What does a 30-second story need?
questions.a: One character, one simple goal or problem, and a quick resolution.

days.guide: Draw a 12-panel storyboard.

questions.q: What is a storyboard?
questions.a: A sequence of sketches showing each shot or key moment, with notes on action and sound.

days.guide: Build characters and set.

questions.q: Why build sturdy characters?
questions.a: They must hold poses for many frames without falling.

weeks.assessment_key: Storyboard and test animation: 4 = 12 panels showing beginning-middle-end with shot notes; test animation 3 seconds, smooth motion with spacing changes, steady camera; 3 = minor jumps; 2 = rough; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Stop Motion Studio, figures, set, steady lighting (close curtains to avoid flicker), free music/sound effects (YouTube Audio Library or recorded).
misconceptions: Flickering from changing daylight. Correct: use lamps and block window light.
Using copyrighted music for a shared video. Correct: use royalty-free or original sound.

days.guide: Shoot first half.

questions.q: Why use onion-skinning?
questions.a: It shows the previous frame faintly so you can make small, consistent moves.

days.guide: Shoot second half.

questions.q: How many frames should you have by the end?
questions.a: About 360 for 30 seconds at 12 fps.

days.guide: Edit frames and add sound.

questions.q: Why might you duplicate frames?
questions.a: To hold a pose longer (a pause) without reshooting.

days.guide: Add titles and credits.

questions.q: What should credits include?
questions.a: Title, creator, helpers and music sources.

days.guide: Screen and collect feedback.

questions.q: What feedback would help most?
questions.a: Was the story clear? Was the motion smooth? What was most memorable?

weeks.assessment_key: Completed animation: 4 = ~30 seconds, clear story following storyboard, smooth motion, steady lighting, sound and titles/credits; 3 = minor jumps or flicker; 2 = short or unclear; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Open space, music; video of Alvin Ailey's 'Revelations' (1960) excerpt (e.g., 'Wade in the Water' or 'Rocka My Soul') and a folk dance. Elements of dance: Body, Energy, Space, Time (BEST).
misconceptions: Thinking dance is only steps. Correct: dance uses body, energy, space and time to express meaning.
Improvising the same movement to every song. Correct: respond to changes in tempo, mood and dynamics.

days.guide: Explore BEST through movement.

questions.q: Name the four elements of dance.
questions.a: Body, Energy, Space, Time.

days.guide: Compare 'Revelations' and a folk dance.

questions.q: What music is 'Revelations' set to and what does it express?
questions.a: African American spirituals, gospel and blues; it expresses African American experience, grief, faith and joy.

days.guide: Improvise to three contrasting pieces.

questions.q: How might energy change between music pieces?
questions.a: Sharp, strong movement for driving music; smooth, light movement for gentle music.

days.guide: Create a 16-count phrase.

questions.q: How many 8-counts is 16 counts?
questions.a: Two.

days.guide: Perform and describe using BEST.

questions.q: Describe a movement using 'Space.'
questions.a: Example: low level, curved pathway, moving backward.

weeks.assessment_key: Phrase performance: 4 = 16 counts performed on the beat, uses at least three elements intentionally (e.g., level changes, sharp vs smooth energy, tempo change), described accurately with BEST vocabulary; 3 = minor timing; 2 = few elements; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Open space, music, recording device.
misconceptions: Confusing canon and unison. Correct: unison = everyone together; canon = same movement starting at staggered times.
Random pathways. Correct: plan pathways and levels with intent.

days.guide: Apply repetition, canon, unison and retrograde to the phrase.

questions.q: What is retrograde?
questions.a: Performing a movement phrase in reverse order, like rewinding.

days.guide: Organize into ABA.

questions.q: What makes the B section contrast?
questions.a: Different tempo, energy, level or movement vocabulary.

days.guide: Use levels and pathways intentionally.

questions.q: Name three levels.
questions.a: High, middle, low.

days.guide: Teach part to a family member; create a duet.

questions.q: Give a duet device.
questions.a: Mirroring, canon, call-and-response, counterbalance.

days.guide: Record the draft.

questions.q: Why record drafts?
questions.a: To check spacing, timing and whether devices read clearly.

weeks.assessment_key: Recorded draft: 4 = ABA structure, at least three devices (repetition, canon, unison, retrograde) clearly visible, intentional levels and pathways, duet section; 3 = two devices; 2 = one device; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Music, costume pieces, lamp(s) for simple lighting, recording device.
misconceptions: Blank faces during performance. Correct: facial expression and focus are part of expression.
Skipping a full dress rehearsal. Correct: run it with costume and lighting.

days.guide: Rehearse for expression.

questions.q: What is performance 'focus'?
questions.a: Where the dancer directs their eyes and attention to communicate intention.

days.guide: Add costume and lighting.

questions.q: How can a costume support a dance?
questions.a: Color and movement of fabric can reinforce mood and theme.

days.guide: Dress rehearsal run-through.

questions.q: What is a dress rehearsal?
questions.a: A full run with all costumes and production elements as in performance.

days.guide: Perform and record.

questions.q: What should you do if you forget a step?
questions.a: Keep going with confident movement in the style until you find your place.

days.guide: Write about choices.

questions.q: What should the reflection explain?
questions.a: Why you chose specific movements, devices, music, costumes and lighting and how they express your idea.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance and reflection: 4 = confident, expressive, accurate performance with production elements; reflection explains intent and choices with dance vocabulary; 3 = minor errors; 2 = hesitant/partial; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: All year's artwork (drawings, paintings, photos, scripts, recordings, animation, dance video), mats or cardstock, glue stick, label cards.
misconceptions: Choosing only 'favorite' pieces. Correct: show range and growth across art forms.
Labels without information. Correct: include title, artist, medium, date and size.

days.guide: Select 8–10 pieces.

questions.q: What criteria should guide selection?
questions.a: Quality, variety of media/art forms, growth over time and personal meaning.

days.guide: Mount or mat 2-D works.

questions.q: Why mat artwork?
questions.a: It frames the piece, protects it and gives a finished, professional look.

days.guide: Write labels.

questions.q: What goes on a museum label?
questions.a: Title, artist name, date, medium and size (plus a short description if desired).

days.guide: Write an artist statement.

questions.q: What does an artist statement do?
questions.a: Explains the artist's themes, process and intent for viewers.

days.guide: Plan the exhibit layout.

questions.q: How should you arrange an exhibit?
questions.a: Group by theme or medium, hang at eye level (center about 57–60 inches), leave space between works, plan a viewing path.

weeks.assessment_key: Portfolio selection and statements: 4 = 8–10 works across at least three art forms showing growth, neatly mounted, complete labels, thoughtful artist statement (themes, growth, intent); 3 = minor gaps; 2 = limited range; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Artwork, performance pieces, space for exhibit, guest invitations, feedback cards.
misconceptions: Treating the showcase as only display. Correct: talk with guests about choices and process.
Ignoring feedback. Correct: use it to set goals.

days.guide: Set up the exhibit.

questions.q: What should you check during setup?
questions.a: Labels match works, lighting, spacing, viewing path, performance area.

days.guide: Rehearse performance pieces.

questions.q: Why rehearse in the actual space?
questions.a: To adjust to space, sound and sightlines.

days.guide: Host the showcase.

questions.q: How should an artist talk to guests?
questions.a: Welcome them, explain intent and process briefly and listen to their responses.

days.guide: Collect guest feedback.

questions.q: What makes feedback useful?
questions.a: Specific comments about what was effective and what was memorable.

days.guide: Write a reflection.

questions.q: What should the reflection include?
questions.a: Growth across art forms, favorite piece and why, feedback received and goals for next year.

weeks.assessment_key: Showcase and reflection: 4 = organized exhibit and performance, engages guests, reflection uses guest feedback and specific works to describe growth and set goals; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = disorganized; 1 = incomplete.

WL.overview: Spanish 1B finishes Spanish I, moving from Novice Mid toward Novice High: restaurants, home and chores, clothing and shopping, travel in the preterite, community service, movies and technology. Keep the 1A routine of daily Spanish (date, weather, a quick question) and add one new structure per week: model it, drill it briefly online (Conjuguemos or StudySpanish), then use it in a real conversation or writing task. Answers below give the correct Spanish so a non-fluent parent can check; in speaking, reward communication first and correct one pattern at a time.

weeks.prep: Pull out the 1A can-do checklist. Set a place setting (plate, glass, cup, fork, knife, spoon, napkin, bowl, tablecloth, salt and pepper). Write a 15-item 1A diagnostic quiz (ser, gustar, -ar/-er/-ir present, tener, ir a, dates/time).
misconceptions: Saying 'el camarero' for women. Use la camarera (or el/la mesero/a in Mexico).
Ordering with 'Yo quiero' only. In restaurants use '¿Me trae…?' or 'Quisiera…' — more polite.

days.guide: Hold a 3-minute conversation about summer, family and likes; give the diagnostic quiz and note weak areas.

questions.q: Answer: ¿Qué te gusta hacer en el verano?
questions.a: En el verano me gusta ___ (infinitive), e.g., nadar y leer.

questions.q: Answer: ¿Cuántos hermanos tienes?
questions.a: Tengo ___ hermanos (or No tengo hermanos).

days.guide: Learn 12 table words; set the table naming items: Pongo el tenedor a la izquierda del plato.

questions.q: Say: 'I put the knife to the right of the plate.'
questions.a: Pongo el cuchillo a la derecha del plato.

questions.q: What is 'la servilleta'?
questions.a: The napkin.

days.guide: Learn main dishes, desserts and drinks (el bistec, el pollo asado, el arroz, la ensalada, el flan, el helado, el pastel, el agua mineral, el té helado); build a three-course menu.

questions.q: What is 'el flan'?
questions.a: A caramel custard dessert.

questions.q: How do you say 'main dish'?
questions.a: el plato principal.

days.guide: Practice requests with you as camarero: ¿Me trae…?, ¿Me puede traer…?, ¿Algo más?, La cuenta, por favor.

questions.q: Ask the waiter to bring you a spoon.
questions.a: ¿Me trae una cuchara, por favor? (or ¿Me puede traer una cuchara?)

days.guide: Give the vocabulary quiz; set two goals from the diagnostic.

questions.q: Translate: 'Anything else?' 'No, thank you. The check, please.'
questions.a: ¿Algo más? —No, gracias. La cuenta, por favor.

weeks.assessment_key: Restaurant vocabulary quiz key: el plato (plate), el vaso (glass), la taza (cup), el tenedor (fork), el cuchillo (knife), la cuchara (spoon), la servilleta (napkin), el tazón (bowl), el mantel (tablecloth), la sal, la pimienta, el camarero/la camarera (waiter/waitress), el plato principal (main dish), el postre (dessert), la cuenta (check). Phrases: ¿Me trae…, por favor? (Can you bring me…?); ¿Algo más? (Anything else?). 80% proficient. Diagnostic conversation: 3 minutes using present tense, gustar and ir a; note gaps for goals.

weeks.prep: Conjuguemos account; plan a real family meal for day 3. A short restaurant scene video in Spanish (textbook video or YouTube).
misconceptions: Conjugating venir as regular: 'yo veno.' The yo form is vengo; it is also e→ie: vienes, viene, vienen (venimos, venís unchanged).
Saying 'La comida es rica' when you mean it tastes good right now. 'Está rica' = it tastes delicious (this dish); 'es rica' can describe a type of food or mean rich (wealthy) for people.

days.guide: Teach venir forms; Conjuguemos to 90%.

questions.q: Conjugate venir for yo and ellos.
questions.a: vengo; vienen.

questions.q: Complete: Nosotros ___ a las ocho.
questions.a: venimos.

days.guide: Write dinner invitations and who comes from where.

questions.q: Write: 'My aunt comes from San Diego on Saturday.'
questions.a: Mi tía viene de San Diego el sábado.

days.guide: Describe five foods during a real meal.

questions.q: Say: 'The salsa is very spicy.'
questions.a: La salsa está muy picante.

questions.q: Say: 'The cake is sweet and delicious.'
questions.a: El pastel está dulce y delicioso.

days.guide: Watch a restaurant scene; list what each customer orders and how they describe it.

questions.q: If a customer says 'La sopa está un poco salada,' what's the complaint?
questions.a: The soup is a little salty.

days.guide: Give the venir and description quiz.

questions.q: Ask: 'Are you coming to dinner?'
questions.a: ¿Vienes a la cena?

weeks.assessment_key: Venir quiz: vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, venís, vienen. Samples: Mis abuelos (venir) de Texas → vienen; ¿(venir) tú a la fiesta? → vienes; Nosotros (venir) a las seis → venimos; Yo (venir) en coche → vengo. Food words: delicioso, picante (spicy), salado (salty), dulce (sweet), rico (tasty). 80% passing.

weeks.prep: Make 20 sentence cards mixing ser and estar uses. StudySpanish.com ser/estar lesson.
misconceptions: Using estar for professions: 'Está doctora.' Occupation uses ser: Es doctora.
Using ser for location of things/people: location uses estar (El restaurante está en la calle Main). Exception: events — La fiesta es en mi casa.

days.guide: Teach DOCTOR and PLACE; sort 20 cards.

questions.q: Which verb for 'Ella ___ abogada'? Why?
questions.a: es — occupation (DOCTOR).

questions.q: Which verb for 'Yo ___ nervioso hoy'? Why?
questions.a: estoy — emotion/condition (PLACE).

days.guide: Study meaning-change adjectives: es aburrido (is boring) vs está aburrido (is bored); es listo (is clever) vs está listo (is ready); es rico (is rich) vs está rico (tastes good); write 6 pairs.

questions.q: Translate: 'The movie is boring' and 'I am bored.'
questions.a: La película es aburrida. Estoy aburrido/a.

questions.q: What's the difference between 'es listo' and 'está listo'?
questions.a: Es listo = he is clever; está listo = he is ready.

days.guide: Describe a meal: what food is (ser) and how it tastes today (estar), plus diners' feelings.

questions.q: Write: 'Paella is a typical dish; today it is delicious.'
questions.a: La paella es un plato típico; hoy está deliciosa.

days.guide: Complete the StudySpanish lesson and exercises.

questions.q: Choose: ¿Dónde ___ los baños? (son/están)
questions.a: están — location.

days.guide: Give the 25-item quiz.

questions.q: Choose: ___ las diez de la noche. (Son/Están)
questions.a: Son — time.

weeks.assessment_key: 25-item quiz guide: ser for DOCTOR — Description (permanent traits), Occupation, Characteristic, Time/date, Origin, Relationship; estar for PLACE — Position, Location, Action (progressive), Condition, Emotion. Samples: Mi madre ___ profesora (es); La sopa ___ fría (está); ___ las dos (son); Nosotros ___ cansados (estamos); El museo ___ cerca (está); Él ___ mi primo (es); Ellos ___ de Chile (son); Yo ___ comiendo (estoy); Hoy ___ lunes (es); La fiesta ___ en el parque (es). 20/25 = 80%.

weeks.prep: Print an authentic menu from a Spanish or Mexican restaurant's website. Write cue cards template. Read about tapas, comida corrida and sobremesa.
misconceptions: Assuming tipping customs match the U.S. In Spain tips are small or optional (service is included); in Mexico about 10–15% is common.
Using tú with the waiter. Use usted: ¿Qué me recomienda?

days.guide: Read about tapas, comida corrida and sobremesa; compare meal times with yours.

questions.q: What is 'la sobremesa'?
questions.a: Relaxing and talking at the table after a meal.

questions.q: When do many Spaniards eat dinner?
questions.a: Late — around 9 to 10 p.m. (lunch, the main meal, around 2–3 p.m.).

days.guide: Read the authentic menu; answer 10 questions about dishes and prices.

questions.q: What are 'entradas' or 'entrantes' on a menu?
questions.a: Appetizers/starters.

days.guide: Write cue cards for the role-play.

questions.q: Ask the waiter what he recommends.
questions.a: ¿Qué me recomienda?

days.guide: Perform the role-play from arrival to paying.

questions.q: Say: 'The chicken is delicious, thank you.'
questions.a: El pollo está delicioso, gracias.

days.guide: Give the unit 1 test.

questions.q: Translate: 'My friends come from the restaurant.'
questions.a: Mis amigos vienen del restaurante.

weeks.assessment_key: Role-play rubric (1–4 each): greeting and seating, ordering with polite requests and usted (¿Qué me recomienda? Quisiera… ¿Me trae…?), describing food with ser/estar, asking for and paying la cuenta, comprehensibility. Unit 1 test: restaurant listening, menu reading, venir conjugation, ser vs estar. Culture: tapas = small shared plates in Spain; comida corrida = affordable fixed-price multi-course lunch in Mexico; sobremesa = time spent talking at the table after a meal; main meal in Spain around 2–3 p.m., dinner around 9–10 p.m.

weeks.prep: Floor plan paper, sticky notes. Vocabulary: la cocina, la sala, el comedor, el dormitorio, el baño, el garaje, el sótano, el jardín, la escalera, el pasillo; furniture: la cama, la cómoda, el armario, la alfombra, el sofá, la lámpara, el escritorio, el estante, la mesita, el espejo, la cortina, el sillón, la silla, la mesa, el televisor.
misconceptions: Colors not agreeing. Rojo/roja/rojos/rojas; azul/azules (no gender); marrón/marrones; naranja and rosa often don't change.
Placing color before the noun. Colors follow nouns: la alfombra roja.

days.guide: Learn 10 rooms; draw and label a floor plan.

questions.q: How do you say 'the kitchen' and 'the living room'?
questions.a: la cocina; la sala.

days.guide: Learn 15 furniture items; label your bedroom.

questions.q: What is 'la cómoda'?
questions.a: The dresser/chest of drawers.

days.guide: Learn colors with agreement; describe 10 items.

questions.q: Write: 'The rug is red and the curtains are yellow.'
questions.a: La alfombra es roja y las cortinas son amarillas.

days.guide: Write a 10-sentence bedroom description with hay, estar + prepositions, colors.

questions.q: Write: 'The lamp is on top of the desk.'
questions.a: La lámpara está encima del escritorio.

days.guide: Give the house vocabulary quiz.

questions.q: Translate: 'There are two black chairs.'
questions.a: Hay dos sillas negras.

weeks.assessment_key: House vocabulary quiz: 10 rooms, 15 furniture items with articles, colors with agreement. Samples: the green curtains → las cortinas verdes; the white bed → la cama blanca; the blue lamps → las lámparas azules; 'In my bedroom there is a desk next to the bed' → En mi dormitorio hay un escritorio al lado de la cama. 80% proficient.

weeks.prep: Photos of rooms or Spanish real-estate ads (e.g., from Idealista or Inmuebles24).
misconceptions: Saying 'más bueno' and 'más malo.' Use mejor and peor.
Using 'que' with tan. Equal comparisons use tan… como: tan grande como.

days.guide: Teach más/menos…que, tan…como; compare 10 pairs.

questions.q: Compare: the sofa (big) vs the chair.
questions.a: El sofá es más grande que la silla.

questions.q: Write: 'The lamp is as tall as the shelf.'
questions.a: La lámpara es tan alta como el estante.

days.guide: Teach mejor, peor, mayor, menor; compare family.

questions.q: Write: 'My sister is younger than me.'
questions.a: Mi hermana es menor que yo.

questions.q: Write: 'My dad cooks better than I do.'
questions.a: Mi papá cocina mejor que yo.

days.guide: Teach el/la más… de; write superlatives.

questions.q: Write: 'My room is the smallest in the house.'
questions.a: Mi cuarto es el más pequeño de la casa.

days.guide: Read three apartment ads; compare in 8 sentences.

questions.q: What does 'tres dormitorios, dos baños' mean?
questions.a: Three bedrooms, two bathrooms.

days.guide: Give the comparisons quiz.

questions.q: Translate: 'She is the best student in the class.'
questions.a: Ella es la mejor estudiante de la clase.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparisons quiz samples: The kitchen is bigger than the bathroom → La cocina es más grande que el baño; My room is as small as yours → Mi cuarto es tan pequeño como el tuyo; My brother is older than I → Mi hermano es mayor que yo; This apartment is the best in the city → Este apartamento es el mejor de la ciudad; The sofa is less comfortable than the armchair → El sofá es menos cómodo que el sillón. 80% proficient.

weeks.prep: Boot-chart template (draw a boot around yo, tú, él, ellos forms), Conjuguemos stem-changer practice.
misconceptions: Changing the stem in nosotros: 'puedemos.' Nosotros and vosotros keep the original stem: podemos.
Changing the ending vowel instead of the stem: 'dormo.' The change is in the stem: duermo.

days.guide: Teach the boot; conjugate poder and dormir.

questions.q: Conjugate dormir for yo and nosotros.
questions.a: duermo; dormimos.

questions.q: Which forms don't change in a boot verb?
questions.a: Nosotros and vosotros.

days.guide: Add costar, volver, encontrar, almorzar, jugar (u→ue); Conjuguemos drill.

questions.q: Conjugate jugar for tú.
questions.a: juegas.

questions.q: Complete: ¿Cuánto ___ la lámpara? (costar)
questions.a: cuesta.

days.guide: Survey family: ¿Cuántas horas duermes? ¿A qué hora vuelves a casa? Graph.

questions.q: Report: 'My dad sleeps seven hours.'
questions.a: Mi papá duerme siete horas.

days.guide: Write 10 puedo/no puedo sentences about the house.

questions.q: Write: 'I can't play ball in the living room.'
questions.a: No puedo jugar a la pelota en la sala.

days.guide: Give the o→ue quiz.

questions.q: Translate: 'We can eat lunch at noon.'
questions.a: Podemos almorzar a mediodía.

weeks.assessment_key: Stem-changer quiz: poder — puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden; dormir — duermo, duermes, duerme, dormimos, dormís, duermen; jugar — juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis, juegan. Samples: ¿Cuánto (costar) los zapatos? → cuestan; Nosotros (volver) a las cinco → volvemos; Yo (almorzar) a la una → almuerzo; Ella no (encontrar) sus llaves → encuentra. 80% passing.

weeks.prep: Chore chart. Chores: hacer la cama, lavar los platos, sacar la basura, pasar la aspiradora, poner la mesa, quitar la mesa, limpiar el baño, cortar el césped, dar de comer al perro, lavar la ropa, sacudir los muebles, cocinar, arreglar el cuarto, planchar.
misconceptions: Using the infinitive as a command: 'Lavar los platos.' The tú command is the él form: Lava los platos.
Forgetting irregulars: 'hace la cama' (he makes) vs 'haz la cama' (make the bed!).

days.guide: Learn 14 chores; make a family chore chart.

questions.q: How do you say 'to take out the trash'?
questions.a: sacar la basura.

questions.q: What does 'pasar la aspiradora' mean?
questions.a: To vacuum.

days.guide: Teach regular tú commands (= él form); write a command for each chore.

questions.q: Command: wash the dishes.
questions.a: Lava los platos.

questions.q: Command: clean the bathroom.
questions.a: Limpia el baño.

days.guide: Teach di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven; 20-item practice.

questions.q: Command: set the table.
questions.a: Pon la mesa.

questions.q: Command: go to your room.
questions.a: Ve a tu cuarto.

days.guide: Play Simón dice with 20 commands; do three chores as commanded.

questions.q: Command: come to the kitchen.
questions.a: Ven a la cocina.

days.guide: Give the commands quiz.

questions.q: Command: make the bed.
questions.a: Haz la cama.

weeks.assessment_key: Commands quiz key: regular — limpia, lava, saca, pasa, cocina, come, bebe, escribe, barre; irregular — decir → di, hacer → haz, ir → ve, poner → pon, salir → sal, ser → sé, tener → ten, venir → ven. Samples: Make your bed → Haz tu cama; Put the table (set it) → Pon la mesa; Take out the trash → Saca la basura; Come here → Ven aquí; Be good → Sé bueno. Chore role-play: gives and follows 5 commands correctly.

weeks.prep: Phone for the home tour. A busy-house illustration (search 'Spanish present progressive picture'). Read about homes in Spain and Latin America.
misconceptions: Using -ando with -er/-ir verbs: 'comando.' -ar → -ando; -er/-ir → -iendo (comiendo, escribiendo).
Missing the irregulars: leer → leyendo, dormir → durmiendo.

days.guide: Teach estar + -ando/-iendo; describe what family members are doing now.

questions.q: Say: 'My mom is reading.'
questions.a: Mi mamá está leyendo.

questions.q: Say: 'We are cleaning the kitchen.'
questions.a: Estamos limpiando la cocina.

days.guide: Describe a busy house picture in 10 sentences.

questions.q: Say: 'The baby is sleeping.'
questions.a: El bebé está durmiendo.

days.guide: Read about homes; write five comparisons.

questions.q: What is an 'azotea'?
questions.a: A flat rooftop terrace used for laundry, plants or gathering.

questions.q: Write: 'In Spain many families live in apartments.'
questions.a: En España muchas familias viven en pisos (apartamentos).

days.guide: Record a 2-minute home tour.

questions.q: Say: 'This is the living room. It is bigger than the kitchen.'
questions.a: Esta es la sala. Es más grande que la cocina.

days.guide: Give the unit 2 test.

questions.q: Translate: 'My brother is washing the dishes.'
questions.a: Mi hermano está lavando los platos.

weeks.assessment_key: Home tour rubric (1–4): 2 minutes, names rooms and furniture, uses comparisons (más/menos…que), mentions chores with present tense or commands, uses estar + prepositions, pronunciation. Unit 2 test: house vocabulary, comparisons, o→ue verbs, tú commands, present progressive (estoy limpiando, está leyendo, están durmiendo). Culture: interior patios (Spain/colonial Latin America), rooftop azoteas, many families live in apartments (pisos) in cities.

weeks.prep: Closet items, catalog photos, a short teen fashion blog in Spanish. Vocabulary: la camisa, la camiseta, los pantalones, los jeans/vaqueros, la falda, el vestido, los zapatos, los tenis, las botas, la chaqueta, el abrigo, el suéter, la gorra, el sombrero, los calcetines, la sudadera, los pantalones cortos, el traje de baño, la bufanda, los guantes.
misconceptions: Using 'usar' and 'llevar' interchangeably is fine, but 'llevar' is the standard for wearing; don't use 'tener' for wearing.
Color agreement with plurals: los pantalones negros.

days.guide: Learn 20 clothing words; label closet items.

questions.q: How do you say 'the jacket' and 'the socks'?
questions.a: la chaqueta; los calcetines.

days.guide: Describe what five family members wear with llevar + colors.

questions.q: Write: 'My dad is wearing blue jeans and a white shirt.'
questions.a: Mi papá lleva unos jeans azules y una camisa blanca.

days.guide: Connect weather to clothes; write 8 sentences.

questions.q: Write: 'When it's cold, I wear a coat.'
questions.a: Cuando hace frío, llevo un abrigo.

questions.q: Write: 'When it's hot, I wear shorts.'
questions.a: Cuando hace calor, llevo pantalones cortos.

days.guide: Read a teen fashion blog; list items and opinions.

questions.q: What does 'está de moda' mean?
questions.a: It's in style/fashionable.

days.guide: Give the clothing quiz with listening.

questions.q: Translate: 'She wears a green cap.'
questions.a: Ella lleva una gorra verde.

weeks.assessment_key: Clothing quiz: 20 items with articles; listening — child identifies what a person is wearing. Samples: She is wearing a red dress → Ella lleva un vestido rojo; I wear boots when it's cold → Llevo botas cuando hace frío; a black jacket → una chaqueta negra. 80% proficient.

weeks.prep: Conjuguemos e→ie practice.
misconceptions: Changing nosotros: 'queremos' (correct), not 'quieremos.'
Confusing pensar + infinitive (plan to) with pensar en (think about).

days.guide: Teach e→ie verbs in the boot; Conjuguemos drill.

questions.q: Conjugate querer for yo and nosotros.
questions.a: quiero; queremos.

questions.q: Conjugate empezar for la clase.
questions.a: empieza.

days.guide: Write 10 preference sentences.

questions.q: Write: 'I prefer the red shirt, but my brother wants the blue one.'
questions.a: Prefiero la camisa roja, pero mi hermano quiere la azul.

days.guide: Use pensar + infinitive for three plans; compare with ir a.

questions.q: Write: 'I plan to buy new shoes.'
questions.a: Pienso comprar zapatos nuevos.

days.guide: Discuss clothes you want, prefer and plan to buy.

questions.q: Ask: 'What do you prefer, the jacket or the sweater?'
questions.a: ¿Qué prefieres, la chaqueta o el suéter?

days.guide: Give the e→ie quiz with mixed o→ue items.

questions.q: Translate: 'They don't understand the question.'
questions.a: Ellos no entienden la pregunta.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: pensar — pienso, piensas, piensa, pensamos, pensáis, piensan; querer — quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, queréis, quieren; preferir — prefiero, prefieres, prefiere, preferimos, preferís, prefieren; empezar — empiezo…; entender — entiendo…; cerrar — cierro… Mixed o→ue: puedo, duermes, vuelven. Samples: La tienda (cerrar) a las nueve → cierra; Nosotros (preferir) la camisa azul → preferimos; ¿Tú (entender)? → entiendes. 80% proficient.

weeks.prep: Price tags on household items, a currency converter website (check current rates). Demonstratives chart.
misconceptions: Using 'doscientos' with feminine nouns. Hundreds agree: doscientas camisas.
Saying 'un mil.' 1,000 is mil; 1,000,000 is un millón (de): un millón de dólares.

days.guide: Teach demonstratives at three distances; 12 sentences.

questions.q: Say: 'This shirt and those shoes (over there).'
questions.a: Esta camisa y aquellos zapatos.

questions.q: Say: 'those pants (near you).'
questions.a: esos pantalones.

days.guide: Teach 100–1,000,000; read 20 prices.

questions.q: Write 750 in words.
questions.a: setecientos cincuenta.

questions.q: Write 2.500 in words.
questions.a: dos mil quinientos.

days.guide: Learn currencies of eight countries; convert three prices with a current rate.

questions.q: What is the currency of Guatemala? Of Peru?
questions.a: The quetzal; the sol.

days.guide: Practice ¿Cuánto cuesta(n)? with tagged items.

questions.q: Ask how much these boots cost and answer 'They cost 80 dollars.'
questions.a: ¿Cuánto cuestan estas botas? —Cuestan ochenta dólares.

days.guide: Give the demonstratives and number dictation quiz.

questions.q: Write 500 and 900.
questions.a: quinientos; novecientos.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: este/esta/estos/estas (this/these, near speaker), ese/esa/esos/esas (that/those, near listener), aquel/aquella/aquellos/aquellas (that/those over there). Numbers: 100 cien, 101 ciento uno, 200 doscientos, 300 trescientos, 400 cuatrocientos, 500 quinientos, 600 seiscientos, 700 setecientos, 800 ochocientos, 900 novecientos, 1.000 mil, 2.000 dos mil, 1.000.000 un millón. Dictation samples: 550 quinientos cincuenta; 1.975 mil novecientos setenta y cinco; 25.000 veinticinco mil. Currencies: México — peso; España — euro; Guatemala — quetzal; Perú — sol; Costa Rica — colón; Argentina — peso; Colombia — peso; Ecuador and El Salvador — U.S. dollar; Venezuela — bolívar; Paraguay — guaraní; Honduras — lempira. 80% proficient.

weeks.prep: Play money, clothing items. Read about the Chichicastenango market (Guatemala) and El Rastro (Madrid). A short video on Guatemalan Maya weaving (huipiles).
misconceptions: Bargaining everywhere. Bargaining (regatear) is expected at many open-air markets and street stalls, not in department stores or fixed-price shops.
Saying 'Me queda bueno.' Use 'Me queda bien' (it fits well); 'Me queda grande/pequeño' for size.

days.guide: Learn store phrases; practice a fitting-room dialogue.

questions.q: A clerk asks '¿Qué talla usa?' What is she asking?
questions.a: What size do you wear?

questions.q: Say: 'These pants are too big on me.'
questions.a: Estos pantalones me quedan grandes.

days.guide: Read about markets and when bargaining is appropriate.

questions.q: Where is bargaining usually acceptable?
questions.a: At open-air markets and street stalls, not in department stores or chain shops.

days.guide: Watch the weaving video; write five sentences about huipiles.

questions.q: What is a huipil?
questions.a: A traditional handwoven tunic/blouse worn by Maya women; its patterns can show the weaver's village and beliefs.

days.guide: Role-play a store purchase and market bargaining with play money.

questions.q: Bargain: 'It's very expensive. Can you give me a discount?'
questions.a: Es muy caro. ¿Me puede dar un descuento?

days.guide: Give the shopping listening quiz.

questions.q: What does 'barato' mean?
questions.a: Cheap/inexpensive.

weeks.assessment_key: Shopping role-play rubric (1–4): clerk/customer phrases (¿En qué puedo servirle? ¿Qué talla usa? Me queda bien/grande), asks and states prices, uses demonstratives, bargains politely (¿Me puede dar un descuento? Es muy caro), closing. Listening quiz: identifies item, size, color, price and whether it fits from a dialogue. Culture: Chichicastenango — large Maya market in the Guatemalan highlands (Thursdays and Sundays) with textiles, masks, produce; El Rastro — Madrid's Sunday open-air flea market; huipil — handwoven blouse whose designs and colors often identify the weaver's community and carry symbolic meaning.

weeks.prep: Paper or slide software for a catalog. An authentic online store page in Spanish (e.g., a Spanish clothing retailer's site).
misconceptions: Copying store-page text. Write your own descriptions using structures learned.
Forgetting euros use a comma for decimals in Spain (19,99 €).

days.guide: Design a catalog page with 8 items, colors, sizes, prices.

questions.q: Write a price: 45 euros and 99 cents.
questions.a: cuarenta y cinco euros con noventa y nueve (céntimos).

days.guide: Write descriptions with demonstratives, comparisons and e→ie verbs.

questions.q: Write: 'These boots are better than those shoes.'
questions.a: Estas botas son mejores que esos zapatos.

days.guide: Read an authentic store page; answer questions.

questions.q: What does 'añadir a la cesta' mean on a store site?
questions.a: Add to cart/basket.

days.guide: Present a 90-second TV shopping segment.

questions.q: Say: 'Do you want a modern style? This sweater is perfect.'
questions.a: ¿Quieres un estilo moderno? Este suéter es perfecto.

days.guide: Give the unit 3 test.

questions.q: Translate: 'That dress (over there) costs 300 dollars.'
questions.a: Aquel vestido cuesta trescientos dólares.

weeks.assessment_key: Catalog project rubric (1–4): 8 items with colors, sizes and prices; descriptions use demonstratives, comparisons and e→ie verbs (e.g., 'Esta chaqueta es más cómoda que aquel abrigo. ¿Prefieres el color azul?'); accurate agreement; attractive layout; 90-second TV segment with enthusiasm and clear pronunciation. Unit 3 test: clothing, e→ie/o→ue, demonstratives, numbers to 1,000,000, shopping phrases.

weeks.prep: Conjuguemos preterite -ar practice; three store receipts.
misconceptions: Dropping accents: 'compro' (I buy) vs 'compró' (he bought). The accent changes meaning and tense.
Confusing nosotros forms. -ar nosotros is the same in present and preterite (hablamos); context (ayer) tells the tense.

days.guide: Teach preterite -ar endings; conjugate comprar, hablar, mirar.

questions.q: Conjugate hablar for yo and ella.
questions.a: hablé; habló.

questions.q: Conjugate mirar for ellos.
questions.a: miraron.

days.guide: Teach time expressions; write 10 sentences about last weekend.

questions.q: Write: 'Last night I studied Spanish.'
questions.a: Anoche estudié español.

questions.q: Write: 'Two days ago we bought shoes.'
questions.a: Hace dos días compramos zapatos.

days.guide: Identify present vs past from context in 15 sentences.

questions.q: Is 'Hablamos con el profesor ayer' present or past?
questions.a: Past (preterite) — 'ayer' signals yesterday.

days.guide: Write what people bought and paid from receipts.

questions.q: Write: 'My mom paid 50 dollars.'
questions.a: Mi mamá pagó cincuenta dólares.

days.guide: Give the preterite -ar quiz.

questions.q: Translate: 'Did you (tú) buy the jacket?'
questions.a: ¿Compraste la chaqueta?

weeks.assessment_key: Preterite -ar quiz: comprar — compré, compraste, compró, compramos, comprasteis, compraron. Samples: Ayer yo (hablar) con mi abuela → hablé; Ellos (mirar) la tele anoche → miraron; ¿Tú (comprar) la camisa? → compraste; La semana pasada nosotros (caminar) al parque → caminamos; Ella (trabajar) el sábado → trabajó. 80% proficient.

weeks.prep: StudySpanish.com preterite exercises.
misconceptions: Applying the spelling change to all persons. It occurs only in the yo form: busqué but buscaste, buscó.
Forgetting why: c→qu and g→gu keep the hard sound before é; z→c because Spanish writes ce, not ze.

days.guide: Teach the spelling rules; practice 15 yo forms.

questions.q: Give the yo preterite of buscar, pagar and almorzar.
questions.a: busqué, pagué, almorcé.

questions.q: Why does 'pagar' become 'pagué'?
questions.a: To keep the hard g sound before e (ge would sound like h).

days.guide: Complete StudySpanish exercises; correct errors.

questions.q: Give the tú preterite of tocar.
questions.a: tocaste (no spelling change).

days.guide: Write a 10-sentence shopping diary with five spelling-change verbs.

questions.q: Write: 'I arrived at the store and I looked for a gift.'
questions.a: Llegué a la tienda y busqué un regalo.

days.guide: Interview a family member about yesterday; record answers.

questions.q: Ask: 'What time did you arrive home?'
questions.a: ¿A qué hora llegaste a casa?

days.guide: Give the spelling-change quiz.

questions.q: Give the yo preterite of practicar.
questions.a: practiqué.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: -car → -qué (buscar → busqué, tocar → toqué, practicar → practiqué, sacar → saqué); -gar → -gué (pagar → pagué, llegar → llegué, jugar → jugué); -zar → -cé (empezar → empecé, almorzar → almorcé, organizar → organicé). Samples: Yo (llegar) tarde → llegué; Él (pagar) → pagó (no change); Yo (empezar) la tarea → empecé; Tú (jugar) → jugaste. 80% proficient.

weeks.prep: A shopping bag with items (a shirt, shoes, a book, socks).
misconceptions: Placing the pronoun after a conjugated verb: 'Compré la.' It goes before: La compré.
Choosing gender by the person, not the noun. The pronoun matches the object: los zapatos → los.

days.guide: Teach lo/la/los/las; replace objects in 15 sentences.

questions.q: Replace: Compré los zapatos.
questions.a: Los compré.

questions.q: Replace: Busco la chaqueta.
questions.a: La busco.

days.guide: Teach placement: before conjugated verb, or attached to infinitive/gerund (add accent on gerund).

questions.q: Rewrite two ways: Voy a comprar la falda.
questions.a: La voy a comprar. / Voy a comprarla.

questions.q: Rewrite: Estoy leyendo el libro.
questions.a: Lo estoy leyendo. / Estoy leyéndolo.

days.guide: Answer your questions with pronouns.

questions.q: ¿Compraste los calcetines?
questions.a: Sí, los compré. (or No, no los compré.)

days.guide: Write a gift story with preterite and DOPs.

questions.q: Write: 'I bought a scarf for my mom. I bought it at the market.'
questions.a: Compré una bufanda para mi mamá. La compré en el mercado.

days.guide: Give the DOP quiz.

questions.q: Replace: ¿Dónde compraste el vestido?
questions.a: ¿Dónde lo compraste?

weeks.assessment_key: DOP quiz samples: Compré la camisa → La compré; ¿Tienes los libros? → Sí, los tengo; Voy a comprar el regalo → Lo voy a comprar / Voy a comprarlo; Estoy lavando los platos → Los estoy lavando / Estoy lavándolos; ¿Viste a María? → Sí, la vi. 80% proficient.

weeks.prep: Semester flashcards, unit tests, Conjuguemos.
misconceptions: Mixing tenses mid-story. Decide if it's now (present) or completed past (preterite) and keep consistent.
Forgetting boot verbs on the exam. Review the boot chart before writing.

days.guide: Review units 1–2 with a practice test.

questions.q: Command your brother to set the table and take out the trash.
questions.a: Pon la mesa y saca la basura.

days.guide: Review units 3–4 with Conjuguemos.

questions.q: Translate: 'I prefer these jeans; I bought them yesterday.'
questions.a: Prefiero estos jeans; los compré ayer.

days.guide: 4-minute interview: home, chores, clothes, shopping trip.

questions.q: Answer: ¿Qué compraste la semana pasada?
questions.a: La semana pasada compré ___, e.g., unos tenis.

days.guide: Give the written exam.

questions.q: Conjugate dormir (present) for ellos and comprar (preterite) for yo.
questions.a: duermen; compré.

days.guide: Complete a can-do checklist; set two goals.

questions.q: Write one goal.
questions.a: Example: 'Master preterite endings with 90% on Conjuguemos.'

weeks.assessment_key: Semester exam (suggested): Listening 10 (restaurant/shopping dialogues), Reading 10 (menu/apartment ad), Grammar 25 (venir, ser/estar, comparisons, o→ue/e→ie, tú commands, progressive, demonstratives, numbers, preterite -ar and spelling changes, DOPs), Writing 15 (12 sentences on home, chores, clothes and a past shopping trip — rubric for content, accuracy, variety). Oral interview rubric (1–4): comprehension, sentence-level answers, asks questions, uses present and preterite, pronunciation. 80% proficient.

weeks.prep: Travel photos, world map, a Spanish tourism brochure for Puerto Rico (Discover Puerto Rico has Spanish content).
misconceptions: Confusing 'visitar a' (people) and 'visitar' (places): Visité a mi abuela; Visité el museo.
Using present tense in past-trip sentences. Use the preterite: Nadé en el lago.

days.guide: Learn 20 vacation words; caption travel photos.

questions.q: What does 'bucear' mean?
questions.a: To scuba dive/snorkel.

questions.q: How do you say 'amusement park'?
questions.a: el parque de diversiones.

days.guide: Write 10 past-trip sentences with -ar preterite.

questions.q: Write: 'I took many photos.'
questions.a: Saqué muchas fotos.

questions.q: Write: 'We swam in the lake.'
questions.a: Nadamos en el lago.

days.guide: Read a Puerto Rico brochure; list five attractions.

questions.q: Name two attractions in Puerto Rico.
questions.a: El Viejo San Juan, El Morro, El Yunque rainforest, bioluminescent bays (e.g., Mosquito Bay in Vieques), beaches.

days.guide: Choose a dream destination; list ten activities.

questions.q: Write: 'In Costa Rica I can visit volcanoes.'
questions.a: En Costa Rica puedo visitar volcanes.

days.guide: Give the vacation vocabulary quiz.

questions.q: Translate: 'She bought souvenirs.'
questions.a: Ella compró recuerdos.

weeks.assessment_key: Vacation vocabulary quiz: el museo, el parque de diversiones, el zoológico, el lago, las montañas, el mar, la playa, el estadio, el parque nacional, el monumento, tomar el sol, bucear, montar a caballo, pasear en bote, acampar, ir de pesca, visitar, sacar fotos, comprar recuerdos, el hotel. Samples: I sunbathed at the beach → Tomé el sol en la playa; We visited the zoo → Visitamos el zoológico. 80% proficient.

weeks.prep: Conjuguemos preterite -er/-ir practice.
misconceptions: Using -ar endings for -er/-ir verbs: 'comé.' Use comí, comió.
Forgetting the y in leer/oír/creer third person: leyó, leyeron (not leió).

days.guide: Teach shared -er/-ir endings; conjugate comer and salir.

questions.q: Conjugate salir for ella and ellos.
questions.a: salió; salieron.

questions.q: Conjugate comer for yo.
questions.a: comí.

days.guide: Conjuguemos drill to 90%.

questions.q: Conjugate vivir for nosotros (preterite).
questions.a: vivimos (same as present — context decides).

days.guide: Teach leyó/leyeron, oyó/oyeron; five sentences.

questions.q: Write: 'My sister read the brochure.'
questions.a: Mi hermana leyó el folleto.

questions.q: Write: 'They heard the music.'
questions.a: Ellos oyeron la música.

days.guide: Interview a parent about their best vacation.

questions.q: Ask: 'What did you eat on the trip?'
questions.a: ¿Qué comiste en el viaje?

days.guide: Give the mixed regular preterite quiz.

questions.q: Translate: 'We left at seven and returned at ten.'
questions.a: Salimos a las siete y volvimos a las diez.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: comer — comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron; salir — salí, saliste, salió, salimos, salisteis, salieron; leer — leí, leíste, leyó, leímos, leísteis, leyeron; oír — oí, oíste, oyó, oímos, oísteis, oyeron. Samples: Ayer nosotros (beber) limonada → bebimos; Ellos (escribir) postales → escribieron; Mi padre (volver) tarde → volvió; ¿Tú (aprender) a bucear? → aprendiste. 80% proficient.

weeks.prep: Photo album. A Spanish Proficiency Exercises clip about a trip (UT Austin, e.g., 'Describe a trip').
misconceptions: Thinking 'fue' always means 'went.' Ir and ser share preterite forms: 'Fue a Madrid' (went) vs 'Fue divertido' (was).
Adding accents: fui, fue have no accent.

days.guide: Teach the shared forms; determine meaning in 15 sentences.

questions.q: Translate: 'Fui al zoológico. Fue muy divertido.'
questions.a: I went to the zoo. It was very fun.

questions.q: Conjugate ir (preterite) for nosotros.
questions.a: fuimos.

days.guide: Write where family members went last summer and how it was.

questions.q: Write: 'My parents went to Mexico; it was fantastic.'
questions.a: Mis padres fueron a México; fue fantástico.

days.guide: Listen to a native speaker; note where they went and what they did.

questions.q: If you hear 'Fuimos a las montañas y acampamos,' what did they do?
questions.a: They went to the mountains and camped.

days.guide: Unscripted conversation with five follow-up questions.

questions.q: Ask: 'Where did you go and with whom?'
questions.a: ¿Adónde fuiste y con quién?

days.guide: Give the ir/ser quiz.

questions.q: Ask: 'How was the trip?'
questions.a: ¿Qué tal fue el viaje? (or ¿Cómo fue el viaje?)

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: ir/ser — fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron. Context items: 'Fuimos a la playa' = we went; 'El viaje fue fantástico' = was; 'Ellos fueron al museo' = went; '¿Qué tal fue?' = how was it. Conversation rubric (1–4): describes a past trip in the preterite, asks/answers 5 follow-up questions (¿Adónde fuiste? ¿Con quién? ¿Qué hiciste? ¿Qué comiste? ¿Qué tal fue?), comprehensibility.

weeks.prep: World map, library books/websites. A Spanish article about Machu Picchu (e.g., from a tourism or encyclopedia site for students).
misconceptions: Placing Machu Picchu in Mexico or Chichén Itzá in Peru. Machu Picchu (Inca) is in Peru; Chichén Itzá (Maya) is in Mexico's Yucatán.
Copying research sentences in Spanish verbatim. Take notes in key words and rewrite.

days.guide: Locate eight sites and identify their landforms.

questions.q: Where is the Salar de Uyuni and what is it?
questions.a: In Bolivia; the world's largest salt flat.

questions.q: Who built Machu Picchu?
questions.a: The Inca, in the 1400s, in the Andes of Peru.

days.guide: Read the Machu Picchu article; answer questions.

questions.q: What does 'las ruinas' mean?
questions.a: The ruins.

days.guide: Research one destination; take notes in Spanish.

questions.q: Write: 'Chichén Itzá is in Mexico; it has a famous pyramid.'
questions.a: Chichén Itzá está en México; tiene una pirámide famosa.

days.guide: Compare with a California landmark in six sentences.

questions.q: Write: 'Death Valley is hotter than Machu Picchu.'
questions.a: El Valle de la Muerte es más caluroso que Machu Picchu (or hace más calor en el Valle de la Muerte que en Machu Picchu).

days.guide: Give a 1-minute oral summary.

questions.q: What is 'el patrimonio' (as in Patrimonio de la Humanidad)?
questions.a: Heritage — UNESCO World Heritage Site.

weeks.assessment_key: Site key: Machu Picchu — Inca citadel (15th century) high in the Andes of Peru near Cusco, mountains; Chichén Itzá — Maya city with the pyramid El Castillo (Temple of Kukulcán), Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico, flat limestone plain with cenotes; Salar de Uyuni — world's largest salt flat, Bolivia, high plateau (Altiplano); El Yunque — tropical rainforest, Puerto Rico; La Alhambra — Moorish palace-fortress in Granada, Spain, on a hill below the Sierra Nevada. Oral summary rubric: 1 minute, 5+ facts in Spanish (location, landform, history, food, festival), pronunciation.

weeks.prep: Slides or a blog template; photos of the destination.
misconceptions: Listing events without sequence words. Use primero, luego, después, más tarde, por fin.
Mixing ir/ser preterite with present: 'Voy a Perú y fue…' — keep it all past.

days.guide: Teach sequencing words; outline a trip story.

questions.q: Write: 'First we went to Cusco, then we visited Machu Picchu.'
